crypto gives a C++20 program the cryptographic primitives that Boost does not provide, on every target webcpp has: native (Linux, macOS, Windows with MSVC), wasip2, wasip3 and Emscripten. It is one of the libraries of webcpp. The algorithms are those of widely used, reviewed C libraries, BearSSL, OpenSSL, ctaes, libsecp256k1 and libsodium, each a backend that the program names in its own Jamfile.

The page is written for two readers at once: a developer who knows little cryptography, and a language model that must pick the right tool for a person’s application from this page alone. Choose by use case answers "what do I use for …​" in one table; each chapter opens with a table that compares what it holds; every program shown is an example of the library’s example directory, built and run on every target with the output printed beside it. The same content, as a machine-readable index, is llms.txt, beside this page.

Why crypto

Cryptography is what keeps a program’s secrets secret and its data honest when someone else can read or change the bytes: a database copied by an intruder, a message passed through a relay, a cookie handed to a browser, a key that controls money. A program that gets it wrong rarely fails a test; it fails when an attacker reads what was meant to be secret, or forges what was meant to be trusted. crypto exists so that a C++ program gets it right on every target, with the same code.

It offers:

  • Authenticated encryption. AES-GCM with keys of 16, 24 and 32 bytes, which keeps a message secret and detects any change to it.

  • Randomness. A random_device that reads the operating system’s or the browser’s generator, and nothing else.

  • secp256k1. BIP 340 Schnorr signatures, ECDSA signatures, their verification, ECDH, ECDSA’s strict DER and low-S forms, and the x-only tweak, through libsecp256k1.

  • A constant-time equal for tags and MACs, Boost.Hash2’s included.

  • The AES block cipher, a building block for the rare case that needs one.

The algorithms are not webcpp’s. Each runs on a backend, a C library that webcpp wraps behind an interface shaped as Boost.Hash2’s. A backend is named after its library: backends::bearssl, backends::openssl, backends::ctaes and backends::secp256k1. Every call is synchronous: with C code on every target, nothing waits.

Three rules

Three rules run through every chapter, each because its absence is how real programs were broken.

  • Never write your own cryptographic primitive. crypto writes none either: every cipher, mode and curve is a C library that has been reviewed and used for years. webcpp adds a uniform C++ interface on top, and the checks that the C interfaces leave to their caller.

  • Every failure is a value. Each operation returns boost::system::result<T>. Nothing fails silently: a wrong key size, a forged message or an empty entropy pool each has its own error (Errors).

  • Secrets do not outlive their use. Keys and key schedules are wiped when an object is destroyed or moved from, a failed open zeroes the bytes it decrypted, and an object moved from refuses every operation instead of using a wiped key.

Namespaces and headers

crypto holds primitives only; a protocol built on them (a Bitcoin, Ethereum or Nostr rule) belongs to a domain library, which Wallets shows how to build. Its names are grouped by kind, one chapter each, and the headers mirror the namespaces as <webcpp/crypto/<group>/<name>.hpp>:

  • webcpp::crypto: random_device, equal, error and the configuration (The root utilities: webcpp::crypto);

  • webcpp::crypto::ciphers: aes128, aes192, aes256, gcm, aes128_gcm and aes256_gcm (Ciphers: webcpp::crypto::ciphers);

  • webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1: key pairs, signatures, ECDH, the encodings and the x-only tweak on secp256k1 (Curves: webcpp::crypto::curves);

  • webcpp::crypto::backends: the backends (The backends).

<webcpp/crypto.hpp> includes every header whose backend the program links.

What stays with Boost.Hash2

Hashing and HMAC are Boost.Hash2’s: SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, RIPEMD, BLAKE2 and boost::hash2::hmac<H>. crypto offers no second interface for them, and its examples use Hash2 wherever a hash is needed: a key derived with HKDF (RFC 5869) is written on Hash2’s hmac in a few lines (Agreeing on a key in public). What crypto adds for Hash2’s users is equal: the operator== of Hash2’s digests is memcmp, which is not constant time, so a MAC is never checked with it (Comparing tags).

Choose by use case

Find the row that says what the program needs, and follow it: the name to use, in the namespace under webcpp::crypto that holds it (no namespace is written for webcpp::crypto itself), the backend that runs it, the Jamfile line that links it, and the example that does it, built and run on every target. The backend column gives the default; The backends says which backend runs where, and Using webcpp::crypto in your Jamfile how to name another.

Read the rows as rules. A need that is not in the table is not met by this version of crypto, and the program must not improvise one from the primitives here: encryption without authentication, a hand-made random generator and a signature on another curve are each how a program loses its users’ data.

Using webcpp::crypto in your Jamfile

The rule, in three lines:

  1. A program names /webcpp/crypto//crypto and the library of each backend it uses: /third_party//bearssl, /webcpp/crypto//openssl, /third_party//ctaes or /third_party//secp256k1. A program that only draws random bytes or compares tags names /webcpp/crypto//crypto alone.

  2. BearSSL, ctaes and libsecp256k1 build for every target; OpenSSL builds natively, on wasip2 and on wasip3, and never for Emscripten, where the build stops and says to name BearSSL.

  3. A backend named and never called adds no byte to the program.

crypto is header-only, and webcpp builds every backend from its sources, file by file: OpenSSL statically, from the superproject’s third_party/libs/openssl, never the system’s. The target /webcpp/crypto//crypto adds crypto’s include directory, Boost’s headers and webcpp’s configuration, and on Windows the system library bcrypt, through which random_device reads Windows’ generator.

In C++, a program names a backend by including its header, <webcpp/crypto/backends/<name>.hpp>, and using its tag type, backends::<name>, as a template argument: ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>>. The default backend needs no include of its own: <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes256_gcm.hpp> brings it when it is linked.

The default backend, and choosing another

aes128_gcm, aes256_gcm and aes256<> name AES-GCM’s default backend: natively OpenSSL, on WebAssembly BearSSL, whatever else the program links (The default backend per target). A program that wants another backend names it in the type, as ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>>, and links it; no define chooses a default. A native program that links BearSSL alone and uses aes256_gcm stops where it calls it, with the line that links its default, /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, and the type that names BearSSL. Version 0.1’s WEBCPP_CRYPTO_DEFAULT_BACKEND_BEARSSL and WEBCPP_CRYPTO_DEFAULT_BACKEND_OPENSSL stop the build with the type to write (Every message, and its fix).

A program built for every target links its default with one line, /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, which links OpenSSL natively and BearSSL on WebAssembly, the library of the backend aes256_gcm names on each target; the examples of this page link it so. The whole Jamfile of the fixture gcm_default, built and run on native, wasip2, wasip3 and Emscripten (Every Jamfile a user writes):

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default ;

Each family with a default has such a line, /webcpp/crypto//<family>-default, generated with the defaults from the same table; each is built and run on every target where its family has a default by the fixture named in its row:

Alias Family Links Fixture

The source-built OpenSSL is compiled without assembly (no-asm) on MSVC, wasip2 and wasip3: its AES is table-based and its GHASH 4-bit, neither constant time, and there is no AES-NI. A program for which timing attacks matter on MSVC names ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>>.

OpenSSL’s memory option

A native program that sends OpenSSL’s allocations to its own resource (OpenSSL’s allocations in your own memory resource) gives the define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE and /webcpp/crypto//openssl together, in the requirements of its project, not of one target. Every target of the program then gets both: its own libraries, and a tool that only calls random_device or equal, which would otherwise have the define without OpenSSL. The fixture memory_option builds and runs this Jamfile natively:

project app
  : requirements <define>WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE <library>/webcpp/crypto//openssl ;

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto ;

Each mistake stops the build, with the messages of Every message, and its fix: the define on a target without OpenSSL, or in a build for WebAssembly, is refused by config.hpp; openssl_memory_resource() not defined is a link error; and on MSVC, files of one program compiled some with the define and some without are refused by the linker (LNK2038). These requirements cannot be built for WebAssembly, since the option is refused there and /webcpp/crypto//openssl stops an Emscripten build: a WebAssembly build of the same program is a project of its own, in a directory of its own, with neither the define nor OpenSSL, and names /third_party//bearssl.

Every Jamfile a user writes

Each case below is a fixture of the superproject’s tools/test/crypto_jamfiles_test.py: its Jamfile is built on a scratch copy of the superproject, as a user’s would be, on each target named, and the program run; what it prints is checked. The list is generated from the fixtures.

block

The AES block cipher on ctaes: the FIPS 197 block encrypted and decrypted again.

Its Jamfile, built and run on native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten:

exe block : block.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /third_party//ctaes ;

It prints:

ctaes aes256 ok

A user builds a case from its directory with b2 natively, b2 toolset=emscripten for the browser, and b2 toolset=clang-wasip2 or b2 toolset=clang-wasip3 for WASI, and runs the program as each target runs one: ./app, node app.js, or a WASI runtime such as wasmtime. The cases web, server and gcm_default are one program, byte for byte (the test checks the copies), whose output names the backend that ran: BearSSL, the default on WebAssembly, and OpenSSL, the default natively; gcm_default links whichever the target needs. both_bearssl_named links both and names BearSSL in the type where OpenSSL is the default. On WASI the default is BearSSL even when OpenSSL is linked (The default backend per target), so server is a native case; a WASI program that wants OpenSSL names the backend in the type, as openssl_linked does.

The examples of this page are built the same way: example/Jamfile names /webcpp/crypto//crypto in its project’s requirements, and each example the libraries of its backends. The program of AES-GCM, for instance, names BearSSL:

webcpp.example aes256_gcm_bearssl.cpp : <library>/third_party//bearssl ;

Every message, and its fix

A mistake in a Jamfile stops the build with a message that says what to add. At compile time, the first error is the one to read: the lines after it come from it and go away with it. At link time, a symbol whose name is the instruction reports a backend library that is missing, or of another commit or configuration than the headers; with b2 it cannot happen, and it guards builds made by other means. Everything below is generated from the tests that fix each text.

At compile time, checked word for word by the message tests of test/messages with clang:

Case Checked on The message, and its fix

aead_not_a_family

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: ciphers::aead takes an AEAD family: families::chacha20_poly1305, families::chacha20_poly1305_original, families::xchacha20_poly1305, families::secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305 or families::secretbox_xchacha20poly1305.

The fix: Name one of the three ChaCha20-Poly1305 families or the two secret boxes’; AES-GCM is ciphers::gcm, as in aes256_gcm.

aes_on_bearssl

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>: BearSSL exports AES only inside its modes, with no block cipher. Name a backend that exports it, as in ciphers::aes256<backends::ctaes> or ciphers::aes256<backends::openssl>, and add its library to the program's Jamfile.

The fix: Name ciphers::aes256<backends::ctaes>, include <webcpp/crypto/backends/ctaes.hpp> and add /third_party//ctaes.

bearssl_not_linked

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: the backend BearSSL is used and not linked. In the program's Jamfile, add /third_party//bearssl beside /webcpp/crypto//crypto. (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_BEARSSL=1 and link BearSSL built with webcpp's src/canary_bearssl.c)

The fix: Add /third_party//bearssl.

box_default_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: X25519-XSalsa20-Poly1305 sealed box's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//sealed_box-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//sealed_box-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: The secret boxes’, the boxes’ and the sealed boxes’ default is libsodium on every target: add the family’s alias, as /webcpp/crypto//box_xsalsa20poly1305-default, which links /third_party//sodium.

box_not_a_family

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: hybrid::basic_box takes a box family: families::box_xsalsa20poly1305 or families::box_xchacha20poly1305.

The fix: Name families::box_xsalsa20poly1305 or families::box_xchacha20poly1305, or use hybrid::box or hybrid::box_xchacha20poly1305.

chacha_default_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: XChaCha20-Poly1305's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//xchacha20_poly1305-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//xchacha20_poly1305-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: The ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEADs’ default is libsodium on every target: add the family’s alias, as /webcpp/crypto//chacha20_poly1305-default, which links /third_party//sodium.

chacha_header_not_included

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: bearssl's ChaCha20-Poly1305 is in <webcpp/crypto/backends/bearssl.hpp>, which the program does not include. Include it, and add /third_party//bearssl to the program's Jamfile.

The fix: Include the backend’s header the message names, as <webcpp/crypto/backends/bearssl.hpp>, and add its library, as /third_party//bearssl.

chacha_on_ctaes

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: ctaes has no ChaCha20-Poly1305. The backends that have it: sodium (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), bearssl (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), openssl (native, wasip2, wasip3).

The fix: Name a backend that has ChaCha20-Poly1305, as in chacha20_poly1305<backends::bearssl>, or its default, chacha20_poly1305<>, and link its library.

chacha_unknown_backend

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: ChaCha20-Poly1305 has no backend of that name. The backends that have it: sodium (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), bearssl (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), openssl (native, wasip2, wasip3).

The fix: Name a backend of webcpp::crypto::backends that has the family, as backends::bearssl, or leave the backend out for the family’s default: chacha20_poly1305<>.

ctaes_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: the backend ctaes is used and not linked. In the program's Jamfile, add /third_party//ctaes beside /webcpp/crypto//crypto. (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_CTAES=1 and link ctaes.c with webcpp's src/canary_ctaes.c)

The fix: Add /third_party//ctaes.

default_openssl_wasm

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: WEBCPP_CRYPTO_DEFAULT_BACKEND_OPENSSL no longer chooses a default. Write the backend in the type where the program wants it, as in ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::openssl>>.

The fix: Remove the define, and name gcm<aes256<backends::openssl>> where the program wants OpenSSL.

default_selected

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: WEBCPP_CRYPTO_DEFAULT_BACKEND_BEARSSL no longer chooses a default. Write the backend in the type where the program wants it, as in ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>>.

The fix: Remove the define, and name gcm<aes256<backends::bearssl>> where the program wants BearSSL.

ed25519_default_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: Ed25519's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//ed25519-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//ed25519-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: Add /webcpp/crypto//ed25519-default, which links /third_party//sodium on every target.

ed25519_on_bearssl

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: bearssl has no Ed25519. The backends that have it: sodium (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten).

The fix: Leave the backend out, as in curves::ed25519::keypair, or name backends::sodium, and add /third_party//sodium.

ed25519_unknown_policy

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: Ed25519's only verification policy is curves::ed25519::strict.

The fix: Leave the policy out, as in curves::ed25519::verify(public_key, message, signature), or name curves::ed25519::strict.

ed25519ph_sha256

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: Ed25519ph is defined over SHA-512 (RFC 8032 section 5.1); name curves::ed25519::ph<webcpp::hash::sha2_512>.

The fix: Name curves::ed25519::ph<webcpp::hash::sha2_512>: RFC 8032 defines Ed25519ph over SHA-512.

ellswift_other_backend

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: bearssl has no ElligatorSwift. The backends that have it: secp256k1 (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten).

The fix: Name backends::secp256k1, or leave the backend out: curves::secp256k1::ellswift_decode(encoded_key).

gcm_default_openssl_not_linked

native

webcpp::crypto: AES-GCM's default backend on this target is OpenSSL, which is not linked. Add /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default ; or name another backend in the type, as in ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>>. The backends that have it: bearssl (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), openssl (native, wasip2, wasip3). (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 and link libcrypto)

The fix: Natively the default is OpenSSL: add /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, which links /webcpp/crypto//openssl there, or name BearSSL in the type, as in gcm<aes256<backends::bearssl>>.

gcm_on_ctaes

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::ctaes>>: ctaes exports the AES block cipher alone, and webcpp builds no GCM on another library's AES. Use a backend that exports GCM: ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>> or ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::openssl>>.

The fix: Name gcm<aes256<backends::bearssl>> or gcm<aes256<backends::openssl>>, or use aes256_gcm with its default linked.

heavy_without_threads

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: async_slow runs on another thread and needs a build with threads (natively without WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS; on Emscripten -pthread). Without threads, call slow.

The fix: Call the synchronous operation the message names, or build with threads: natively without WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS, on Emscripten with -pthread; WASI has none.

heavy_without_threads_first

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: async_slow runs on another thread and needs a build with threads (natively without WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS; on Emscripten -pthread). Without threads, call slow.

The fix: As heavy_without_threads.

kx_default_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: crypto_kx's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//kx-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//kx-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: Add /webcpp/crypto//kx-default, which links /third_party//sodium on every target.

label_lookup_by_value

native, wasip2

no matching function for call to 'scan_outputs'

The fix: Return std::optional<std::span<std::uint8_t const, 32>>, a span over a tweak the lookup keeps, such as a map’s entry; never the tweak by value.

musig_nonce_copied

native, wasip2

call to deleted constructor of

The fix: Pass the nonce with std::move, once: a secret nonce signs one message.

musig_other_backend

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: bearssl has no MuSig2. The backends that have it: secp256k1 (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten).

The fix: Name backends::secp256k1, or leave the backend out: curves::secp256k1::musig::parse_public_nonce(encoded_nonce).

no_backend_wasm

wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: AES-GCM's default backend on this target is BearSSL, which is not linked. Add /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default ; or name another backend in the type, as in ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::openssl>>. The backends that have it: bearssl (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), openssl (native, wasip2, wasip3). (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_BEARSSL=1 and link BearSSL built with webcpp's src/canary_bearssl.c)

The fix: On WASI the default is BearSSL: add /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, which links /third_party//bearssl there, or, with OpenSSL linked, name it in the type, as in gcm<aes256<backends::openssl>>.

openssl_memory_not_linked

native

webcpp::crypto: WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE routes OpenSSL's allocations, and OpenSSL is not linked. In the program's Jamfile, add /webcpp/crypto//openssl beside /webcpp/crypto//crypto, or remove that define. (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 and link libcrypto)

The fix: A target has the define and not OpenSSL: put <library>/webcpp/crypto//openssl in the same project requirements as the define, or remove the define.

openssl_memory_on_webassembly

wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE is an option of native programs, and this program is built for WebAssembly. Remove that define from the program's Jamfile.

The fix: Remove <define>WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE from the WebAssembly build: give that build a project of its own, without the define and OpenSSL, naming /third_party//bearssl. On WebAssembly the backend is BearSSL, which allocates nothing.

openssl_not_linked

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: the backend OpenSSL is used and not linked. In the program's Jamfile, add /webcpp/crypto//openssl beside /webcpp/crypto//crypto. (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_OPENSSL=1 and link libcrypto)

The fix: Add /webcpp/crypto//openssl.

openssl_old

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: the backend OpenSSL needs OpenSSL 3.0 or later, and the headers found are of an older OpenSSL. In the program's Jamfile, name /webcpp/crypto//openssl, which builds OpenSSL 3.5.9. (without b2: put OpenSSL 3's include/ first)

The fix: Name /webcpp/crypto//openssl, which builds OpenSSL 3.5.9; without b2, put OpenSSL 3’s include/ first.

openssl_only_on_wasi

wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: AES-GCM's default backend on this target is BearSSL, which is not linked. Add /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default ; or name another backend in the type, as in ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::openssl>>. The backends that have it: bearssl (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten), openssl (native, wasip2, wasip3). (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_BEARSSL=1 and link BearSSL built with webcpp's src/canary_bearssl.c)

The fix: On WASI the default is BearSSL: add /webcpp/crypto//gcm-default, which links /third_party//bearssl there, or, with OpenSSL linked, name it in the type, as in gcm<aes256<backends::openssl>>.

pem_default_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: PEM's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//pem-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//pem-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: Add /webcpp/crypto//pem-default, which links /third_party//sodium on every target.

secp256k1_not_linked

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp> needs libsecp256k1, which is not linked. In the program's Jamfile, add /third_party//secp256k1 beside /webcpp/crypto//crypto. (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SECP256K1=1 and link libsecp256k1 built with webcpp's src/canary_secp256k1.c)

The fix: Add /third_party//secp256k1.

secp256k1_other_backend

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: bearssl has no secp256k1. The backends that have it: secp256k1 (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten).

The fix: Name backends::secp256k1, or leave the backend out: curves::secp256k1::keypair.

secret_of_no_bytes

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: a secret of no bytes holds nothing.

The fix: Give secret the number of bytes it holds, at least one, as in secret<32>.

silent_payments_other_backend

native, wasip2

webcpp::crypto: bearssl has no BIP 352 silent payments. The backends that have it: secp256k1 (native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten).

The fix: Name backends::secp256k1, or leave the backend out: curves::secp256k1::silent_payments::make_prevouts_summary(...).

sodium_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: the backend libsodium is used and not linked. In the program's Jamfile, add /third_party//sodium beside /webcpp/crypto//crypto, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /third_party//sodium ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: Add /third_party//sodium.

x25519_default_not_linked

native, wasip2, wasip3

webcpp::crypto: X25519's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//x25519-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//x25519-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

The fix: Add /webcpp/crypto//x25519-default, which links /third_party//sodium on every target.

At build and link time, from the fixtures of the user’s Jamfiles, each built on a scratch superproject: the texts the build’s output contains, per target and linker, as each fixture checks them.

aead_not_a_family_on_emscripten

A program for Emscripten that gives ciphers::aead AES-GCM’s family, which ciphers::gcm serves instead. The fix: As aead_not_a_family.

Its Jamfile:

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /third_party//sodium ;

On each target, the build’s output contains:

  • emscripten:

    • webcpp::crypto: ciphers::aead takes an AEAD family: families::chacha20_poly1305, families::chacha20_poly1305_original, families::xchacha20_poly1305, families::secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305 or families::secretbox_xchacha20poly1305.

box_default_not_linked_on_emscripten

A program for Emscripten that calls the secret boxes, the boxes and the sealed box on their default, libsodium, and links none. The fix: As box_default_not_linked.

Its Jamfile:

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto ;

On each target, the build’s output contains:

  • emscripten:

    • webcpp::crypto: XSalsa20-Poly1305 secret box's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//secretbox_xsalsa20poly1305-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

    • webcpp::crypto: XChaCha20-Poly1305 secret box's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//secretbox_xchacha20poly1305-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//secretbox_xchacha20poly1305-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

    • webcpp::crypto: X25519-XSalsa20-Poly1305 box's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//box_xsalsa20poly1305-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//box_xsalsa20poly1305-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

    • webcpp::crypto: X25519-XChaCha20-Poly1305 box's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//box_xchacha20poly1305-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//box_xchacha20poly1305-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

    • webcpp::crypto: X25519-XSalsa20-Poly1305 sealed box's default backend on this target is libsodium, which is not linked, and the one backend that has it there. Add /webcpp/crypto//sealed_box-default, the default's library on every target, to the program's Jamfile, as in: exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//sealed_box-default ; (without b2: define WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM=1 and link libsodium built with webcpp's src/canary_sodium.c)

box_not_a_family_on_emscripten

A program for Emscripten that gives hybrid::basic_box a type that is no box family. The fix: As box_not_a_family.

canary_without

A BearSSL built from its sources without webcpp’s src/canary_bearssl.c. The fix: Compile webcpp’s src/canary_bearssl.c with the library, or link it through b2.

Its Jamfile:

path-constant BEARSSL : ../../third_party/libs/bearssl ;
lib bearssl-plain : [ glob $(BEARSSL)/src/*.c $(BEARSSL)/src/*/*.c ]
  : <link>static <warnings>off <include>$(BEARSSL)/inc <include>$(BEARSSL)/src
  : : <include>$(BEARSSL)/inc <define>WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_BEARSSL=1 ;
exe app : app.cpp bearssl-plain /webcpp/crypto//crypto ;

On each target, the build’s output contains:

  • native, macOS:

    • Undefined symbols for architecture

    • _webcpp_crypto_bearssl_7bea48e_getentropy__add_third_party_bearssl_to_your_link

    • undefined reference to `webcpp_crypto_bearssl_7bea48e_getentropy__add_third_party_bearssl_to_your_link'

Elsewhere than MSVC these mistakes build, and nothing stops them; the fixtures record it:

memory_two_files

Two files of one program, one compiled with the memory option and one without.

Its Jamfile, which builds on native:

obj with : with.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//openssl
  : <define>WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE ;

exe app : main.cpp with /webcpp/crypto//crypto /webcpp/crypto//openssl ;

Windows

crypto’s headers include <windows.h> under NOMINMAX and WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN when the program has not defined them, and write (min)() and (max)() so that the macros never matter. A program that wants the macros min and max, or what WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN leaves out, includes <windows.h> itself before any header of crypto.

The root utilities: webcpp::crypto

The namespace webcpp::crypto holds what every other chapter relies on: where secrets come from (random_device), how a secret is checked (equal) and how a failure is told apart (error), none of which needs a backend; and how a key’s standard form becomes text and back (pem, on libsodium; Key formats: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM). It also declares, for a native program on OpenSSL that turns the memory option on, the resource every allocation of OpenSSL’s goes to (openssl_memory_resource, OpenSSL’s allocations in your own memory resource).

Name random_device equal error pem openssl_memory_resource

What it is for

Keys, IVs, tokens, nonces: every secret a program draws

Checking a tag, a MAC or a token

Telling failures apart

A key’s SPKI or PKCS#8 as text, to paste, store or exchange with OpenSSL

Keeping every allocation of OpenSSL’s in the program’s own resource, natively

Header

<webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>

<webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>

<webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

<webcpp/crypto/pem.hpp>

<webcpp/crypto/backends/openssl.hpp>

Errors

entropy_unavailable, errc::not_supported

none: it returns bool

its values are the errors

invalid_encoding, invalid_input_size

memory_functions_refused, memory_functions_not_installed

Standards and sources

POSIX.1-2024, getentropy, Microsoft, BCryptGenRandom, W3C Web Cryptography API, getRandomValues, WASI, wasi:random

CWE-208, observable timing discrepancy

none

RFC 7468, textual encodings of PKIX, PKCS and CMS structures (PEM), libsodium’s documentation, helpers: base64 encoding and decoding

OpenSSL 3.5’s OPENSSL_malloc(3), CRYPTO_set_mem_functions

Choose it when

you need a random number an attacker must not predict; never std::mt19937 or rand (CWE-338, a weak generator used for security)

you compare anything secret; never == or memcmp on a MAC

you branch on a failure: forged data, a wrong size, no entropy

a key goes to or comes from a file, a form or a tool as -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- text; with the encode_spki and encode_pkcs8 of curves::ed25519, curves::x25519 or curves::secp256k1

a native program on OpenSSL must allocate only from its own arena; on WebAssembly, BearSSL allocates nothing

Entropy

A cryptographically secure random number generator produces numbers that an attacker cannot predict, even after seeing many of them (Wikipedia). Every secret a program makes starts there: a key, an IV, a session token, a password-reset link. A general-purpose generator such as std::mt19937 or rand is built to look random, not to resist an attacker: a few outputs reveal its state and every output after them (CWE-338). A token drawn from one can be computed by anyone who has seen a few others, and the account it protects is taken over.

random_device, in <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>, reads the operating system’s or the browser’s generator, and nothing else. Every call reads the source: there is no cache and no generator of webcpp’s in between. There is one source per platform, each with its documented contract:

  • getentropy on Linux, macOS and WASI (POSIX.1-2024); on WASI it is the host’s generator (wasi:random);

  • crypto.getRandomValues through Emscripten, in the browser and in node (W3C);

  • BCryptGenRandom with the system’s preferred generator on Windows (Microsoft).

There is no weaker fallback, ever: no clock, no rand, no address. When the source fails, fill returns entropy_unavailable and zeroes its output, so that nothing the caller could use by mistake is left in it; where there is no source at all (an Emscripten audio worklet, which has no crypto), it returns errc::not_supported. The function asks in pieces of at most 256 bytes, the limit of getentropy, and checks every call.

fill(bytes) is the interface. With exceptions, random_device is also a standard random bit generator, shaped as std::random_device: its operator() throws boost::system::system_error when the source fails, so it plugs into std::uniform_int_distribution for an unbiased number in a range. Without exceptions operator() is not declared, since it would have no way to report a failure, and fill is the whole interface.

The backends of random_device, from the test programs that run it:

Backend Jamfile Header Targets

the system’s generator

/webcpp/crypto//crypto

<webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>

native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten (tested by random_device)

Example. A password-reset token of 32 bytes, sent as 64 hex digits in a link, and a six-digit one-time code:

// 32 random bytes are 256 bits: far beyond any guessing, written as 64 hex digits.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> raw{};
if (!device.fill(raw)) {
    return 1;
}
std::string token;
for (std::uint8_t const byte : raw) {
    char const* const hex = "0123456789abcdef";
    token += hex[byte >> 4U];
    token += hex[byte & 0x0FU];
}
// The distribution removes the bias a plain modulo would add.
std::uniform_int_distribution<unsigned> digits(0, 999999);
unsigned const number = digits(device);
std::array<char, 8> code{};
if (std::snprintf(code.data(), code.size(), "%06u", number) != 6) {
    return 1;
}
token: 64 hex digits
code: 6 digits

Pitfalls.

  • Never seed std::mt19937 from random_device and use the mt19937 for secrets: its state is recoverable from its output.

  • Never shorten a token for convenience: 128 bits is the floor, and 256 costs nothing.

  • Never take a number modulo a range by hand: % 1000000 of a 32-bit value favours small codes. std::uniform_int_distribution does not.

  • Never ignore the result of fill: on entropy_unavailable there is no safe value to use, and the operation that needed one fails.

Seeding BearSSL’s own generator

A program that calls BearSSL’s C API directly, for something crypto does not wrap, seeds BearSSL’s generators from random_device: crypto builds BearSSL without a seeder of its own on Windows, and no backend ever chooses its own entropy source. 32 bytes from fill seed BearSSL’s HMAC-DRBG:

#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>

#include <bearssl.h>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> seed{};
    webcpp::crypto::random_device device;
    if (!device.fill(seed)) {
        return 1;
    }

    br_hmac_drbg_context drbg;
    br_hmac_drbg_init(&drbg, &br_sha256_vtable, seed.data(), seed.size());
    // The generator holds what it needs: the seed goes now.
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(seed)));

    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> bytes{};
    br_hmac_drbg_generate(&drbg, bytes.data(), bytes.size());
    // The bytes are random, so the program never prints them.
    // The generator's state predicts its next outputs: wipe it, and what it gave, after use.
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(&drbg, 1)));
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(bytes)));
    std::printf("seeded\n");
    return 0;
}
seeded

Comparing tags

A timing attack recovers a secret by measuring how long a program takes to handle different inputs (Wikipedia). The commonest target is a comparison: == and memcmp stop at the first byte that differs, so they take longer the more leading bytes match. A server that checks a request’s MAC that way tells an attacker, through its response time, how many bytes of a forged MAC are right; with enough requests the attacker builds a valid one byte by byte (CWE-208).

equal, in <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>, compares in constant time: it reads every byte, combines the differences without a branch, and its running time depends only on the length. It takes two Hash2 digests of one size, or two spans; spans of different sizes compare unequal without reading their contents, since a size is public. HMAC itself (RFC 2104) is Boost.Hash2’s; crypto adds the comparison that makes it safe to check.

The backends of equal, from the test programs that run it:

Backend Jamfile Header Targets

no backend

/webcpp/crypto//crypto

<webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>, <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

native, wasip2, wasip3, emscripten (tested by equal)

Example. A payment provider signs each webhook call with HMAC-SHA-256 under a shared secret. The program recomputes the MAC over the body and compares it with equal; here the key, the body and the MAC are RFC 4231’s test case 2 (RFC 4231):

// The receiver recomputes the tag and compares it in constant time.
hash2::hmac_sha2_256 mac(key.data(), key.size());
mac.update(data.data(), data.size());
auto const computed = mac.result();
bool const valid =
    crypto::equal(std::span<std::uint8_t const>(computed.data(), computed.size()), sent_tag);
hmac verified with equal
altered tag refused

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/hmac.hpp>
#include <boost/hash2/sha2.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace hash2 = boost::hash2;

int main() {
    // RFC 4231, test case 2.
    std::string_view const key = "Jefe";
    std::string_view const data = "what do ya want for nothing?";
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const sent_tag{
        0x5b, 0xdc, 0xc1, 0x46, 0xbf, 0x60, 0x75, 0x4e, 0x6a, 0x04, 0x24,
        0x26, 0x08, 0x95, 0x75, 0xc7, 0x5a, 0x00, 0x3f, 0x08, 0x9d, 0x27,
        0x39, 0x83, 0x9d, 0xec, 0x58, 0xb9, 0x64, 0xec, 0x38, 0x43,
    };

    // The receiver recomputes the tag and compares it in constant time.
    hash2::hmac_sha2_256 mac(key.data(), key.size());
    mac.update(data.data(), data.size());
    auto const computed = mac.result();
    bool const valid =
        crypto::equal(std::span<std::uint8_t const>(computed.data(), computed.size()), sent_tag);
    if (!valid) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("hmac verified with equal\n");

    // A tag with one changed byte must be refused.
    auto altered = sent_tag;
    altered[31] ^= 1U;
    if (crypto::equal(std::span<std::uint8_t const>(computed.data(), computed.size()), altered)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("altered tag refused\n");
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls.

  • Comparing the hex strings of two MACs with == brings the leak back.

  • Returning early when the lengths differ is fine, since a length is public; reading the contents first is not.

  • A MAC checked after the request has been acted on protects nothing: check first.

Errors

Every operation of crypto that can fail returns boost::system::result<T>, and reports the failure with an error of the category webcpp.crypto, as a boost::system::error_code, never by throwing on its own. The values are fixed and never reused, so a program may store them.

A program tells failures apart because they call for different answers. authentication_failed means the data, its additional data or its tag changed since it was sealed, or the key is another: someone may be attacking, and the message is dropped. A size error means the caller or the wire format is wrong: a bug to fix, not an attack. entropy_unavailable means there is no safe random value to use: the operation that needed one fails.

Value Name Raised when

1

invalid_key_size

A key of another size than the algorithm’s key_size, or a secret key not of 32 bytes.

2

invalid_iv_size

A GCM IV that is empty or longer than 128 bytes.

3

invalid_tag_size

A tag given to open that is not of 16 bytes.

4

invalid_input_size

Data given to a block cipher that is not a whole number of blocks, or a DER output shorter than max_der_size.

5

message_too_long

A message or additional data longer than the algorithm allows.

6

authentication_failed

The tag does not match: the message or its additional data changed, or the key differs.

7

invalid_state

An object moved from, or the incremental seal called out of order.

8

entropy_unavailable

The system’s or the browser’s generator failed.

9

invalid_secret_key

A secret key or a tweak that is zero or not below the group order, or a tweak that gives no valid key.

10

invalid_public_key

A public key of the wrong size, with a prefix other than 02 or 03 (33 bytes) or 04 (65 bytes), or not a point of the curve.

11

invalid_signature

A signature that does not verify, or is not a valid encoding: not strict DER, or an r or an s that is zero or not below the group order.

12

backend_failure

A backend failed where its contract says it does not.

13

memory_functions_refused

OpenSSL’s memory functions could not be installed: OpenSSL has already allocated, or another party installed its own. From backends::openssl::install_memory_functions, with WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE.

14

memory_functions_not_installed

OpenSSL’s memory functions are not webcpp::crypto’s. From every make of the OpenSSL backend, with WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE.

15

weak_public_key

A public key of small order, or one that gives an all-zero shared secret.

16

invalid_point

An encoding that is not a canonical element of the group.

17

invalid_scalar

A scalar that is not reduced, or zero where zero is refused.

18

invalid_padding

Padding that cannot be removed, whatever the cause: one value for every cause, so that no padding oracle is built from it.

19

invalid_encoding

Hexadecimal, base64, PEM, or a key’s DER form that does not decode, or is not the one encoding the format allows.

20

invalid_ciphertext_size

A KEM or RSA ciphertext of another size than the key’s.

A value that error does not define has the message "unknown webcpp.crypto error". random_device also returns errc::not_supported where there is no generator at all, and OpenSSL’s make errc::not_enough_memory when OpenSSL cannot allocate its context. memory_functions_refused and memory_functions_not_installed come only with OpenSSL’s memory option, natively: OpenSSL’s allocations in your own memory resource says what each means and what to do.

Example. A message is sealed, then opened three ways: with a flipped bit, with an empty IV and with a short tag. Only the first is an attack, and only the first decrypted anything, which open has zeroed:

if (opened) {
    return 1;
}
if (opened.error() == crypto::error::authentication_failed) {
    // Someone changed the data or used another key: drop the message.
    std::printf("tampered: authentication_failed%s\n",
                all_zero(tampered) ? ", data zeroed" : "");
    std::string const message = opened.error().message();
    std::printf("message: %s\n", message.c_str());
} else {
    // Anything else is a mistake of the caller, not an attack.
    return 1;
}
tampered: authentication_failed, data zeroed
message: the authentication tag does not match
empty iv: invalid_iv_size, data untouched
short tag: invalid_tag_size

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes256_gcm.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
using aead_type = crypto::ciphers::aes256_gcm;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

bool all_zero(std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    return std::ranges::all_of(bytes, [](std::uint8_t b) { return b == 0; });
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // A demonstration key and IV, so that the output is the same on every run; a real program
    // draws the key from random_device and never reuses an IV under it.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    key.fill(0x2a);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> iv{};
    iv.fill(0x07);
    std::string_view const text = "attack at dawn!";
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 15> sealed{};
    std::ranges::copy(text, sealed.begin());

    auto aead = aead_type::make(key);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(key)));
    if (!aead) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const tag = aead->seal(iv, {}, sealed);
    if (!tag) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::span<std::uint8_t const> const tag_bytes(tag->data(), tag->size());

    // (a) One flipped bit in the ciphertext.
    auto tampered = sealed;
    tampered[3] ^= 1U;
    auto const opened = aead->open(iv, {}, tampered, tag_bytes);
    if (opened) {
        return 1;
    }
    if (opened.error() == crypto::error::authentication_failed) {
        // Someone changed the data or used another key: drop the message.
        std::printf("tampered: authentication_failed%s\n",
                    all_zero(tampered) ? ", data zeroed" : "");
        std::string const message = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("message: %s\n", message.c_str());
    } else {
        // Anything else is a mistake of the caller, not an attack.
        return 1;
    }
    if (!all_zero(tampered)) {
        return 1;
    }

    // (b) An empty IV is refused before anything is touched.
    auto copy = sealed;
    auto const no_iv = aead->open({}, {}, copy, tag_bytes);
    if (no_iv || no_iv.error() != crypto::error::invalid_iv_size || copy != sealed) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("empty iv: invalid_iv_size, data untouched\n");

    // (c) A tag of 15 bytes instead of 16.
    auto const short_tag = aead->open(iv, {}, copy, tag_bytes.first(15));
    if (short_tag || short_tag.error() != crypto::error::invalid_tag_size) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("short tag: invalid_tag_size\n");
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls.

  • Never use the bytes of a failed open: crypto zeroes them on purpose.

  • Never tell a remote party which check failed: "could not decrypt" is enough, and more detail helps an attacker.

  • Never treat entropy_unavailable as a reason to fall back on a weaker value: fail the operation.

Exceptions

Every operation reports its errors as values, whether or not the program has exceptions. <webcpp/crypto/config.hpp>, which every header of crypto includes first, defines WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_EXCEPTIONS when webcpp has no exceptions (the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), and a program may define it for crypto alone. One function throws: random_device::operator(), through boost::throw_exception, because the standard’s random bit generator has no other way to report a failure; it is declared only when the macro is not defined. keypair::make lets the program’s memory resource report a failed allocation as the resource does.

Ciphers: webcpp::crypto::ciphers

A cipher turns readable data into bytes that reveal nothing without the key, and back. A chat app encrypts each message, a password manager its vault, a file-sharing app each file; without a cipher, anyone who reads the network, the server’s disk or a backup reads the data. Every cipher a program uses for data must also be authenticated: an AEAD adds a tag that detects any change, since an attacker who can flip bits of an unauthenticated ciphertext changes the plaintext the program acts on (Wikipedia).

The namespace webcpp::crypto::ciphers holds the AEADs of this version and one building block. AES-GCM is the cipher the industry standardised on (FIPS 197; SP 800-38D), fast where the CPU has AES instructions and the one browsers’ WebCrypto offers. ChaCha20-Poly1305 needs no such instructions to be fast and constant time (RFC 8439); its XChaCha20 form takes a 24-byte nonce that is safe to draw at random for every message, and libsodium’s secret boxes are the same idea in NaCl’s format. The raw AES block cipher is a building block, never encryption of data.

Which one. When in doubt, xchacha20_poly1305<>: a random nonce per message and nothing to count, the same code and the same bytes on the web and natively. AES-GCM when a protocol, a standard or a browser’s WebCrypto names it, or to read what such a party wrote; RFC 8439’s ChaCha20-Poly1305 when a protocol names it, TLS 1.3 or WireGuard; a secret box to read or write libsodium’s crypto_secretbox. The table compares them; each row’s "choose it when" is the rule.

AES-GCM

Authenticated encryption keeps data secret and proves it unchanged with one key (Wikipedia). Encryption alone does not: with counter mode alone, flipping a bit of a ciphertext flips the same bit of the plaintext, and the receiver cannot tell; a forged "amount" field in an encrypted cookie goes through. AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) encrypts with AES in counter mode and computes a 16-byte tag over the ciphertext and over additional data that travels in clear (Wikipedia; NIST SP 800-38D). Opening recomputes the tag and returns the plaintext only if it matches; on a mismatch the data is zeroed. It is the mandatory cipher of TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and the AEAD of browsers’ WebCrypto (W3C).

gcm<Cipher>, in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/gcm.hpp>, is AES-GCM with the key size of Cipher, on the backend of Cipher, which must export GCM over its own AES: BearSSL or OpenSSL. aes128_gcm and aes256_gcm, in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes256_gcm.hpp>, name it on the default backend, OpenSSL natively and BearSSL on WebAssembly. It is made with make(key_bytes), and works in place:

  • seal(iv_bytes, additional_data_bytes, data_bytes) encrypts data_bytes in place and returns its 16-byte tag, a boost::hash2::digest<16>;

  • open(iv_bytes, additional_data_bytes, data_bytes, tag_bytes) checks the tag and decrypts data_bytes in place;

  • begin_seal(iv_bytes, additional_data_bytes), update(data_bytes) and result() seal a message in pieces.

Example. A program stores users’ API tokens in a database. Each token is sealed under a storage key with the user’s id as additional data, so that the row opens only for that user: a row copied onto another user’s record does not open.

std::string_view const token = "api-token-0123456789";
row stored;
// A fresh IV for every row: reusing one under the same key breaks GCM.
if (!device.fill(stored.iv)) {
    return 1;
}
stored.ciphertext.assign(token.begin(), token.end());
auto const tag = aead->seal(stored.iv, bytes_of("user-42"), stored.ciphertext);
if (!tag) {
    return 1;
}
std::ranges::copy(*tag, stored.tag.begin());
// Reading the row back: the id comes from the session, not from the row.
auto plain = stored.ciphertext;
if (!aead->open(stored.iv, bytes_of("user-42"), plain, stored.tag)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("opened for user-42: %.*s\n", static_cast<int>(plain.size()),
            reinterpret_cast<char const*>(plain.data()));
// The decrypted token is a secret: once used, wipe it.
wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(plain)));
opened for user-42: api-token-0123456789
refused for user-43: authentication_failed

The same, with the backend named rather than the default: AES-256-GCM on BearSSL against the GCM specification’s test case 14. Naming BearSSL lets one Jamfile line serve every target, at a cost natively: on an ARM server BearSSL runs its portable AES, where the default, OpenSSL, uses the CPU’s (A warning for ARM servers).

#include <webcpp/crypto/backends/bearssl.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/gcm.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;

// The backend is part of the type: no default, no surprise.
using aead_type = crypto::ciphers::gcm<crypto::ciphers::aes256<crypto::backends::bearssl>>;

int main() {
    // The test vector's zero key and IV: a real program draws its key from random_device and
    // never reuses an IV under it.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const key{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> const iv{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> data{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> const expected_cipher{
        0xce, 0xa7, 0x40, 0x3d, 0x4d, 0x60, 0x6b, 0x6e,
        0x07, 0x4e, 0xc5, 0xd3, 0xba, 0xf3, 0x9d, 0x18,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> const expected_tag{
        0xd0, 0xd1, 0xc8, 0xa7, 0x99, 0x99, 0x6b, 0xf0,
        0x26, 0x5b, 0x98, 0xb5, 0xd4, 0x8a, 0xb9, 0x19,
    };

    auto aead = aead_type::make(key);
    if (!aead) {
        return 1;
    }
    // Seal encrypts in place and returns the tag.
    auto const tag = aead->seal(iv, {}, data);
    if (!tag || data != expected_cipher || !crypto::equal(*tag, expected_tag)) {
        return 1;
    }
    // Open decrypts in place and checks the tag; on a mismatch it zeroes data and returns
    // authentication_failed.
    if (!aead->open(iv, {}, data, expected_tag) || data != std::array<std::uint8_t, 16>{}) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const name = aead_type::backend_type::name;
    std::printf("aes256_gcm ok backend=%.*s\n", static_cast<int>(name.size()), name.data());
    return 0;
}
aes256_gcm ok backend=bearssl

The rules of AES-GCM

Each rule is how crypto behaves, and what it asks of the program.

  • Never reuse an IV under one key. Two messages under one key and one IV reveal the XOR of their plaintexts, and let an attacker recover the authentication key and forge tags for every later message (Joux, 2006; Boeck et al., 2016; CWE-323). AES-GCM does not resist this misuse: the program must prevent it.

  • The usage limit. With random IVs, or IVs other than 12 bytes, at most 232 messages are sealed under one key (NIST SP 800-38D, section 8.3). A counter IV (message 0, 1, 2 …​) is safe until the counter repeats, which it must never do, a restart included. Rotate the key before either limit.

  • IVs of 1 to 128 bytes; 12 recommended. An IV of another size than 12 bytes is hashed into the first counter block, as every backend does; the cap of 128 bytes is OpenSSL’s, applied on every backend so that a call succeeds or fails the same way everywhere.

  • Keys of 16, 24 or 32 bytes. A key shared with a browser’s WebCrypto is of 16 or 32 bytes: Chromium refuses 192-bit AES keys (Chromium).

  • In place, the tag apart. data_bytes is both input and output, so no buffer is copied; the tag is separate, so that a wire format that appends it or sends it apart is a matter of the caller’s spans.

  • A failed open zeroes data_bytes. Every backend decrypts and checks the tag in one pass; when the tag does not match, crypto zeroes the whole of data_bytes, so that no unauthenticated plaintext is left. A caller who needs the ciphertext after a failure keeps a copy. A guard’s refusal (invalid_state, invalid_iv_size, invalid_tag_size, message_too_long) comes before any work and leaves data_bytes untouched. Whether the tag matched is the one value derived from the key that crypto treats as public (Constant time).

  • Plaintext is in data_bytes while open runs. The decrypted bytes sit in data_bytes before the tag is checked. When data_bytes is memory another party can read during the call (a shared segment, a SharedArrayBuffer that JavaScript sees), open into private memory and copy the result out.

  • No incremental open. Decrypting piece by piece would hand out plaintext before the tag is known, and code that acts on unverified plaintext is how many protocols were broken. A large message is split into records, each sealed and opened whole (Encrypting what does not fit in memory).

  • One thread at a time, and not shareable. A gcm holds the state of a message, so it is used by one thread at a time, as a Hash2 algorithm is. It holds a key, and OpenSSL’s holds pointers into OpenSSL’s heap: it is never placed in memory shared with another process, and a key never should be.

  • An object moved from is empty. Every function of it returns invalid_state, so that a moved-from object never seals under a wiped key.

The guards

Each function checks its guards first, in the order of the table, and returns before it reads a secret byte; the last three rows are the failures of the work itself, which come after the guards:

Condition Error

make: a key of another size than key_size

invalid_key_size

any other function: the object was moved from

invalid_state

begin_seal while a message is in progress; update or result with no message begun

invalid_state

an empty IV, or one longer than max_iv_size, 128 bytes

invalid_iv_size

open: a tag of another size than 16

invalid_tag_size

a message longer than max_message_size, 236 - 32 bytes, in one call or summed over update, or additional data longer than 261 - 1 bytes (NIST SP 800-38D, section 5.2.1.1)

message_too_long

open: the tag does not match

authentication_failed

the backend fails where it should not

A warning for ARM servers

Natively the default is OpenSSL. A program that names BearSSL there gets AES-NI code for x86 but none for ARM’s AES instructions (BearSSL): on an ARM server it runs its portable constant-time code, while OpenSSL’s assembly uses ARMv8’s AES and polynomial multiplication instructions (OpenSSL’s AES; OpenSSL’s GHASH). Throughput records how much slower, measured by hand on an arm64 machine. A server on ARM keeps the default and links /webcpp/crypto//openssl (The default backend per target).

Encrypting what does not fit in memory

A 2 GB video before an upload, or a log as it is written, cannot be held whole. begin_seal takes the IV and the additional data, update encrypts each piece in place as it arrives, and result returns the tag at the end. The object refuses another message while one is in progress, and any error abandons the message: its pieces have no tag and are not to be sent.

// The header is authenticated up front, then the buffer is encrypted chunk by chunk in place.
if (!aead->begin_seal(iv, header)) {
    return false;
}
std::span<std::uint8_t> const whole(buffer);
for (std::size_t chunk = 0; chunk < 3; ++chunk) {
    if (!aead->update(whole.subspan(chunk * 16, 16))) {
        return false;
    }
}
auto const tag = aead->result();

What is sealed in pieces is opened whole. To open a large file piece by piece, split it into records, each sealed alone with its own IV, and with two things in its additional data: its number, so that a record cannot be reordered or replayed at another position, and a flag that is 1 for the last record and 0 for every other, so that a stream cut after any record does not open: the receiver opens the last record it got as the last, and a record that was not sealed as the last fails. The STREAM construction binds the same two (Hoang, Reyhanitabar, Rogaway and Vizár, 2015).

The record’s number is its IV, so each stream has a key of its own. Every stream numbers its records from 0: two files sealed under one key would both seal record 0 with the same IV, which reveals the XOR of the two records and lets an attacker forge tags under that key (The rules of AES-GCM), and a record of one file could be spliced into the other at the same position. The example draws a fresh random key per stream. A program that keeps one long-lived storage key derives the stream’s key from it, for example with HKDF of the storage key and a random salt of 32 bytes stored in the file’s header (RFC 5869); or it makes the IV’s first 8 bytes a random identifier drawn for the stream and its last 4 the record number, and counts every record against the key’s usage limit of 232 messages, since the identifiers are random.

// The stream's own key, drawn for it alone: every stream numbers its records from 0, so two
// streams under one key would seal record 0 twice with one IV. The receiver gets this key
// from the protocol, for example sealed under a long-lived key or agreed with ECDH.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
if (!crypto::random_device().fill(key)) {
    return false;
}
auto aead = aead_type::make(key);
wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(key)));
if (!aead) {
    return false;
}

std::vector<record> sent;
std::size_t const piece = (message.size() + 2) / 3;
for (std::uint64_t number = 0; number < 3; ++number) {
    auto const part = message.substr(number * piece, piece);
    record made;
    made.data.assign(part.begin(), part.end());
    bool const last = number == 2;
    auto const tag = aead->seal(counter_iv(number), record_data(number, last), made.data);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    std::ranges::copy(*tag, made.tag.begin());
    sent.push_back(std::move(made));
}

// The whole stream opens, record by record.
auto const whole = open_stream(*aead, sent);
if (!whole || *whole != message) {
    return false;
}
std::printf("3 records opened, the last as the last\n");

// A record presented at another position fails: its number is authenticated.
auto moved = sent[2].data;
auto const reordered = aead->open(counter_iv(1), record_data(1, false), moved, sent[2].tag);

// A stream cut after record 1 fails: record 1 was not sealed as the last.
auto const truncated = open_stream(*aead, std::span<record const>(sent).first(2));
incremental seal opened whole: 3 chunks
3 records opened, the last as the last
record 2 as record 1: authentication_failed
stream cut after record 1: authentication_failed

Pitfalls. Without the last-record flag, an attacker who drops the final records leaves a stream that opens record by record, shorter than the one sent. Never send the pieces of an abandoned message.

ChaCha20-Poly1305

ChaCha20-Poly1305 is authenticated encryption built from two of Daniel J. Bernstein’s designs: the stream cipher ChaCha20 encrypts, and the one-time authenticator Poly1305 computes a 16-byte tag over the ciphertext and the additional data (Wikipedia; RFC 8439). A chat app seals each message with it, a password manager each entry of its vault: whoever copies the ciphertext learns nothing of the text, and a single changed bit makes open refuse it. ChaCha20 is made of additions, XORs and rotations of 32-bit words (RFC 8439, section 2.1), with no table indexed by a secret, so it needs no AES instructions to be fast and is not sensitive to timing attacks in plain portable code, as libsodium’s documentation says (libsodium, AEAD constructions): on a phone or a WebAssembly page without AES hardware it is the safe choice. It is a cipher suite of TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and the AEAD of WireGuard (WireGuard).

ciphers::aead<Family, Backend>, in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aead.hpp>, is one-shot authenticated encryption in place over a family; three aliases, in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/chacha20_poly1305.hpp>, name its three ChaCha20-Poly1305 families on their default backend, libsodium on every target:

  • chacha20_poly1305<>, RFC 8439’s form: a 32-byte key, a 12-byte nonce, and messages of at most 238 - 64 bytes;

  • chacha20_poly1305_original<>, the original form libsodium keeps: an 8-byte nonce, too short to draw at random, which a counter numbers (libsodium);

  • xchacha20_poly1305<>: a 24-byte nonce, safe to draw at random for every message (the XChaCha draft). When in doubt, this one, as Ciphers: webcpp::crypto::ciphers says: a program that draws each nonce at random has nothing to count and nothing to store, on the web and natively alike.

Each is made with make(key_bytes) and works in place, as AES-GCM’s one-shot calls do: seal(iv_bytes, additional_data_bytes, data_bytes) encrypts data_bytes and returns the 16-byte tag; open(iv_bytes, additional_data_bytes, data_bytes, tag_bytes) checks the tag and decrypts. A failed open zeroes data_bytes; a guard’s refusal leaves it untouched. The nonce may lie in data_bytes, and the additional data may touch it, as a wire format that puts it just before the message does, but not overlap it.

RFC 8439’s form also runs on BearSSL, on every target, and on OpenSSL, natively and on WASI, with the same results byte for byte: name the backend in the type, as in chacha20_poly1305<backends::bearssl>, and link its library. On BearSSL nothing allocates; on OpenSSL make allocates and a message does not.

Limits. Each form bounds how much one key may seal, and how many messages may take a nonce drawn at random before two of them risk the same one, which would reveal both plaintexts’ XOR and let tags be forged:

Form One message, at most Messages with random nonces, per key

chacha20_poly1305

238 - 64 bytes, about 256 GB

232

chacha20_poly1305_original

no practical limit

216: use a counter

xchacha20_poly1305

no practical limit

no practical limit

A program changes keys periodically. A large message is no reason to improvise: splitting a message into chunks is safe only when each chunk’s tag also covers its number and a flag marking the last chunk, in the additional data or in a nonce built from them, and a reader refuses chunks out of order and a stream that ends without the last flag: otherwise whoever holds the ciphertext reorders, drops, repeats or truncates chunks and each one still opens. The STREAM construction (Hoang, Reyhanitabar, Rogaway and Vizár, 2015) and libsodium’s secretstream (libsodium’s documentation) do this; this version of crypto offers neither.

Example. A chat app’s messages under one conversation key, each sealed with a nonce drawn for it and the conversation’s id as additional data, so that a message moved to another conversation does not open:

// Seals text under the conversation's key, with a nonce drawn for this message alone.
bool seal(xchacha& cipher, crypto::random_device& device, std::span<std::uint8_t const> id,
          std::string_view text, sealed_message& out) {
    if (!device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    out.ciphertext.assign(text.begin(), text.end());
    auto const tag = cipher.seal(out.nonce, id, out.ciphertext);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return true;
}
// Opens a message in place; prints it, or why it was refused.
void open(xchacha& cipher, std::span<std::uint8_t const> id, sealed_message message) {
    auto const opened = cipher.open(message.nonce, id, message.ciphertext, message.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("refused: %s\n", reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("read: %.*s\n", static_cast<int>(message.ciphertext.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(message.ciphertext.data()));
}
read: see you at noon
read: bring the keys
refused: the authentication tag does not match
refused: the authentication tag does not match

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/chacha20_poly1305.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
using xchacha = crypto::ciphers::xchacha20_poly1305<>;

namespace {

// A message as it travels: the nonce, the tag and the ciphertext, all public.
struct sealed_message {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, xchacha::iv_size> nonce{};
    xchacha::result_type tag{};
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> ciphertext;
};

// Seals text under the conversation's key, with a nonce drawn for this message alone.
bool seal(xchacha& cipher, crypto::random_device& device, std::span<std::uint8_t const> id,
          std::string_view text, sealed_message& out) {
    if (!device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    out.ciphertext.assign(text.begin(), text.end());
    auto const tag = cipher.seal(out.nonce, id, out.ciphertext);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return true;
}


// Opens a message in place; prints it, or why it was refused.
void open(xchacha& cipher, std::span<std::uint8_t const> id, sealed_message message) {
    auto const opened = cipher.open(message.nonce, id, message.ciphertext, message.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("refused: %s\n", reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("read: %.*s\n", static_cast<int>(message.ciphertext.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(message.ciphertext.data()));
}


}  // namespace

int main() {
    crypto::random_device device;
    // The conversation's key: in a real app, agreed with the contact (curves::x25519) or
    // derived from a key the app already keeps; here, drawn once.
    crypto::secret<32> key;
    if (!device.fill(key.writable())) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto cipher = xchacha::make(key.bytes());
    if (!cipher) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> const conversation{'c', 'h', 'a', 't', '-', '0', '4', '2'};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 8> const other{'c', 'h', 'a', 't', '-', '0', '0', '7'};

    sealed_message first;
    sealed_message second;
    if (!seal(*cipher, device, conversation, "see you at noon", first) ||
        !seal(*cipher, device, conversation, "bring the keys", second)) {
        return 1;
    }
    open(*cipher, conversation, first);
    open(*cipher, conversation, second);

    // A relay flips one bit of the ciphertext.
    sealed_message changed = first;
    changed.ciphertext[0] ^= 0x01U;
    open(*cipher, conversation, changed);
    // A message replayed into another conversation.
    open(*cipher, other, second);
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls

  • A nonce is never repeated under one key: two messages under one key and one nonce reveal the XOR of their plaintexts and let an attacker forge tags for every later message (RFC 8439, section 4). With xchacha20_poly1305 draw 24 bytes at random per message; with chacha20_poly1305 count, a restart included, or draw at random within the limit above; with the original form, count.

  • The tag covers the ciphertext and the additional data, nothing else: what the message belongs to (a conversation, a user, a record’s id) goes in the additional data, or a message can be moved there unnoticed.

  • A failed open zeroes the data: keep the ciphertext if it is needed after a failure, and never act on a message before open succeeds.

Parts of this section, the limits, are adapted from libsodium’s documentation (jedisct1/libsodium-doc at 6d1ea27, ISC, LICENSE-LIBSODIUM-DOC.txt).

Secret boxes

A secret box is NaCl’s name for authenticated encryption under one secret key, with no additional data: the box hides the message and its tag proves it unchanged (NaCl; libsodium’s documentation). Its cipher is XSalsa20, Salsa20 with a 24-byte nonce (Extending the Salsa20 nonce), and its authenticator Poly1305. A program that stores records or files under one key, each with a nonce drawn at random, and a program that must read what libsodium’s crypto_secretbox wrote, use it.

ciphers::secretbox<> and ciphers::secretbox_xchacha20poly1305<>, in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/secretbox.hpp>, are ciphers::aead over libsodium’s crypto_secretbox and its XChaCha20 twin, crypto_secretbox_xchacha20poly1305, on libsodium, their default on every target: a 32-byte key, a 24-byte nonce safe to draw at random for every message, a 16-byte tag. They are made and used as the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEADs are (ChaCha20-Poly1305), with one difference: a secret box has no additional data, so their max_additional_data_size is 0 and seal and open refuse a non-empty one with invalid_input_size, after the nonce and the tag are checked and before the length. The nonce may lie in the data: libsodium reads it again after it writes the first bytes of the ciphertext, so it is copied first.
