Pitfalls.

  • The secret box’s tag covers the ciphertext alone: a field that travels in clear and must not change, a record’s id for instance, belongs in an AEAD’s additional data (ChaCha20-Poly1305), not beside a secret box.

  • A nonce is never repeated under one key: draw 24 bytes at random for every message, which never collide in practice.

Example. A file-sharing app seals each file in a secret box under a key drawn for that file, and sends the key to the recipient in a sealed box (Sealed boxes); the recipient opens the key, then the file, and a changed upload does not open:

// The sender: a key for this file alone, the file in a secret box under it, the key sealed to
// the recipient.
bool share(crypto::random_device& device, std::span<std::uint8_t const> recipient_public_key,
           std::string_view contents, upload& out) {
    crypto::secret<32> file_key;
    if (!device.fill(file_key.writable()) || !device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    auto box = secretbox<>::make(file_key.bytes());
    if (!box) {
        return false;
    }
    out.file.assign(contents.begin(), contents.end());
    auto const tag = box->seal(out.nonce, {}, out.file);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return sealed_box::seal(recipient_public_key, file_key.bytes(), out.sealed_key).has_value();
}
// The recipient: the file key out of the sealed box, then the file out of the secret box.
void receive(char const* who, std::span<std::uint8_t const> public_key,
             std::span<std::uint8_t const> secret_key, upload received) {
    crypto::secret<32> file_key;
    auto const key_opened =
        sealed_box::open(public_key, secret_key, received.sealed_key, file_key.writable());
    if (!key_opened) {
        std::string const reason = key_opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s: the file key refused: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    auto box = secretbox<>::make(file_key.bytes());
    if (!box) {
        return;
    }
    auto const opened = box->open(received.nonce, {}, received.file, received.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s: the file refused: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("%s read: %.*s\n", who, static_cast<int>(received.file.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(received.file.data()));
}
on the wire: 80 bytes of sealed key, 24 of nonce, 16 of tag, 25 of file
the recipient read: quarterly report, draft 3
the recipient, the upload changed: the file refused: the authentication tag does not match
another key pair: the file key refused: the authentication tag does not match

A file-sharing app: secret boxes and sealed boxes shows the whole program.

Parts of this section, the nonce’s size and its advice, are adapted from libsodium’s documentation (jedisct1/libsodium-doc at 6d1ea27, ISC, LICENSE-LIBSODIUM-DOC.txt).

The block cipher

A block cipher is a keyed permutation of fixed-size blocks: with the key, each 16-byte block maps to one other block and back; without it, the output looks random (Wikipedia; FIPS 197). It is the building block of every AES mode, GCM’s included, and not encryption by itself: applied to each block of a message alone, equal blocks give equal ciphertext, and the shape of the data shows through, the mode called ECB (Wikipedia).

aes128, aes192 and aes256, in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes.hpp>, are the AES block cipher with keys of 16, 24 and 32 bytes. They work in place on whole blocks: encrypt and decrypt take a span whose size is a multiple of block_size, 16, and give invalid_input_size for a partial block. Each is made with make(key_bytes), which gives invalid_key_size for a key of another size; an object moved from is wiped and empty, and returns invalid_state.

BearSSL

BearSSL exports AES only inside its modes, with no single-block class, so aes256<backends::bearssl> is a complete type, which gcm needs to name its cipher, but its make does not compile, and a static_assert says which backends to use (Every message, and its fix). aes256<> is the cipher of aes256_gcm, so it follows AES-GCM’s default backend, OpenSSL natively and BearSSL on WebAssembly, where aes256<>::make does not compile: a program that wants the block cipher there names aes256<backends::ctaes> and includes <webcpp/crypto/backends/ctaes.hpp>. ctaes is a constant-time bitsliced AES, the one Bitcoin Core ships (ctaes): the block cipher alone, which allocates nothing and wipes its key schedule. GCM is not built on it: webcpp writes no mode of its own on another library’s AES.

Example. A shop’s database hands out sequential order ids. In a URL they reveal how many orders the shop takes a day, and let anyone try the next customer’s order. One AES block turns each id into an opaque reference and back, and a forged reference decrypts to a block whose padding is not zero:

// The id goes big-endian in the first 8 bytes of a block; the other 8 stay zero.
std::uint64_t const order = 1234;
std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> block{};
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
    block[7 - i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(order >> (8U * i));
}
if (!cipher->encrypt(block)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("reference ");
for (std::uint8_t const byte : block) {
    std::printf("%02x", byte);
}
std::printf("\n");
auto const reference = block;

if (!cipher->decrypt(block) || !padding_is_zero(block)) {
    return 1;
}
std::uint64_t decoded = 0;
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
    decoded = (decoded << 8U) | block[i];
}
std::printf("order %llu\n", static_cast<unsigned long long>(decoded));
reference d2b566be92e4f77a5fd7b9bf4d484994
order 1234
forged reference refused

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/backends/ctaes.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
using cipher_type = crypto::ciphers::aes256<crypto::backends::ctaes>;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

bool padding_is_zero(std::span<std::uint8_t const, 16> block) {
    return std::ranges::all_of(block.last<8>(), [](std::uint8_t b) { return b == 0; });
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // A demonstration key, so that the output is the same on every run. A real program draws
    // it once from random_device and keeps it secret.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < key.size(); ++i) {
        key[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    auto cipher = cipher_type::make(key);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(key)));
    if (!cipher) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The id goes big-endian in the first 8 bytes of a block; the other 8 stay zero.
    std::uint64_t const order = 1234;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> block{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
        block[7 - i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(order >> (8U * i));
    }
    if (!cipher->encrypt(block)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("reference ");
    for (std::uint8_t const byte : block) {
        std::printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
    auto const reference = block;

    if (!cipher->decrypt(block) || !padding_is_zero(block)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::uint64_t decoded = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
        decoded = (decoded << 8U) | block[i];
    }
    std::printf("order %llu\n", static_cast<unsigned long long>(decoded));
    if (decoded != order) {
        return 1;
    }

    // A forged reference decrypts to a block whose padding is not zero.
    auto forged = reference;
    forged[0] ^= 1U;
    if (!cipher->decrypt(forged) || padding_is_zero(forged)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("forged reference refused\n");
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls.

  • Encrypting several blocks one by one is ECB, and leaks every repeated block: use AES-GCM for anything longer than one block.

  • An opaque reference hides the id; it does not authorise the request. Check that the order belongs to the user who asks for it.

Curves: webcpp::crypto::curves

An elliptic curve gives public-key cryptography with short keys: a secret key is a number, its public key a point of the curve computed from it, and going back from the point to the number is infeasible. On a curve a program can sign, so that anyone with the public key can check who wrote a message (Wikipedia), and agree on a key, so that two parties who only exchanged public keys share a secret (Wikipedia).

The namespace webcpp::crypto::curves holds three curves in this version, the three columns of the table below. The first is secp256k1 (SEC 2; Bitcoin Wiki), the curve of Bitcoin, Ethereum and Nostr (secp256k1). This version covers Bitcoin’s keys and signatures, Nostr’s event signatures (NIP-01) and the raw x-coordinate ECDH of its encrypted messages (NIP-44, Three forms of ECDH), and Ethereum’s ECDSA: recoverable signatures, the recovery of a signer’s public key from a signature, and the uncompressed key (Recoverable signatures). Its functions, by header:

  • secp256k1.hpp, the key pair and its signatures and ECDH: keypair::make, and the key pair’s xonly_public_key, public_key, public_key_uncompressed, sign_schnorr, sign_ecdsa, sign_recoverable, ecdh, ecdh_x, ecdh_point and tweak_xonly; verify_schnorr, verify_ecdsa, recover, parse_public_key, serialize_public_key, to_der, from_der, normalize_ecdsa and the x-only key’s tweak_xonly;

  • secp256k1/tweak.hpp, tweaks of whole keys, the arithmetic of BIP 32’s derivation and of watch-only wallets: seckey_tweak_add, seckey_tweak_mul, seckey_negate, pubkey_tweak_add, pubkey_tweak_mul, pubkey_negate and pubkey_combine (Tweaks, negation and combination);

  • secp256k1/formats.hpp, keys in the SPKI and PKCS#8 files that OpenSSL exchanges: encode_spki, decode_spki, encode_pkcs8 and decode_pkcs8 (Keys in files: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM);

  • secp256k1/ellswift.hpp, keys sent as random-looking bytes, BIP 324’s ElligatorSwift: ellswift_create, ellswift_encode, ellswift_decode and ellswift_xdh (ElligatorSwift: keys that look like noise);

  • secp256k1/musig.hpp, many signers’ keys and signatures aggregated into one, BIP 327’s MuSig2: key_aggregate, nonce_gen, nonce_aggregate, nonce_process, partial_sign, partial_signature_verify, partial_signature_aggregate, and the parse_ and serialize_ functions of what the signers send (MuSig2: many signers, one signature);

  • secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp, one reusable address whose payments look unrelated, BIP 352’s silent payments: create_outputs, create_label, create_labeled_spend_key, make_prevouts_summary and scan_outputs (Silent payments).

Ethereum’s v encoding of the recovery id, the hash it signs, its transactions and its addresses are a domain library’s, and so is BIP 32’s derivation, its HMAC-SHA-512 and its paths, which only adds a tweak computed there to a whole key (BIP 32). The second is Ed25519, RFC 8032’s signatures on edwards25519, with Ed25519ph for a message given in pieces (RFC 8032; Ed25519). The third is X25519, RFC 7748’s key agreement on Curve25519, the same curve in another form, with the conversion of an Ed25519 key to it (RFC 7748; X25519), and libsodium’s key exchange on it, crypto_kx (Key exchange: crypto_kx). A program chooses a curve for compatibility: a signature on one curve is checked only with that curve, and the curve of passkeys and TLS certificates, P-256, is another, which this version does not offer. Ed25519’s and X25519’s keys leave a program, and enter it, in the standard forms OpenSSL and WebCrypto use, SPKI and PKCS#8, as DER or PEM text (Key formats: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM).

The cause is Apple silicon’s DIT (data-independent timing), which wasmtime does not set (Apple, Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms: enable DIT for constant-time cryptographic operations): with DIT set in wasmtime’s main thread, an experiment and not the lane, the same case reads |t| 1.5 to 2.1; no branch on a secret was found in the WebAssembly or in wasmtime’s compiled code. The lane cannot set DIT from inside the WebAssembly, so it prints this value on wasip2 without judging it; the CI’s x86-64 run measures it next; not measured yet on wasip3, emscripten (Constant time)

Choose it for compatibility with

Bitcoin’s keys and signatures; Nostr’s event signatures (Nostr NIP-01, events signed with BIP 340 on secp256k1); Ethereum’s ECDSA verification with a known key; ECDH in the raw x-coordinate form of Nostr’s encrypted messages (Nostr NIP-44, encrypted payloads); Ethereum’s recoverable signatures and uncompressed keys (The Ethereum yellow paper, appendix F: ECDSA on secp256k1), the address hashing being a domain library’s; BIP 32’s tweaks of the full key, its derivation of the tweak being a domain library’s (BIP 32, hierarchical deterministic wallets); keys exchanged with OpenSSL as SPKI or PKCS#8 (RFC 5480, Elliptic Curve Cryptography Subject Public Key Information, RFC 5915, Elliptic Curve Private Key Structure), in DER or PEM (RFC 7468, textual encodings of PKIX, PKCS and CMS structures (PEM)); Bitcoin’s version 2 transport, whose keys are ElligatorSwift encodings (BIP 324, version 2 P2P encrypted transport protocol); MuSig2’s multisignatures (BIP 327, MuSig2 for BIP340-compatible multi-signatures); silent payments (BIP 352, Silent Payments), the addresses and transactions being a domain library’s

SSH, Tor and Solana keys and signatures, and any protocol that names RFC 8032’s Ed25519 or Ed25519ph; verification is strict (libsodium’s rules), which some lenient verifiers are not. Not Bitcoin, Ethereum or Nostr, whose keys are secp256k1’s

TLS 1.3’s and SSH’s key exchange, WireGuard, Signal; libsodium’s crypto_box keys, and the session keys of crypto_kx with kx_keypair (libsodium’s documentation, key exchange). The Ed25519 public key of a peer converts with curves::ed25519::to_x25519_public. A shared secret goes through a KDF before it keys a cipher. Every case of Wycheproof’s X25519 file is tested (Project Wycheproof, test vectors for cryptographic libraries)

secp256k1

<webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp> is secp256k1 on libsecp256k1 (/third_party//secp256k1), in the namespace webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1. It offers two signature schemes and one key agreement:

  • BIP 340 Schnorr signatures, 64 bytes over a message of any length, with a 32-byte x-only public key: Bitcoin’s Taproot and Nostr’s events (BIP 340; NIP-01; Wikipedia);

  • ECDSA signatures, 64 bytes over a 32-byte hash, with a 33-byte compressed public key: Bitcoin before Taproot and Ethereum (Wikipedia; Ethereum’s yellow paper). Each signature’s nonce is RFC 6979’s, derived from the key and the hash, so that no weak generator can leak the key (RFC 6979), and each is in low-S form. A signature is also made hedged, with the caller’s fresh randomness mixed into the nonce, or recoverable, with the id from which a reader finds the signer’s key (Recoverable signatures);

  • ECDH, a shared secret: ecdh gives libsecp256k1’s hashed form, the SHA-256 of the shared point in its 33-byte compressed encoding, one of three forms (Three forms of ECDH). It interoperates only with peers that hash the same way, such as another program on libsecp256k1’s default; ecdh_x gives the raw x coordinate that Nostr’s encrypted messages (NIP-44) take.

A keypair is made from a 32-byte secret key with make(secret), which allocates its signing context in the std::pmr::memory_resource it is given, and randomises it from random_device; crypto’s own code allocates nothing else (Allocation). The namespace’s functions, by header:

  • <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>: the key pair’s make, its public keys (xonly_public_key, public_key, public_key_uncompressed), its signatures (sign_schnorr, sign_ecdsa, hedged or not, and sign_recoverable), its ECDH (ecdh, ecdh_x, ecdh_point) and its tweak in place (tweak_xonly); verify_schnorr and verify_ecdsa, which check a signature with a public key alone; recover, which finds the key of a recoverable signature (Recoverable signatures); parse_public_key and serialize_public_key, which read and write a public_key (Public keys and their two forms); to_der, from_der (strict DER) and normalize_ecdsa, ECDSA’s DER and low-S forms; and tweak_xonly, the tweak of an x-only public key;

  • <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/tweak.hpp>: seckey_tweak_add, seckey_tweak_mul and seckey_negate, pubkey_tweak_add, pubkey_tweak_mul and pubkey_negate, and pubkey_combine with its combine_workspace_size: the tweaks, negation and combination of whole keys (Tweaks, negation and combination);

  • <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/formats.hpp>: encode_spki, decode_spki, encode_pkcs8 and decode_pkcs8, the keys’ SPKI and PKCS#8, which pem writes as PEM text (Keys in files: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM);

  • <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/ellswift.hpp>: ellswift_create, ellswift_encode, ellswift_decode and ellswift_xdh, keys sent as random-looking bytes (ElligatorSwift: keys that look like noise);

  • <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>, namespace musig: key_aggregate (and the aggregate key’s xonly_public_key, full_public_key, tweak_add and tweak_xonly_add), nonce_gen, nonce_aggregate, nonce_process, partial_sign, partial_signature_verify and partial_signature_aggregate, the parse_ and serialize_ functions of the public nonce, the aggregate nonce and the partial signature, and workspace_size: many signers’ one signature (MuSig2: many signers, one signature);

  • <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp>, namespace silent_payments: create_outputs, create_label, create_labeled_spend_key, make_prevouts_summary and scan_outputs, with send_workspace_size, summary_workspace_size and scan_workspace_size: one reusable address whose payments look unrelated (Silent payments).

Every function reads libsecp256k1’s canary, so that a program linked with another build of the library does not link.

Example. BIP 340’s first test vector, signed and verified; then the key pair tweaked and used again, its signature verified under the tweaked key:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

// Prints bytes in hex after a name, 32 bytes (64 digits) to a line, the lines after the first
// indented under the first, so that a long value stays readable on a narrow page.
void print(char const* name, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    int const indent = std::printf("%s ", name);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < bytes.size(); ++i) {
        if (i != 0 && i % 32 == 0) {
            std::printf("\n%*s", indent, "");
        }
        std::printf("%02x", bytes[i]);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// Signs message with key and checks the signature under the key's x-only public key.
bool sign_and_verify(secp256k1::keypair const& key, std::span<std::uint8_t const> message) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const aux{};
    auto const public_key = key.xonly_public_key();
    auto const signature = key.sign_schnorr(message, aux);
    if (!public_key || !signature) {
        return false;
    }
    print("public key", *public_key);
    print("signature ", *signature);
    return secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, *public_key).has_value();
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // BIP340's first test vector key, public on purpose; a real secret is drawn from
    // random_device.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
    secret.back() = 3;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const message{};
    auto key = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
    if (!key || !sign_and_verify(*key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tweak{};
    tweak.fill(0x01);
    if (!key->tweak_xonly(tweak) || !sign_and_verify(*key, message)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("verified\n");
    return 0;
}

A tweak is a primitive: crypto does not compute one. A protocol that defines a tweak (Bitcoin’s Taproot output key, for one) belongs to a domain library, which computes the tweak from its own hash and passes it here (A tweaked key: Taproot).

Pitfalls.

  • A secret key drawn from random_device is below the group order with overwhelming probability, but not always: make returns invalid_secret_key then, and the program draws again (Making and keeping a key).

  • Keep the secret key out of logs, crash reports and source control: the key pair wipes its copy, the program wipes its own.

  • BIP 340’s auxiliary randomness is fresh for each signature; a fixed value is safe only because the nonce also depends on the key and the message, and the examples use zeros only to print fixed signatures.

  • verify_ecdsa refuses a high-S signature, as libsecp256k1 does: normalize_ecdsa gives the low-S form of a signature from a signer that does not enforce it. A verifier that normalizes before verifying accepts both forms of a signature, so it must not rely on the signature’s bytes being unique (BIP 146).

Three forms of ECDH

Two users of a chat app who have never met want to talk without the server reading along. Each publishes a public key; with elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) each combines its own secret key with the other’s public key and both arrive at the same shared secret, which nobody who sees only the public keys can compute (Wikipedia). The shared secret is a point on the curve, the secret key of one side times the public key of the other; what a program takes of that point is a choice of the protocol, and a key pair gives the three that protocols use:

  • ecdh: the SHA-256 of the point’s compressed encoding, 32 bytes, libsecp256k1’s default (libsecp256k1). Two programs on webcpp, or one on libsecp256k1’s default, agree on it; it is the form of the chat session of Agreeing on a key in public.

  • ecdh_x: the point’s x coordinate, 32 bytes, unhashed. Nostr’s encrypted messages (NIP-44) and Wycheproof’s ECDH test vectors (Project Wycheproof, test vectors for cryptographic libraries) take this form; the protocol then hashes it its own way.

  • ecdh_point: the point itself, 65 bytes in SEC1’s uncompressed encoding (0x04, x, y; SEC 1, sections 2.3.3 and 2.3.4): both coordinates, of which the other two forms keep x alone.

Each is returned as a secret<N>, which wipes its bytes when it is destroyed or moved from: a program reads it with bytes() and makes no copy of its own to forget. Each refuses a moved-from key pair with invalid_state, and a peer key that is not a point of the curve, or not 33 bytes compressed or 65 bytes uncompressed with the prefix 04, with invalid_public_key. They are members of the key pair, whose backends are listed above.

Example. Two key pairs agree on the x coordinate, and a Nostr library’s first step follows: NIP-44’s conversation key, HKDF-extract (RFC 5869) of the x coordinate with the salt nip44-v2. The rest of NIP-44 (message keys, padding, the payload) is a domain library’s, not crypto’s:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/sha2.hpp>
#include <boost/system/result.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>
#include <type_traits>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace hash2 = boost::hash2;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

// Wipes an object of key-derived state, such as an HMAC whose inner and outer states hold the
// key: its bytes are all it is, so overwriting them leaves nothing of the key.
template <class T>
void wipe_object(T& object) {
    static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(&object, 1)));
}

std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes_of(std::string_view text) {
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-reinterpret-cast)
    return {reinterpret_cast<std::uint8_t const*>(text.data()), text.size()};
}

void print_hex(char const* label, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    std::printf("%s", label);
    for (std::uint8_t const octet : bytes) {
        std::printf("%02x", static_cast<unsigned>(octet));
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// NIP-44's conversation key: HKDF-extract (RFC 5869), an HMAC-SHA-256 keyed with the salt
// "nip44-v2" over the shared x coordinate. A NIP-44 library computes it; the message keys,
// the padding and the payload's format that follow are the protocol's too.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> conversation_key(crypto::secret<32> const& shared_x) {
    auto const salt = bytes_of("nip44-v2");
    hash2::hmac_sha2_256 extract(salt.data(), salt.size());
    extract.update(shared_x.bytes().data(), crypto::secret<32>::size());
    auto digest = extract.result();
    wipe_object(extract);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    std::span<std::uint8_t const> const digest_bytes(digest.data(), digest.size());
    std::ranges::copy(digest_bytes, key.begin());
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(digest.data(), digest.size())));
    return key;
}

boost::system::result<secp256k1::keypair> from_secret(std::uint8_t fill) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
    secret.fill(fill);
    auto made = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
    // The key pair keeps its own copy, which it wipes; this one goes now.
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
    return made;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Fixed secrets, so that the output is fixed. A real program draws its secret keys from
    // random_device, as wallet_key.cpp does.
    auto const alice = from_secret(0x11);
    auto const bob = from_secret(0x22);
    if (!alice || !bob) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const alice_public = alice->public_key();
    auto const bob_public = bob->public_key();
    if (!alice_public || !bob_public) {
        return 1;
    }
    // Each side combines its secret key with the other's public key: the same x coordinate,
    // a secret<32> that wipes itself.
    auto const alice_x = alice->ecdh_x(*bob_public);
    auto const bob_x = bob->ecdh_x(*alice_public);
    if (!alice_x || !bob_x || !crypto::equal(alice_x->bytes(), bob_x->bytes())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("shared x coordinates match\n");

    // A real program never prints a shared secret; this one does to show the fixed value.
    print_hex("x: ", alice_x->bytes());
    auto key = conversation_key(*alice_x);
    print_hex("conversation key (what a NIP-44 library derives): ", key);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(key)));
    return 0;
}
shared x coordinates match
x: 77e0510d5042e2f5e9e59c977b81eeed590cf7d20c1c51da451a8eaa9fdc45ff
conversation key (what a NIP-44 library derives): 2cbdf074f601178c24da3f829b504507a1f550f97d472af0f3f2cc59ab7757d1

Pitfalls.

  • The raw x coordinate is not a key: a Diffie-Hellman value is not uniformly random (RFC 5869, section 3.3). It is always below the field’s prime and always the x of a point, which not every 32-byte value is (SEC 1, sections 2.3.3 and 2.3.4), so its 256 bits hold less than 256 bits of entropy. A protocol’s key derivation function (HKDF in NIP-44) turns it into keys. Used directly as an AES key, it is the same key in every protocol that uses the same two key pairs that way: a key that leaks from one leaks from all of them.

  • Two programs must agree on the form. One that takes ecdh and one that takes ecdh_x derive different keys from the same key pairs, and fail silently: every message is refused as forged, with nothing pointing at the cause. Read the protocol’s specification for the form it names.

  • Never use one shared secret as two keys, one per direction or one for encryption and one for authentication: derive one key per purpose with the KDF, each with its own label (Agreeing on a key in public).

Public keys and their two forms

A public key arrives as bytes: from a peer, from a file, from a transaction. A program that checks many signatures with one key, or compares keys, parses it once into a public_key, a point of the curve that the type guarantees, and uses that from then on. The check matters: a peer’s key that is not on the curve is how invalid-curve attacks begin, in which a key off the curve, combined with a secret key, leaks that secret bit by bit, which is why the holder of a long-lived secret key validates the other side’s public key (Wikipedia). parse_public_key makes the only public_key there is, so a program that holds one holds a valid point.

A point is written in one of two forms (SEC 1, sections 2.3.3 and 2.3.4):

  • compressed, 33 bytes: 02 or 03 by the parity of y, then x. Bitcoin writes keys this way, and its SegWit outputs take no other form by default (BIP 143);

  • uncompressed, 65 bytes: 04, x, y. Ethereum’s keys are x and y, 64 bytes, the uncompressed form without its prefix (Ethereum’s yellow paper).

serialize_public_key writes either (point_form::compressed, the default, or point_form::uncompressed); a key pair gives its own key in both forms, public_key and public_key_uncompressed. Two public_key values compare with ==, and order with <=> as their compressed encodings do, the order MuSig2’s key sorting uses (BIP 327). A public_key holds nothing secret and is copied freely.

Pitfalls.

  • X9.62’s hybrid form, prefix 06 or 07 then x and y, is refused with invalid_public_key, though libsecp256k1 reads it: SEC 1 defines only the two forms above and refuses every other prefix (SEC 1, section 2.3.4), so a key webcpp takes is one every SEC 1 parser takes, and one key has one encoding of each form.

  • A key compared as bytes, rather than parsed, differs between its two forms: the same key compressed and uncompressed are different bytes. Parse both and compare the public_key values.

  • Ethereum’s 64-byte key is the uncompressed form without its 04: add the prefix before parse_public_key, and drop it after serialize_public_key.

Recoverable signatures

Ethereum names an account by the hash of its public key, and a transaction carries no key: only the signature, from which a node recovers the key that made it (Ethereum’s yellow paper, appendix F). An ECDSA signature fits up to four keys, and the recovery id, 0 to 3, names the one that made it (SEC 1, section 4.1.6). sign_recoverable writes 65 bytes, r, s and the id, with the same r and s as sign_ecdsa, and recover returns the public_key from those 65 bytes and the hash. It refuses with invalid_signature an id above 3, an r or an s not below the group order, and a signature from which no key is recovered.

Example. A wallet signs a message’s hash; a reader that holds no key of the wallet’s recovers the signer’s key and compares it with the key the wallet published; a changed message recovers a different key:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/sha2.hpp>
#include <boost/system/result.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

// The message's SHA-256. Ethereum's own message hash is EIP-191's (a prefix, then Keccak-256),
// which a domain library computes; crypto signs and recovers whatever 32-byte hash it is given.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> sha256(std::string_view text) {
    boost::hash2::sha2_256 hash;
    hash.update(text.data(), text.size());
    auto const digest = hash.result();
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> out{};
    std::copy_n(digest.data(), out.size(), out.begin());
    return out;
}

boost::system::result<secp256k1::keypair> generate_key() {
    crypto::random_device device;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
    for (;;) {
        auto const filled = device.fill(secret);
        if (!filled) {
            return filled.error();
        }
        auto key = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
        if (key || key.error() != crypto::error::invalid_secret_key) {
            // The key pair keeps its own copy, which it wipes; this one goes now.
            wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
            return key;
        }
    }
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // The wallet publishes its key once, uncompressed as Ethereum writes it, and signs.
    auto wallet = generate_key();
    if (!wallet) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const published = wallet->public_key_uncompressed();
    std::string message = "pay 10 to bob";
    auto const signature = wallet->sign_recoverable(sha256(message));
    if (!published || !signature) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The reader holds no key of the wallet's: it parses the published key once, recovers the
    // signer's key from the 65-byte signature and the hash, and compares the two.
    auto const expected = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*published);
    auto const signer = secp256k1::recover(*signature, sha256(message));
    if (!expected || !signer || *signer != *expected) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("recovered the wallet's key\n");

    // A changed message still recovers a key, but not the wallet's.
    message = "pay 99 to bob";
    auto const other = secp256k1::recover(*signature, sha256(message));
    if (other && *other == *expected) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("a changed message names another signer\n");
    return 0;
}
recovered the wallet's key
a changed message names another signer

sign_ecdsa also has a hedged form, which takes 32 more bytes, drawn from random_device and new for each signature, and mixes them into RFC 6979’s nonce, as the RFC’s variant with additional data allows (RFC 6979, section 3.6) and libsecp256k1’s ndata takes (libsecp256k1). The signature verifies as any other.

Pitfalls.

  • Recovery always yields some key for almost every signature and hash, a forged one included: a program that trusts the recovered key alone accepts anything. Compare it with the key expected, as the example does, or with the account the key’s hash must name.

  • Ethereum’s v is the recovery id plus 27, or plus an offset of the chain’s (Ethereum’s yellow paper, appendix F): passing v as the id makes recover refuse it. That encoding, and the message hash Ethereum signs, are a domain library’s.

  • The hedged form gives a different signature each time, so a test that compares signatures with fixed bytes uses the unhedged form. Use the hedged form where the signer runs on hardware an attacker can fault or observe: the nonce then no longer depends on the key and the hash alone, so two signings of one hash do not repeat the same computation. Never reuse the 32 bytes: fixed extra data leaves the signature deterministic, as plain RFC 6979.

Tweaks, negation and combination

A wallet app gives every payment a new address, so that strangers cannot link the payments to one person, yet keeps a single backup. A shop’s web server that hands out those addresses holds no secret key at all: if it is broken into, the thief sees payments but cannot spend them (BIP 32). Both rest on one property of the curve: adding a number t, the tweak, to a secret key d adds t times the generator G to its public key, so that the public key of d + t is P + tG. The server computes P + tG from the public key P alone; the signing device computes d + t from the secret; and both arrive at the same key pair without the server ever holding a secret.

<webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/tweak.hpp> offers that arithmetic on whole keys, each function a call of libsecp256k1:

  • seckey_tweak_add and seckey_tweak_mul: a secret key plus or times a 32-byte tweak, modulo the group order, returned as a secret<32>; pubkey_tweak_add and pubkey_tweak_mul: P + tG and tP, the public keys of those two secrets;

  • seckey_negate and pubkey_negate: the negation of either, n - d and -P;

  • pubkey_combine: the sum of public keys, the public key of the sum of their secrets. libsecp256k1 takes an array of pointers to the keys, which crypto builds in a workspace the caller lends, of combine_workspace_size(n) bytes, so that nothing is allocated; the workspace is wiped before the call returns.

A secret key that is zero or not below the group order is refused with invalid_secret_key before the tweak runs; so are a tweak not below the order, a zero multiplier, and a result that is no key (a zero secret, the point at infinity). pubkey_combine refuses no keys and a short workspace with invalid_input_size, and a sum at infinity with invalid_public_key.

Example. A watch-only wallet: the server adds a payment’s tweak to the wallet’s public key, the device adds the same tweak to the secret key, and a signature of the device’s tweaked key pair verifies under the server’s key. The tweak is an HMAC of the public key and the payment’s number under a chain code both sides share, as BIP 32 extends each key with a chain code so that child keys do not depend on the key alone; BIP 32’s own derivation, with HMAC-SHA-512, is a domain library’s (BIP 32):

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/tweak.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/sha2.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <type_traits>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace hash2 = boost::hash2;

namespace {

// Overwrites an object's bytes through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a
// dead store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
template <class T>
void wipe(T& object) {
    static_assert(std::is_trivially_destructible_v<T>, "an object whose bytes are all its state");
    auto* const data = reinterpret_cast<unsigned char volatile*>(&object);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(T); ++i) {
        data[i] = 0;
    }
}

// 32 secret bytes the program holds, wiped when the scope ends, on every path, an early return's
// included.
struct wiped_bytes {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};

    wiped_bytes() = default;
    wiped_bytes(wiped_bytes const&) = delete;
    wiped_bytes& operator=(wiped_bytes const&) = delete;

    ~wiped_bytes() { wipe(bytes); }
};

// The tweak of payment `number`: HMAC-SHA-256 under the chain code of the compressed public key
// and the number, written into `tweak`. Both sides compute it; an outsider without the chain
// code cannot, and so cannot tell that two payment keys belong to one wallet. The HMAC's state,
// keyed by the chain code, and its digest, the tweak itself, are wiped before it returns.
void payment_tweak(std::span<std::uint8_t const, 32> chain_code,
                   std::span<std::uint8_t const, 33> public_key, std::uint32_t number,
                   wiped_bytes& tweak) {
    hash2::hmac_sha2_256 mac(chain_code.data(), chain_code.size());
    mac.update(public_key.data(), public_key.size());
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 4> const index{
        static_cast<std::uint8_t>(number >> 24U),
        static_cast<std::uint8_t>(number >> 16U),
        static_cast<std::uint8_t>(number >> 8U),
        static_cast<std::uint8_t>(number),
    };
    mac.update(index.data(), index.size());
    auto digest = mac.result();
    std::copy_n(digest.data(), tweak.bytes.size(), tweak.bytes.begin());
    wipe(digest);
    wipe(mac);
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // The device's secret and the chain code, drawn once; the device keeps both, the server
    // gets the chain code and the public key.
    crypto::random_device device;
    wiped_bytes secret;
    wiped_bytes chain_code;
    if (!device.fill(secret.bytes) || !device.fill(chain_code.bytes)) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const wallet = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret.bytes);
    if (!wallet) {
        // A secret not below the group order: negligible, and a real wallet draws again.
        return 1;
    }
    auto const wallet_public = wallet->public_key();
    if (!wallet_public) {
        return 1;
    }
    // The tweak and the tweaked secret give back the secret: the tweak is wiped too.
    wiped_bytes tweak;
    payment_tweak(chain_code.bytes, *wallet_public, 7, tweak);

    // The server: the wallet's public key plus the tweak, with no secret anywhere.
    auto const parsed = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*wallet_public);
    if (!parsed) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const watched = secp256k1::pubkey_tweak_add(*parsed, tweak.bytes);

    // The device: the secret key plus the same tweak, a secret<32> it makes a key pair of.
    auto const tweaked_secret = secp256k1::seckey_tweak_add(secret.bytes, tweak.bytes);
    if (!watched || !tweaked_secret) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const payment_key = secp256k1::keypair::make(tweaked_secret->bytes());
    if (!payment_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const payment_public = payment_key->public_key();
    if (!payment_public || secp256k1::serialize_public_key(*watched) != *payment_public) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("tweaked keys match\n");

    // The device signs a spend with the payment's key pair; the server verifies under the
    // x-only form of the key it derived alone (the compressed key without its prefix byte).
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const message{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> aux{};
    if (!device.fill(aux)) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const signature = payment_key->sign_schnorr(message, aux);
    auto const watched_bytes = secp256k1::serialize_public_key(*watched);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> xonly{};
    std::copy_n(watched_bytes.begin() + 1, xonly.size(), xonly.begin());
    if (!signature || !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, xonly)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("signature verifies under the tweaked public key\n");
    return 0;
}
tweaked keys match
signature verifies under the tweaked public key

Pitfalls.

  • A tweak computed from public data alone (the public key and a counter) links every derived key to the wallet: anyone who sees the public key computes the same tweaks and recognises each payment. Mix in a value only the two sides hold, as BIP 32’s chain code is (BIP 32).

  • A tweaked secret is a secret, which is why it is returned as a secret<32>: whoever knows the tweak and the tweaked secret key computes the original. With BIP 32’s public derivation, one leaked child secret key and the parent’s extended public key give away the parent’s secret key, and with it every key of the wallet (BIP 32).

  • The sum of keys others choose is not a multisignature. A participant who picks its key after seeing yours can choose its own key minus yours, and the sum is then its key alone, which it signs for without you. MuSig2 weighs each key with a coefficient hashed from all the keys, so that no participant can cancel another’s (BIP 327).

Keys in files: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM

A server’s key lives in a configuration file, a peer’s public key arrives in a certificate or a handshake, and other tools, OpenSSL among them, must read both. Two DER structures carry them. SPKI, SubjectPublicKeyInfo, is a public key with the name of its algorithm and curve (RFC 5480); PKCS#8 is a private key with the same name (RFC 5208), which for an elliptic curve holds RFC 5915’s ECPrivateKey: the secret, and optionally the curve and the public key (RFC 5915).

<webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/formats.hpp> writes and reads them:

  • encode_spki writes the SPKI of a public_key with the secp256k1 OID, its point compressed, 56 bytes (the default), or uncompressed, 88 bytes, into a buffer of at least max_spki_size bytes; decode_spki reads either back;

  • encode_pkcs8 writes a key pair’s PKCS#8, 135 bytes, into a buffer of at least max_pkcs8_size: version 0, and an ECPrivateKey of version 1 with the uncompressed public key and no curve inside it, which is the form OpenSSL writes for a key in its default uncompressed form: OpenSSL’s point form is uncompressed unless a program sets it, and it includes the public key when it encodes a private key unless told not to (OpenSSL’s EVP_PKEY-EC); decode_pkcs8 reads it into a key pair, made as keypair::make makes one.

The decoders are strict: they accept exactly the bytes the encoders write, and refuse anything else with invalid_encoding. The point must be on the curve, the secret below the group order, and the public key inside a PKCS#8 the secret’s own: decode_pkcs8 makes the key pair, encodes it again and compares the whole input. The encoders refuse a short buffer with invalid_input_size and a moved-from key pair with invalid_state, and write nothing then. The tests read OpenSSL’s keys and give OpenSSL webcpp’s, natively and on WASI, and under Emscripten round-trip every encoding through node’s crypto module.

A configuration file, a terminal or a form carries text, not DER. PEM is the DER in base64 between a -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- or -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY----- line and its -----END line (RFC 7468), the form OpenSSL’s -pubout and genpkey write. pem::armour and pem::unarmour (<webcpp/crypto/pem.hpp>, Key formats: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM) write and read it around these functions’ bytes, with the labels pem::public_key_label and pem::private_key_label, as strictly as the decoders read DER: another label, lines of another length than 64 or a carriage return are invalid_encoding. PEM needs libsodium’s target, whose base64 runs in a time that does not depend on the bytes, those of a private key included: a program that writes or reads PEM links /webcpp/crypto//pem-default (or /third_party//sodium) beside /third_party//secp256k1. The tests compare the text that pem::armour writes with that of OpenSSL’s PEM_write_bio_PUBKEY and PEM_write_bio_PrivateKey, character for character.

Example. A server’s key pair from the fixed secret 0x11 repeated: its public key written as PEM SPKI for a configuration file and read back, and its key pair written as PEM PKCS#8 for its own key file, never printed, and read back:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/formats.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/pem.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace pem = webcpp::crypto::pem;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;

namespace {

// The public key as PEM SPKI, compressed, printed as the configuration file holds it, and read
// back from that text: the same key.
bool public_key_to_pem(secp256k1::public_key const& key) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, secp256k1::max_spki_size> spki{};
    auto const size = secp256k1::encode_spki(key, spki);
    if (!size) {
        return false;
    }
    std::array<char, pem::armoured_size(pem::public_key_label.size(), secp256k1::max_spki_size)>
        text{};
    auto const written = pem::armour(pem::public_key_label, std::span(spki).first(*size), text);
    if (!written) {
        return false;
    }
    std::string_view const config(text.data(), *written);
    std::printf("%.*s", static_cast<int>(config.size()), config.data());

    std::array<std::uint8_t, secp256k1::max_spki_size> read{};
    auto const read_size = pem::unarmour(pem::public_key_label, config, read);
    if (!read_size) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const back = secp256k1::decode_spki(std::span(read).first(*read_size));
    return back && *back == key;
}

// The key pair as PEM PKCS#8, which holds the secret: the DER and the text are kept in
// secret<N>, which wipes itself, the text as its bytes' characters. Read back, it is a key pair
// of the same public key.
bool key_pair_to_pem(secp256k1::keypair const& key_pair) {
    crypto::secret<secp256k1::max_pkcs8_size> pkcs8;
    auto const size = secp256k1::encode_pkcs8(key_pair, pkcs8.writable());
    if (!size) {
        return false;
    }
    constexpr std::size_t file_size =
        pem::armoured_size(pem::private_key_label.size(), secp256k1::max_pkcs8_size);
    crypto::secret<file_size> file;
    std::span<char> const text(reinterpret_cast<char*>(file.writable().data()), file_size);
    auto const written = pem::armour(pem::private_key_label, pkcs8.bytes().first(*size), text);
    if (!written) {
        return false;
    }

    crypto::secret<secp256k1::max_pkcs8_size> read;
    auto const read_size = pem::unarmour(pem::private_key_label,
                                         std::string_view(text.data(), *written), read.writable());
    if (!read_size) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const back = secp256k1::decode_pkcs8(read.bytes().first(*read_size));
    if (!back) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const back_key = back->public_key();
    auto const original_key = key_pair.public_key();
    return back_key && original_key && *back_key == *original_key;
}

// The server's files written and read back.
bool store_and_read(secp256k1::keypair const& key_pair) {
    auto const encoded = key_pair.public_key();
    if (!encoded) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*encoded);
    return key && public_key_to_pem(*key) && key_pair_to_pem(key_pair);
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret_key{};
    secret_key.fill(0x11);
    auto const key_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret_key);
    if (!key_pair || !store_and_read(*key_pair)) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("read back: same key\n");
    return 0;
}
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MDYwEAYHKoZIzj0CAQYFK4EEAAoDIgADTzVb3LfMCvco7zzOuWFdkGhLtbLKX4Wa
sPC3BAdYcao=
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----
read back: same key

Pitfalls.

  • A lenient parser gives one key many encodings, and lets a file say two things at once. RFC 5915 makes the curve and the public key optional inside ECPrivateKey (RFC 5915), so a PKCS#8 can carry a public key that is not its secret’s; a program that shows or checks that key, rather than the one the secret gives, trusts the wrong key. decode_pkcs8 refuses such a file.

  • X9.62’s hybrid point form, prefix 06 or 07, is refused: RFC 5480 forbids it in an SPKI (RFC 5480).

  • OpenSSL keeps a key’s point form through its DER and PEM encodings (OpenSSL’s EVP_PKEY-EC), so a key set to the compressed form carries its compressed point inside the PKCS#8 too, 102 bytes, which decode_pkcs8 refuses: export the key in OpenSSL’s default uncompressed form, and choose the SPKI’s form when writing it.

  • The PKCS#8 these functions write holds the secret key in clear, and so does its PEM text: base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Keep both where only the program reads them, out of source control, or seal them at rest (Making and keeping a key), and wipe the buffers when done, as secret<N> does.

ElligatorSwift: keys that look like noise

A peer-to-peer program, a Bitcoin node or a messenger, opens connections that a censor or a middlebox on the path may want to block or throttle. Such a box recognises a protocol by its first bytes, and a handshake that starts with a public key is easy to spot: a compressed key starts with 02 or 03, and the 32 bytes after it are always the x coordinate of a point of the curve, which only about half of all random strings are. BIP 324 sends each peer’s key instead as 64 bytes that cannot be told from random ones, so that the first bytes of the connection look like noise (BIP 324).

ElligatorSwift is the encoding that makes this work. It maps every string of 64 bytes to a point of the curve, and each point has many such strings; an encoding drawn at random among those of a key is uniform among all 64-byte strings, so a key sent this way looks like any other random bytes (Chavez-Saab, Rodríguez-Henríquez and Tibouchi, SwiftEC, 2022). <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/ellswift.hpp> offers libsecp256k1’s functions:

  • ellswift_create makes the encoding of a key pair’s own public key from its secret and 32 bytes of fresh randomness, so that the key is never computed apart; ellswift_encode encodes any public_key;

  • ellswift_decode returns the public_key of any 64 bytes: it never fails;

  • ellswift_xdh is the key exchange: the x coordinate of the shared point, hashed with both encodings as BIP 324 hashes it, a tagged SHA-256, into a secret<32>. It takes the initiator’s encoding, then the responder’s, and which of the two the key pair is (ellswift_party).

A moved-from key pair is refused with invalid_state. The tests check BIP 324’s own vectors: every encoding of its decoding list, and the shared secret of each of its packet vectors.

Example. Two peers each send the 64 bytes ellswift_create makes; each message decodes to its sender’s key, and the two shared secrets agree:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/ellswift.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Each peer's key pair and the randomness of its encoding (random_device in a real program).
    auto const initiator = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x11));
    auto const responder = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x22));
    if (!initiator || !responder) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Each peer sends the 64 bytes ellswift_create makes from its key pair.
    auto const initiator_message = secp256k1::ellswift_create(*initiator, repeated(0x33));
    auto const responder_message = secp256k1::ellswift_create(*responder, repeated(0x44));
    if (!initiator_message || !responder_message) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Each message decodes to its sender's public key; any 64 bytes decode to some key.
    auto const initiator_key = initiator->public_key();
    auto const responder_key = responder->public_key();
    if (!initiator_key || !responder_key ||
        secp256k1::serialize_public_key(secp256k1::ellswift_decode(*initiator_message)) !=
            *initiator_key ||
        secp256k1::serialize_public_key(secp256k1::ellswift_decode(*responder_message)) !=
            *responder_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("each 64-byte message decodes to its sender's key\n");

    // Both pass the two messages in the same order, the initiator's first, and name their own
    // side; the shared secret is the input of the protocol's key schedule, not a key itself.
    auto const initiator_secret = secp256k1::ellswift_xdh(
        *initiator, *initiator_message, *responder_message, secp256k1::ellswift_party::initiator);
    auto const responder_secret = secp256k1::ellswift_xdh(
        *responder, *initiator_message, *responder_message, secp256k1::ellswift_party::responder);
    if (!initiator_secret || !responder_secret ||
        !crypto::equal(initiator_secret->bytes(), responder_secret->bytes())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("initiator and responder agree\n");
    return 0;
}
each 64-byte message decodes to its sender's key
initiator and responder agree

The messages carry no recognisable prefix, unlike a compressed key’s 02 or 03 (BIP 324). That hides that a key exchange happens, not who takes part: the addresses of both peers stay visible to whoever watches the connection.

Pitfalls.

  • Draw fresh randomness for every encoding. The same key with the same randomness gives the same 64 bytes, so two connections of one node, or one key reused, are linked by anyone who sees both; with fresh randomness each encoding is new.

  • The hash binds both encodings in a fixed order, the initiator’s first. A side that passes them in its own order, ours then theirs, or names the wrong party, computes a different secret, and the connection fails with nothing pointing at the cause.

  • The shared secret is the input of the protocol’s key schedule, never a key by itself: BIP 324 derives its session’s keys from it with HKDF (BIP 324), and that schedule, its packets and its garbage terminators are a domain library’s.

MuSig2: many signers, one signature

Some coins should move only when several parties agree: a company’s treasury that two officers approve, a Lightning channel whose two peers both sign each update, a wallet split across a phone and a laptop so that a thief who takes one device takes nothing. MuSig2 lets those signers aggregate their public keys into one key and their signatures into one BIP 340 signature under it. On the chain the key and the signature look like any single signer’s: they cost no more and tell no one that several parties hold the coins (BIP 327).

It works in two rounds (Nick, Ruffing and Seurin, MuSig2, CRYPTO 2021). First every signer makes a nonce and sends its public half to the others, before the message need be known; then, with every public nonce in, each signs its part of the message, and the parts add up to the signature. <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>, namespace curves::secp256k1::musig, offers libsecp256k1’s functions:

  • key_aggregate aggregates the signers’ keys, in the order given, into an aggregate_key; sort them first with std::ranges::sort, since the order of public_key is BIP 327’s KeySort. Its xonly_public_key is the key the signature verifies under; tweak_add and tweak_xonly_add tweak it as a protocol asks;

  • nonce_gen makes one signer’s nonce for one signature from its key pair, its randomness drawn inside: a secret_nonce to keep and a public_nonce to send;

  • nonce_aggregate sums the public nonces, and nonce_process makes the session of the 32-byte message;

  • partial_sign signs this signer’s part, consuming its secret nonce; partial_signature_verify checks one signer’s part, and partial_signature_aggregate adds the parts into 64 bytes that verify_schnorr checks;

  • parse_public_nonce, parse_aggregate_nonce and parse_partial_signature read what the other signers send, and the serialize_ functions write it.

The functions over many keys, nonces or parts take a workspace of workspace_size(n) bytes for libsecp256k1’s array of pointers, so that nothing is allocated, and wipe it before they return; no items or a short workspace is invalid_input_size. A nonce or a partial signature of the wrong length is invalid_input_size too, and one that does not parse is invalid_point or invalid_signature, a tweak out of range invalid_secret_key, and a moved-from key pair or a used nonce invalid_state. The tests check BIP 327’s own vectors, those that need no secret nonce of the vector’s: a secret_nonce exists only from nonce_gen, and libsecp256k1’s own tests, run in the c-suites lane, check the rest.
