Example. A phone and a laptop hold the two halves of a wallet. They aggregate their keys, exchange public nonces, each signs its part, and the signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature under the wallet’s one key:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace musig = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::musig;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Each device's key pair; each sends the other its public key.
    auto const phone = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x11));
    auto const laptop = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x22));
    if (!phone || !laptop) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*phone->public_key());
    auto const laptop_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*laptop->public_key());
    if (!phone_key || !laptop_key) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Both sort the keys (BIP 327's KeySort) and aggregate them: the same key on both devices.
    // The workspace holds libsecp256k1's array of pointers; nothing is allocated.
    std::array<secp256k1::public_key, 2> keys{*phone_key, *laptop_key};
    std::ranges::sort(keys);
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, musig::workspace_size(2)> space{};
    auto const wallet_key = musig::key_aggregate(keys, space);
    if (!wallet_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("aggregate key made from %zu signers\n", keys.size());

    // The spend both approve: the transaction's 32-byte hash, as a domain library computes it.
    auto const message = repeated(0x5a);

    // Round one: each device makes a nonce for this signature and sends its public half.
    auto phone_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*phone, *wallet_key, message);
    auto laptop_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*laptop, *wallet_key, message);
    if (!phone_nonce || !laptop_nonce) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Once both public nonces are in, each device computes the same session.
    std::array<musig::public_nonce, 2> const nonces{
        phone_nonce->public_part,
        laptop_nonce->public_part,
    };
    auto const nonce_sum = musig::nonce_aggregate(nonces, space);
    if (!nonce_sum) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const signing_session = musig::nonce_process(*nonce_sum, message, *wallet_key);
    if (!signing_session) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Round two: each signs its part, which consumes its secret nonce; the other checks it.
    auto const phone_part = musig::partial_sign(*phone, std::move(phone_nonce->secret_part),
                                                *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    auto const laptop_part = musig::partial_sign(*laptop, std::move(laptop_nonce->secret_part),
                                                 *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    if (!phone_part || !laptop_part ||
        !musig::partial_signature_verify(*phone_part, nonces[0], *phone_key, *wallet_key,
                                         *signing_session) ||
        !musig::partial_signature_verify(*laptop_part, nonces[1], *laptop_key, *wallet_key,
                                         *signing_session)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("both partial signatures verify\n");

    // The parts add up to one BIP 340 signature under the wallet's one x-only key.
    std::array<musig::partial_signature, 2> const parts{*phone_part, *laptop_part};
    auto const signature = musig::partial_signature_aggregate(*signing_session, parts, space);
    if (!signature ||
        !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, wallet_key->xonly_public_key())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the aggregate signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature\n");
    return 0;
}
aggregate key made from 2 signers
both partial signatures verify
the aggregate signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature

Example. The same wallet with its devices apart. Every public piece crosses the network as bytes: each public nonce in 66, the aggregate nonce a coordinator sums in 66, each partial signature in 32. The coordinator, which holds no secret, parses each part and checks it with partial_signature_verify before it adds the parts, so that a part damaged on the way is refused by name:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <boost/system/result.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <utility>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace musig = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::musig;

namespace {

using public_nonce_bytes = std::array<std::uint8_t, musig::public_nonce_size>;
using aggregate_nonce_bytes = std::array<std::uint8_t, musig::aggregate_nonce_size>;
using partial_signature_bytes = std::array<std::uint8_t, musig::partial_signature_size>;

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

// The wallet's key, which each party aggregates from the two public keys it received: sorted
// (BIP 327's KeySort), it is the same key on every party.
std::optional<musig::aggregate_key> wallet_key_of(secp256k1::public_key const& first,
                                                  secp256k1::public_key const& second) {
    std::array<secp256k1::public_key, 2> keys{first, second};
    std::ranges::sort(keys);
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, musig::workspace_size(2)> space{};
    auto aggregated = musig::key_aggregate(keys, space);
    if (!aggregated) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return *aggregated;
}

// The coordinator's checks on what arrived: each part parsed from its 32 bytes, then checked
// against its signer's public nonce and key; the first refusal is returned.
boost::system::result<musig::partial_signature> received_part(
    partial_signature_bytes const& wire, musig::public_nonce const& signer_nonce,
    secp256k1::public_key const& signer_key, musig::aggregate_key const& wallet_key,
    musig::session const& signing_session) {
    auto part = musig::parse_partial_signature(wire);
    if (!part) {
        return part.error();
    }
    auto const checked = musig::partial_signature_verify(*part, signer_nonce, signer_key,
                                                         wallet_key, signing_session);
    if (!checked) {
        return checked.error();
    }
    return part;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Each device's key pair; each publishes its public key, which every party parses.
    auto const phone = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x11));
    auto const laptop = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x22));
    if (!phone || !laptop) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*phone->public_key());
    auto const laptop_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*laptop->public_key());
    if (!phone_key || !laptop_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const wallet_key = wallet_key_of(*phone_key, *laptop_key);
    if (!wallet_key) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The spend both approve: the transaction's 32-byte hash, as a domain library computes it.
    auto const message = repeated(0x5a);

    // Round one, on each device: a nonce for this signature, its public half sent as bytes.
    auto phone_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*phone, *wallet_key, message);
    auto laptop_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*laptop, *wallet_key, message);
    if (!phone_nonce || !laptop_nonce) {
        return 1;
    }
    public_nonce_bytes const phone_nonce_wire =
        musig::serialize_public_nonce(phone_nonce->public_part);
    public_nonce_bytes const laptop_nonce_wire =
        musig::serialize_public_nonce(laptop_nonce->public_part);
    std::printf("each device sends its public nonce: %zu bytes\n", phone_nonce_wire.size());

    // The coordinator parses both public nonces, sums them and sends the sum back as bytes.
    auto const phone_nonce_in = musig::parse_public_nonce(phone_nonce_wire);
    auto const laptop_nonce_in = musig::parse_public_nonce(laptop_nonce_wire);
    if (!phone_nonce_in || !laptop_nonce_in) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<musig::public_nonce, 2> const nonces{*phone_nonce_in, *laptop_nonce_in};
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, musig::workspace_size(2)> space{};
    auto const nonce_sum = musig::nonce_aggregate(nonces, space);
    if (!nonce_sum) {
        return 1;
    }
    aggregate_nonce_bytes const nonce_sum_wire = musig::serialize_aggregate_nonce(*nonce_sum);
    std::printf("the coordinator sends the aggregate nonce: %zu bytes\n", nonce_sum_wire.size());

    // Round two, on each device: the aggregate nonce parsed, the session made (the same on both,
    // so made once here), the part signed (which consumes the secret nonce) and sent as bytes.
    auto const nonce_sum_in = musig::parse_aggregate_nonce(nonce_sum_wire);
    if (!nonce_sum_in) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const device_session = musig::nonce_process(*nonce_sum_in, message, *wallet_key);
    if (!device_session) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_part = musig::partial_sign(*phone, std::move(phone_nonce->secret_part),
                                                *wallet_key, *device_session);
    auto const laptop_part = musig::partial_sign(*laptop, std::move(laptop_nonce->secret_part),
                                                 *wallet_key, *device_session);
    if (!phone_part || !laptop_part) {
        return 1;
    }
    partial_signature_bytes const phone_part_wire = musig::serialize_partial_signature(*phone_part);
    partial_signature_bytes const laptop_part_wire =
        musig::serialize_partial_signature(*laptop_part);
    std::printf("each device sends its partial signature: %zu bytes\n", phone_part_wire.size());

    // The coordinator makes the same session from the nonce sum it sent, and checks each part
    // before it adds them.
    auto const signing_session = musig::nonce_process(*nonce_sum, message, *wallet_key);
    if (!signing_session) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_part_in =
        received_part(phone_part_wire, *phone_nonce_in, *phone_key, *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    auto const laptop_part_in = received_part(laptop_part_wire, *laptop_nonce_in, *laptop_key,
                                              *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    if (!phone_part_in || !laptop_part_in) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("both partial signatures parse and verify\n");

    // The same check refuses the laptop's part with one byte flipped on the way.
    partial_signature_bytes damaged_wire = laptop_part_wire;
    damaged_wire.back() ^= 0x01U;
    auto const damaged =
        received_part(damaged_wire, *laptop_nonce_in, *laptop_key, *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    if (damaged) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::string const reason = damaged.error().message();
    std::printf("a part with one byte flipped is refused: %s\n", reason.c_str());

    // The parts add up to one BIP 340 signature under the wallet's one x-only key.
    std::array<musig::partial_signature, 2> const parts{*phone_part_in, *laptop_part_in};
    auto const signature = musig::partial_signature_aggregate(*signing_session, parts, space);
    if (!signature ||
        !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, wallet_key->xonly_public_key())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the aggregate signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature: %zu bytes\n",
                signature->size());
    return 0;
}
each device sends its public nonce: 66 bytes
the coordinator sends the aggregate nonce: 66 bytes
each device sends its partial signature: 32 bytes
both partial signatures parse and verify
a part with one byte flipped is refused: the signature does not verify or is not a valid encoding
the aggregate signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature: 64 bytes

Example. The wallet’s aggregate key as the internal key of a Taproot output spent by its key path (BIP 341). tweak_xonly_add tweaks it by its TapTweak tagged hash before any nonce is made, since the session and the partial signatures need the key as tweaked, and nonce_gen mixes in the key it is given (BIP 327’s NonceGen takes it only as an optional input); the signature then verifies under the output key and not under the internal one. The hash is the protocol’s, a domain library’s to compute; the example shows it with webcpp::hash’s SHA-256:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <utility>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace musig = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::musig;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

// BIP 340's tagged hash, SHA-256(SHA-256(tag) || SHA-256(tag) || data), with which BIP 341
// derives the tweak: the tag keeps a hash made for one purpose from being valid for another.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> tagged_hash(std::string_view tag, std::span<std::uint8_t const> data) {
    webcpp::hash::sha2_256 tag_hash;
    tag_hash.update(tag.data(), tag.size());
    auto const prefix = tag_hash.result();

    webcpp::hash::sha2_256 hash;
    hash.update(prefix.data(), prefix.size());
    hash.update(prefix.data(), prefix.size());
    hash.update(data.data(), data.size());
    auto const digest = hash.result();
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> out{};
    std::ranges::copy(digest, out.begin());
    return out;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Each device's key pair; each sends the other its public key.
    auto const phone = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x11));
    auto const laptop = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x22));
    if (!phone || !laptop) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*phone->public_key());
    auto const laptop_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*laptop->public_key());
    if (!phone_key || !laptop_key) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The keys sorted and aggregated: the output's internal key.
    std::array<secp256k1::public_key, 2> keys{*phone_key, *laptop_key};
    std::ranges::sort(keys);
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, musig::workspace_size(2)> space{};
    auto wallet_key = musig::key_aggregate(keys, space);
    if (!wallet_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const internal_key = wallet_key->xonly_public_key();
    std::printf("internal key aggregated from %zu signers\n", keys.size());

    // BIP 341's tweak of a key-path-only output, the tagged hash of the internal key, applied
    // as an x-only tweak before any nonce is made: the output key is the key on the chain.
    auto const tweak = tagged_hash("TapTweak", internal_key);
    if (!wallet_key->tweak_xonly_add(tweak)) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const output_key = wallet_key->xonly_public_key();
    if (output_key == internal_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("output key tweaked with TapTweak, a key other than the internal key\n");

    // The spend both approve: the transaction's 32-byte hash (BIP 341's signature message), as
    // a domain library computes it.
    auto const message = repeated(0x5a);

    // MuSig2's two rounds under the tweaked key: a nonce each, the session, a part each.
    auto phone_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*phone, *wallet_key, message);
    auto laptop_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*laptop, *wallet_key, message);
    if (!phone_nonce || !laptop_nonce) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<musig::public_nonce, 2> const nonces{
        phone_nonce->public_part,
        laptop_nonce->public_part,
    };
    auto const nonce_sum = musig::nonce_aggregate(nonces, space);
    if (!nonce_sum) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const signing_session = musig::nonce_process(*nonce_sum, message, *wallet_key);
    if (!signing_session) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_part = musig::partial_sign(*phone, std::move(phone_nonce->secret_part),
                                                *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    auto const laptop_part = musig::partial_sign(*laptop, std::move(laptop_nonce->secret_part),
                                                 *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    if (!phone_part || !laptop_part ||
        !musig::partial_signature_verify(*phone_part, nonces[0], *phone_key, *wallet_key,
                                         *signing_session) ||
        !musig::partial_signature_verify(*laptop_part, nonces[1], *laptop_key, *wallet_key,
                                         *signing_session)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("both partial signatures verify\n");

    // One BIP 340 signature: valid under the output key, which spends the output by its key
    // path, and not under the internal key.
    std::array<musig::partial_signature, 2> const parts{*phone_part, *laptop_part};
    auto const signature = musig::partial_signature_aggregate(*signing_session, parts, space);
    if (!signature || !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, output_key)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the signature verifies under the output key\n");
    auto const under_internal = secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, internal_key);
    if (under_internal) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::string const reason = under_internal.error().message();
    std::printf("under the internal key it is refused: %s\n", reason.c_str());
    return 0;
}
internal key aggregated from 2 signers
output key tweaked with TapTweak, a key other than the internal key
both partial signatures verify
the signature verifies under the output key
under the internal key it is refused: the signature does not verify or is not a valid encoding

Pitfalls.

  • A nonce used for two signatures gives away the secret key: from two partial signatures with the same nonce, anyone solves for it (BIP 327). This is why partial_sign takes the secret_nonce by value, so that passing it needs a std::move, why its copy is deleted (the build stops), and why a second move of the same object is refused with invalid_state. Never store a secret nonce to sign later, after a restart: a nonce restored from a backup signs a second time.

  • Never sign before every public nonce is in. A signer who signs while others can still choose their nonces lets them steer the final nonce, which the two-round design exists to prevent (MuSig2).

  • A key aggregated with an attacker’s key that the attacker chose after seeing yours is safe here: MuSig2 weighs each key with a coefficient hashed from all of them, so that no signer can cancel another’s. The plain sum of keys, pubkey_combine (Tweaks, negation and combination), has no such weight, and is not a multisignature (BIP 327).

  • The tweaks belong to a protocol. Taproot’s output key is the aggregate key tweaked by a tagged hash of it and a script tree’s root (BIP 341); that hash, and every other rule of the protocol, is a domain library’s, which passes the tweak to tweak_xonly_add.

Silent payments

A donation page, an invoice that is paid more than once, a creator’s tip jar: each wants one address to publish for good. With a plain address, every payment to it is on the chain for anyone to list and add up. A silent payment address is two public keys, scan and spend; every payment to it lands on a new output key that only the recipient can tell is theirs, so that an onlooker sees no two payments to one address, and the sender needs no exchange with the recipient first (BIP 352).

It works by ECDH. The sender sums the secret keys of the transaction’s eligible inputs, hashes the transaction’s smallest outpoint with the sum of their public keys, and multiplies the recipient’s scan key by both: a secret only the sender and the holder of the scan key’s secret share. A hash of that secret and of the output’s number tweaks the spend key into the output key, a new one per transaction and per output. The recipient sums the inputs’ public keys instead, multiplies the sum by the same hash and its scan secret, finds the same secret, and recognises its outputs (BIP 352). <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp>, namespace curves::secp256k1::silent_payments, offers libsecp256k1’s functions:

  • create_outputs makes the sender’s output keys, one per recipient (a scan and a spend public_key, which the sender decodes from the address), from the key pairs of the Taproot inputs and of the other eligible inputs, apart, and the smallest outpoint’s 36 bytes;

  • make_prevouts_summary sums the eligible inputs’ public keys for the recipient, into a prevouts_summary, and scan_outputs scans a transaction’s x-only outputs with the scan key pair and the spend key: each found_output holds the output’s key, its spend_tweak (a secret<32>, which seckey_tweak_add adds to the spend secret key to spend the output, Tweaks, negation and combination) and the label it was sent to;

  • create_label makes the scan key’s m-th label, 0 being BIP 352’s change label, and create_labeled_spend_key the spend key of the address with that label; scan_outputs recognises a labelled payment through a lookup the caller gives, a noexcept callable that returns exactly std::optional<std::span<std::uint8_t const, 32>>: a span over the label’s tweak, in bytes the lookup owns for the call, since libsecp256k1 reads them after it returns, or std::nullopt. A tweak returned by value is refused at compile time.

create_outputs, make_prevouts_summary and scan_outputs take a workspace for libsecp256k1’s arrays (send_workspace_size, summary_workspace_size and scan_workspace_size say how many bytes), so that nothing is allocated, and wipe it, the inputs’ secrets and the found tweaks in it, before they return. No recipient, no input, no output, outputs not one per recipient, found shorter than the outputs, a short workspace, or more than group_limit (2323) recipients on one scan key is invalid_input_size; a moved-from key pair or a null input invalid_state; inputs whose keys sum to zero invalid_secret_key for the sender and invalid_public_key for the recipient, as is an output key that does not parse; a label that is not a point invalid_point. The tests check BIP 352’s own vectors, as libsecp256k1’s tests read them from the same file: the input keys, the smallest outpoint and the recipients’ keys, already taken out of the vectors’ transactions and addresses, which are a domain library’s.

The backends of curves::secp256k1::silent_payments::create_outputs, create_label, create_labeled_spend_key, make_prevouts_summary, scan_outputs, send_workspace_size, summary_workspace_size, scan_workspace_size, from the test programs that run it:

Example. A donation page publishes one address. A donor’s wallet pays it with one input; the recipient scans the transaction, finds the payment, and makes the key pair that spends it; a second donation lands on an unrelated key:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/tweak.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace silent_payments = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::silent_payments;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

using output_key = std::array<std::uint8_t, 32>;
using outpoint = std::array<std::uint8_t, silent_payments::outpoint_size>;

// The donor's wallet pays the address with one input: one output key, the transaction's.
bool pay(silent_payments::recipient const& address, secp256k1::keypair const& donor_input,
         outpoint const& smallest_outpoint, output_key& paid_key) {
    std::array<silent_payments::recipient, 1> const recipients{address};
    std::array<secp256k1::keypair const*, 1> const plain_inputs{&donor_input};
    std::array<output_key, 1> outputs{};
    // The workspace holds libsecp256k1's arrays and the input's secret; it is wiped on return.
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, silent_payments::send_workspace_size(1, 0, 1)>
        space{};
    if (!silent_payments::create_outputs(recipients, smallest_outpoint, {}, plain_inputs, outputs,
                                         space)) {
        return false;
    }
    paid_key = outputs[0];
    return true;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // The donation page: its scan and spend key pairs stay with the recipient; the address is
    // their two public keys.
    auto const scan_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x51));
    // The spend secret is kept, in a secret<32> that wipes itself, to spend what is found.
    webcpp::crypto::secret<32> spend_secret;
    std::ranges::fill(spend_secret.writable(), std::uint8_t{0x52});
    auto const spend_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(spend_secret.bytes());
    auto const donor = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x53));
    if (!scan_pair || !spend_pair || !donor) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const scan_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*scan_pair->public_key());
    auto const spend_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*spend_pair->public_key());
    auto const donor_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*donor->public_key());
    if (!scan_key || !spend_key || !donor_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    silent_payments::recipient const address{.scan_key = *scan_key, .spend_key = *spend_key};

    // The donor pays: the transaction spends one input, whose outpoint is its smallest.
    outpoint first_outpoint{};
    first_outpoint.fill(0x01);
    output_key first_payment{};
    if (!pay(address, *donor, first_outpoint, first_payment)) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The recipient sees the transaction: its input's public key and smallest outpoint make the
    // summary, and the scan of its outputs finds the payment.
    std::array<secp256k1::public_key, 1> const input_keys{*donor_key};
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, silent_payments::summary_workspace_size(0, 1)>
        summary_space{};
    auto const summary =
        silent_payments::make_prevouts_summary(first_outpoint, {}, input_keys, summary_space);
    if (!summary) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<output_key, 1> const transaction_outputs{first_payment};
    std::array<silent_payments::found_output, 1> found{};
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, silent_payments::scan_workspace_size(1)>
        scan_space{};
    auto const found_count = silent_payments::scan_outputs(*scan_pair, *spend_key, *summary,
                                                           transaction_outputs, found, scan_space);
    if (!found_count) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the recipient found %zu output\n", *found_count);

    // The spend secret plus the found tweak is the output's secret key.
    auto const output_secret = secp256k1::seckey_tweak_add(spend_secret, found[0].spend_tweak);
    if (!output_secret) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const spending_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(output_secret->bytes());
    if (!spending_pair) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const spending_key = spending_pair->xonly_public_key();
    if (!spending_key || *spending_key != found[0].output_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the spending key matches the output\n");

    // A second donation from the same wallet, another transaction: another outpoint.
    outpoint second_outpoint{};
    second_outpoint.fill(0x02);
    output_key second_payment{};
    if (!pay(address, *donor, second_outpoint, second_payment)) {
        return 1;
    }
    if (second_payment != first_payment) {
        std::printf("two payments to one address share no output key\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
the recipient found 1 output
the spending key matches the output
two payments to one address share no output key

Pitfalls.

  • The smallest outpoint must be the transaction’s, the smallest of all its inputs, eligible or not. A sender who passes another computes another secret, and the recipient is unable to find the payment (libsecp256k1’s silent payments header). Choosing the inputs and the outpoint is the wallet’s, a domain library’s.

  • Every output create_outputs makes must be in the transaction. The recipient looks for the outputs to one scan key in order and stops at the first it does not find, so that a dropped output may hide some or all of the others (libsecp256k1’s silent payments header).

  • Scanning costs one ECDH per transaction with eligible inputs, whether it pays the recipient or not, since only the shared secret tells. A full node does it as blocks arrive; a light client, which must fetch each transaction’s summary data, must plan for that cost (BIP 352).

  • Many labels may slow scanning down badly in some wallets, light clients among them; libsecp256k1 recommends creating the change label alone and handing out no labelled address (libsecp256k1’s silent payments header). The change label itself is never handed out, so that no one else can pay what looks like change (BIP 352).

  • A wallet always scans for the change label, recovery from a seed included, whether it made other labels or not (BIP 352). scan_outputs defaults to no_labels: a wallet that scans so misses every change output it sent itself, and its balance looks short.

  • The workspaces grow with the counts: send_workspace_size(r, t, p) with the recipients and the inputs, scan_workspace_size(n) with the outputs. A workspace on the stack suits a few; a transaction of thousands of outputs needs one the program owns on the heap. On Emscripten the stack is 64 KiB by default and cannot grow, and a program built without assertions that overruns it fails silently, with no check of overflows by default (Emscripten’s settings reference): the workspace then overwrites the program’s other memory instead of stopping it. On wasip2 and wasip3 the stack is likewise a region of the linear memory that grows downward (the WebAssembly tool conventions’ basic C ABI); this page states no default size and no overflow behaviour for it, so a workspace of more than a few recipients or outputs belongs on the heap there too.

Ed25519

<webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519.hpp> is Ed25519, the Edwards-curve signature scheme of RFC 8032 (RFC 8032), on libsodium (/third_party//sodium, or /webcpp/crypto//ed25519-default, which links it on every target), in the namespace webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519. A signature is 64 bytes over a message of any length, made with a 32-byte secret key, the seed, and checked with a 32-byte public key. The signature is deterministic: the same key and message always give the same signature, so no weak generator at signing time can leak the key. Ed25519 is the signature of SSH keys (RFC 8709), of Tor’s identity keys (Tor’s specifications) and of Solana’s accounts (Solana’s documentation); browsers’ WebCrypto has it too (W3C). Bitcoin, Ethereum and Nostr sign on secp256k1 instead (secp256k1).

A keypair is made from a seed with make(seed), or drawn from random_device with generate(); it gives its public key (public_key), signs (sign), and gives its X25519 secret key (x25519_secret, a secret<32>), so that one seed serves for signatures and for key agreement. The key pair wipes its secret key when it is moved from and destroyed. verify(public_key, message, signature) checks a signature with the public key alone.

Ed25519ph signs the SHA-512 of a message instead of the message: a program that signs a large file reads it in pieces, gives each to update, and signs once at the end. Its type names the hash, ph<webcpp::hash::sha2_512>, which the header brings with it, since RFC 8032 fixes it; another hash does not compile. An Ed25519ph signature is not an Ed25519 signature of the same message, and neither verifies as the other: a protocol says which of the two it uses.

Example. RFC 8032’s second test signed and verified, then its Ed25519ph test, the message given in two pieces:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519.hpp>

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace ed25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519;

namespace {

// Prints bytes in hex after a name, 32 bytes (64 digits) to a line, the lines after the first
// indented under the first, so that a long value stays readable on a narrow page.
void print(char const* name, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    int const indent = std::printf("%s ", name);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < bytes.size(); ++i) {
        if (i != 0 && i % 32 == 0) {
            std::printf("\n%*s", indent, "");
        }
        std::printf("%02x", bytes[i]);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// Ed25519: one message in one call.
bool sign_whole() {
    // RFC 8032 section 7.1, TEST 2: a published seed, never a real key; a program draws its
    // own with keypair::generate().
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const seed{
        0x4c, 0xcd, 0x08, 0x9b, 0x28, 0xff, 0x96, 0xda, 0x9d, 0xb6, 0xc3,
        0x46, 0xec, 0x11, 0x4e, 0x0f, 0x5b, 0x8a, 0x31, 0x9f, 0x35, 0xab,
        0xa6, 0x24, 0xda, 0x8c, 0xf6, 0xed, 0x4f, 0xb8, 0xa6, 0xfb,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 1> const message{0x72};
    auto const key = ed25519::keypair::make(seed);
    if (!key) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const public_key = key->public_key();
    auto const signature = key->sign(message);
    if (!public_key || !signature) {
        return false;
    }
    print("public key", *public_key);
    print("signature ", *signature);
    // The verifier holds the public key, the message and the signature; nothing secret.
    return ed25519::verify(*public_key, message, *signature).has_value();
}

// Ed25519ph: the message given in pieces, as a large file is read, signed once at the end,
// over SHA-512, the hash RFC 8032 fixes.
bool sign_in_pieces() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const seed{
        0x83, 0x3f, 0xe6, 0x24, 0x09, 0x23, 0x7b, 0x9d, 0x62, 0xec, 0x77,
        0x58, 0x75, 0x20, 0x91, 0x1e, 0x9a, 0x75, 0x9c, 0xec, 0x1d, 0x19,
        0x75, 0x5b, 0x7d, 0xa9, 0x01, 0xb9, 0x6d, 0xca, 0x3d, 0x42,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 1> const first{'a'};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 2> const second{'b', 'c'};
    using signer = ed25519::ph<webcpp::hash::sha2_512>;
    auto const key = ed25519::keypair::make(seed);
    auto signing = signer::begin();
    if (!key || !signing || !signing->update(first) || !signing->update(second)) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const public_key = key->public_key();
    auto const signature = signing->sign(*key);
    if (!public_key || !signature) {
        return false;
    }
    print("public key", *public_key);
    print("signature ", *signature);
    auto verifying = signer::begin();
    return verifying && verifying->update(first) && verifying->update(second) &&
           verifying->verify(*public_key, *signature).has_value();
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    if (!sign_whole() || !sign_in_pieces()) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("verified\n");
    return 0;
}

Strict verification. Implementations of Ed25519 disagree on some signatures that no honest signer produces: a scalar S not reduced below the group order, a point encoded in a non-canonical form, a public key of small order. verify takes a verification policy, strict by default and the only one in this version: libsodium’s rules, which refuse all three (libsodium’s documentation). Every valid signature of Wycheproof’s EdDSA file is accepted and every invalid one refused (ed25519_wycheproof_sodium).

The twelve edge cases. Chalkias, Garillot and Nikolaenko, "Taming the many EdDSAs" (IACR ePrint 2020/1244), give twelve signatures on which implementations disagree, in their suite (novifinancial/ed25519-speccheck). They run against every Ed25519 backend: its own verdict (raw), and its verdict under strict, which is libsodium’s on every backend. The test ed25519_speccheck asserts the table below, so that a new version of a backend that changes a verdict fails until the table is regenerated. WebCrypto in node is an outside view, recorded with the node and the OpenSSL that gave it (node’s Ed25519 is OpenSSL’s) and never held to strict. The suite’s results of 2021 show OpenSSL 3.0 accepting cases 0 to 2 and 11; the newer OpenSSL of the column’s node refuses them, as libsodium does.

Honest signatures verify everywhere: the cases differ only on signatures no honest signer makes, and a network that mixes verifiers must agree on one rule for them. In the suite’s results of 2021 (the suite’s results, whose Cargo.toml pins them), Rust peers that used the default verify of ed25519-dalek 1.0.0-pre.4 accepted cases 0 to 2 and 11, which strict refuses, and ed25519-zebra 2.1.1, a ZIP-215 verifier (ZIP 215, the rule of Zcash), accepted every case but 6 to 8. ZIP-215 does so by design: it verifies with the cofactor and accepts non-canonical encodings of A and R, so that every ZIP-215 verifier agrees on every signature. strict refuses the cases ZIP-215 accepts beyond it; zip215 is not a policy of this version, and waits for a mature C or C++ implementation of ZIP-215.

Pitfalls.

  • Keep the seed out of logs, crash reports and source control: whoever holds it signs as the key’s owner. The examples use RFC 8032’s published seeds only to print fixed signatures.

  • A signature proves who signed the bytes, not when or for what: a protocol that must refuse a replayed message signs a counter, a time or a context with it.

Parts of this section, libsodium’s rules of strict verification, are adapted from libsodium’s documentation (jedisct1/libsodium-doc at 6d1ea27, ISC, LICENSE-LIBSODIUM-DOC.txt).

X25519

<webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519.hpp> is X25519, the Diffie-Hellman key agreement on Curve25519 of RFC 7748 (RFC 7748), on libsodium (/third_party//sodium, or /webcpp/crypto//x25519-default, which links it on every target), in the namespace webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519. Two parties each keep a 32-byte secret key and send the other its 32-byte public key; each combines its own secret key with the other’s public key and both get the same 32-byte shared secret, which no one who saw only the public keys can compute. A chat app agrees a key this way with each contact, and TLS 1.3, SSH, WireGuard and Signal start their sessions with it (RFC 8446; RFC 8731; WireGuard; X3DH).

public_key(secret_key) gives the public key of any 32 bytes, which a program draws with random_device; agree(secret_key, peer_public_key) gives the shared secret, a secret<32> that wipes itself. A peer’s public key of low order makes the shared secret all zero, whatever the secret key: agree refuses it with weak_public_key, so that an attacker who sends such a key cannot make both sides use a secret it knows (design D8). Every case of Wycheproof’s X25519 file gives its shared secret, and its 31 all-zero cases give weak_public_key (x25519_wycheproof_sodium).

From Ed25519. A program that already holds an Ed25519 key pair (Ed25519) agrees with the same seed: keypair::x25519_secret() is its X25519 secret key, and curves::ed25519::to_x25519_public(public_key) converts a peer’s Ed25519 public key to its X25519 public key, the birational map between the two forms of the curve. The conversion refuses with invalid_public_key a key of small order, off the curve or outside the main subgroup, as libsodium does (libsodium’s documentation).

Example. RFC 7748’s Alice and Bob, then two Ed25519 key pairs that agree through their X25519 forms, then a peer key of low order refused:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace ed25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519;
namespace x25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519;

namespace {

// Prints bytes in hex after a name.
void print(char const* name, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    std::printf("%s ", name);
    for (auto const byte : bytes) {
        std::printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// X25519: each side sends its public key and keeps its secret key.
bool alice_and_bob() {
    // RFC 7748 section 6.1's secret keys: published, never real keys; a program draws its own
    // 32 bytes with random_device.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const alice_secret{
        0x77, 0x07, 0x6d, 0x0a, 0x73, 0x18, 0xa5, 0x7d, 0x3c, 0x16, 0xc1,
        0x72, 0x51, 0xb2, 0x66, 0x45, 0xdf, 0x4c, 0x2f, 0x87, 0xeb, 0xc0,
        0x99, 0x2a, 0xb1, 0x77, 0xfb, 0xa5, 0x1d, 0xb9, 0x2c, 0x2a,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const bob_secret{
        0x5d, 0xab, 0x08, 0x7e, 0x62, 0x4a, 0x8a, 0x4b, 0x79, 0xe1, 0x7f,
        0x8b, 0x83, 0x80, 0x0e, 0xe6, 0x6f, 0x3b, 0xb1, 0x29, 0x26, 0x18,
        0xb6, 0xfd, 0x1c, 0x2f, 0x8b, 0x27, 0xff, 0x88, 0xe0, 0xeb,
    };
    auto const alice_public = x25519::public_key(alice_secret);
    auto const bob_public = x25519::public_key(bob_secret);
    if (!alice_public || !bob_public) {
        return false;
    }
    print("alice public", *alice_public);
    print("bob public  ", *bob_public);
    auto const alice_shared = x25519::agree(alice_secret, *bob_public);
    auto const bob_shared = x25519::agree(bob_secret, *alice_public);
    if (!alice_shared || !bob_shared) {
        return false;
    }
    // Printed here only because RFC 7748 publishes it; a program never prints a shared secret,
    // and derives its keys from it with a KDF.
    print("shared      ", alice_shared->bytes());
    return crypto::equal(alice_shared->bytes(), bob_shared->bytes());
}

// The same agreement from Ed25519 key pairs: one seed for signatures and key agreement.
bool from_ed25519() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const first_seed{
        0x9d, 0x61, 0xb1, 0x9d, 0xef, 0xfd, 0x5a, 0x60, 0xba, 0x84, 0x4a,
        0xf4, 0x92, 0xec, 0x2c, 0xc4, 0x44, 0x49, 0xc5, 0x69, 0x7b, 0x32,
        0x69, 0x19, 0x70, 0x3b, 0xac, 0x03, 0x1c, 0xae, 0x7f, 0x60,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const second_seed{
        0x4c, 0xcd, 0x08, 0x9b, 0x28, 0xff, 0x96, 0xda, 0x9d, 0xb6, 0xc3,
        0x46, 0xec, 0x11, 0x4e, 0x0f, 0x5b, 0x8a, 0x31, 0x9f, 0x35, 0xab,
        0xa6, 0x24, 0xda, 0x8c, 0xf6, 0xed, 0x4f, 0xb8, 0xa6, 0xfb,
    };
    auto const first = ed25519::keypair::make(first_seed);
    auto const second = ed25519::keypair::make(second_seed);
    if (!first || !second) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const first_secret = first->x25519_secret();
    auto const second_secret = second->x25519_secret();
    auto const first_signing = first->public_key();
    auto const second_signing = second->public_key();
    if (!first_secret || !second_secret || !first_signing || !second_signing) {
        return false;
    }
    // Each side knows the other by its Ed25519 public key, and converts it.
    auto const first_peer = ed25519::to_x25519_public(*second_signing);
    auto const second_peer = ed25519::to_x25519_public(*first_signing);
    if (!first_peer || !second_peer) {
        return false;
    }
    print("converted   ", *second_peer);
    auto const first_shared = x25519::agree(first_secret->bytes(), *first_peer);
    auto const second_shared = x25519::agree(second_secret->bytes(), *second_peer);
    return first_shared && second_shared &&
           crypto::equal(first_shared->bytes(), second_shared->bytes());
}

// A peer key of low order gives an all-zero secret, which agree refuses.
bool low_order_refused() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const secret_key{1};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const zero_point{};
    auto const shared = x25519::agree(secret_key, zero_point);
    if (!shared && shared.error() == crypto::error::weak_public_key) {
        std::printf("low order    refused: weak_public_key\n");
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    if (!alice_and_bob() || !from_ed25519() || !low_order_refused()) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("agreed\n");
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls.

  • The shared secret is not a key: a program derives its keys from it, with the two public keys, through a KDF such as webcpp::hash’s HKDF, and never uses its bytes as a cipher’s key directly (libsodium’s documentation, scalar multiplication).

  • X25519 proves nothing about who sent a public key: an attacker in the middle agrees one secret with each side. A protocol signs the public keys, or checks them against keys it already trusts.

  • A peer’s key of low order gives an all-zero shared secret whatever the own secret key: agree refuses it, and a program never replaces the refusal with a secret of its own choosing.

  • On Apple silicon (and other 64-bit ARM CPUs with DIT, data-independent timing), neither webcpp nor libsodium sets DIT, and without it agree took a time that depends on the secret key: about one nanosecond less for the all-zero key, enough for dudect to tell it apart (Constant time). The lane’s dudect sets DIT itself on macOS and Linux on arm64 only, and measures without it elsewhere. A program sets DIT around its secret operations, as Apple describes (Apple, enable DIT for constant-time cryptographic operations; timingsafe_enable_if_supported from macOS 15.2).

  • On WebAssembly, timing is an open finding: under wasmtime, on wasip2, dudect times agree against its secret key above the lane’s threshold, where every native build passes (with DIT set on macOS and Linux on arm64, as the lane runs it). The cause is measured: Apple silicon’s DIT, which wasmtime does not set; with DIT set in wasmtime’s thread, as an experiment, the case passes. The measurement, with its numbers, is in Constant time and in the curves’ comparison table (Curves: webcpp::crypto::curves); a program that agrees keys on WebAssembly where an attacker can time many agreements with one secret key reads it first.

Parts of this section, the warnings on the shared secret and on keys of low order, are adapted from libsodium’s documentation (jedisct1/libsodium-doc at 6d1ea27, ISC, LICENSE-LIBSODIUM-DOC.txt).

Key exchange: crypto_kx

<webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519/kx.hpp> is libsodium’s key exchange, crypto_kx, on libsodium (/third_party//sodium, or /webcpp/crypto//kx-default, which links it on every target), in the namespace webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519. It turns X25519 (X25519) into what a program that talks to one peer needs: two keys ready for a cipher, one for each direction. A chat app’s client and its server each hold a kx_keypair; they send each other their public keys; the client calls client_session_keys(server_public_key) and the server server_session_keys(client_public_key). Each gets a session_keys, a receive and a transmit key, both secret<32> that wipe themselves; the client’s transmit is the server’s receive and the reverse, so that a message each side sends has a key of its own (libsodium’s documentation, key exchange).

The session keys are BLAKE2b-512 of the X25519 shared secret and of both public keys, client first, split in two: unlike the raw shared secret of agree they are keys, and they bind both public keys. Only another crypto_kx, as libsodium’s own in another language, derives the same keys; a protocol that names X25519 and a KDF of its own, as TLS 1.3’s key schedule does (RFC 8446, section 7.1), uses agree instead.

kx_keypair<>::generate() draws the key pair’s 32-byte seed with random_device; kx_keypair<>::make(seed) makes the same key pair from the same seed, as a program that keeps its seed does. A peer’s public key of low order makes the X25519 secret all zero, whatever the secret key: both functions refuse it with weak_public_key, as libsodium does (design D8).

Example. libsodium’s test’s client and server compute their session keys; the client seals a message that the server opens on ChaCha20-Poly1305 (ChaCha20-Poly1305); a peer key of low order is refused:

#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/chacha20_poly1305.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519/kx.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace x25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519;

namespace {

// Prints bytes in hex after a name.
void print(char const* name, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    std::printf("%s ", name);
    for (auto const byte : bytes) {
        std::printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// The client sends "hello" to the server, sealed with the client's transmit key and opened with
// the server's receive key, the same key.
bool message(x25519::session_keys const& client, x25519::session_keys const& server) {
    auto sealer = crypto::ciphers::chacha20_poly1305<>::make(client.transmit.bytes());
    auto opener = crypto::ciphers::chacha20_poly1305<>::make(server.receive.bytes());
    if (!sealer || !opener) {
        return false;
    }
    // The first message of this direction: nonce 0. Each next message takes the next number;
    // a nonce is never used twice under one key.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> const nonce{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 5> data{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'};
    auto const tag = sealer->seal(nonce, {}, data);
    if (!tag || !opener->open(nonce, {}, data, *tag)) {
        return false;
    }
    std::printf("server read   ");
    for (auto const byte : data) {
        std::printf("%c", byte);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
    return true;
}

bool client_and_server() {
    // libsodium's kx test's seeds, published, never real ones: a program calls
    // kx_keypair<>::generate(), which draws its seed with random_device.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> client_seed{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < client_seed.size(); ++i) {
        client_seed[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> server_seed = client_seed;
    server_seed[0] = 1;
    auto const client = x25519::kx_keypair<>::make(client_seed);
    auto const server = x25519::kx_keypair<>::make(server_seed);
    if (!client || !server) {
        return false;
    }
    // Each side sends its public key; the secret keys never leave the key pairs.
    auto const client_public = client->public_key();
    auto const server_public = server->public_key();
    if (!client_public || !server_public) {
        return false;
    }
    print("client public", *client_public);
    print("server public", *server_public);
    auto const client_keys = client->client_session_keys(*server_public);
    auto const server_keys = server->server_session_keys(*client_public);
    if (!client_keys || !server_keys) {
        return false;
    }
    // Printed here only because libsodium's test publishes them; a program never prints a key.
    print("client rx    ", client_keys->receive.bytes());
    print("client tx    ", client_keys->transmit.bytes());
    return crypto::equal(client_keys->transmit.bytes(), server_keys->receive.bytes()) &&
           crypto::equal(client_keys->receive.bytes(), server_keys->transmit.bytes()) &&
           message(*client_keys, *server_keys);
}

// A peer key of low order gives an all-zero X25519 secret, which crypto_kx refuses.
bool low_order_refused() {
    auto const key = x25519::kx_keypair<>::make(std::array<std::uint8_t, 32>{});
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const zero_point{};
    if (!key) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const keys = key->server_session_keys(zero_point);
    if (!keys && keys.error() == crypto::error::weak_public_key) {
        std::printf("low order     refused: weak_public_key\n");
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    if (!client_and_server() || !low_order_refused()) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("agreed\n");
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls.

  • The two sides must agree on who is the client: two clients, or two servers, compute keys that do not match, and every message fails to open.

  • crypto_kx proves nothing about who sent a public key: an attacker in the middle exchanges keys with each side. A protocol signs the public keys, or checks them against keys it already trusts.

  • A session key is used with one nonce per message: a counter that starts at zero is enough for ChaCha20-Poly1305, since each direction has its own key; a key pair kept across sessions gives the same keys again, so a program that reconnects starts from a fresh key pair, or uses XChaCha20-Poly1305 with random nonces.

Parts of this section, how the two session keys are derived and used, are adapted from libsodium’s documentation (jedisct1/libsodium-doc at 6d1ea27, ISC, LICENSE-LIBSODIUM-DOC.txt).

Key formats: SPKI, PKCS#8 and PEM

A key leaves a program in a standard form when another program must read it: OpenSSL’s command line, a browser’s WebCrypto, an SSH or TLS tool, a server that stores a user’s public key. Two forms of DER, the binary encoding of ASN.1, carry a key with the name of its algorithm: SPKI, a public key (SubjectPublicKeyInfo, the form inside every X.509 certificate), and PKCS#8, a private key (RFC 5958’s OneAsymmetricKey, RFC 5958). PEM writes either as text between -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- and -----END PUBLIC KEY-----, or PRIVATE KEY, so that it can be pasted into a file, a form or an e-mail (RFC 7468). A chat app that lets a user export an identity key to another device, or a server that accepts a public key uploaded by a browser, speaks these forms.

For Ed25519 and X25519, RFC 8410 fixes them to one layout each (RFC 8410): an SPKI is 12 bytes that name the curve, then the 32 bytes of the public key, 44 bytes in all; a PKCS#8 is 16 bytes, then the 32 bytes of the seed (Ed25519) or secret key (X25519), 48 bytes in all. These are exactly the bytes OpenSSL’s i2d_PUBKEY and i2d_PrivateKey and WebCrypto’s exportKey("spki") and exportKey("pkcs8") write (W3C), and the PEM texts OpenSSL’s PEM_write_bio_PUBKEY and PEM_write_bio_PrivateKey write: the tests compare every byte with OpenSSL’s natively and on WASI (formats_25519_openssl_oracle) and with node’s WebCrypto on Emscripten (formats_25519_webcrypto_oracle), 200 keys per curve each.

<webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519/formats.hpp> gives, in webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519, encode_spki(public_key, out), decode_spki(spki), encode_pkcs8(keypair, out) and decode_pkcs8(pkcs8), which makes the key pair at once; <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519/formats.hpp> gives the same four in webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519, where a PKCS#8 holds a 32-byte secret key and decode_pkcs8 gives it as a secret<32>, which wipes itself. max_spki_size and max_pkcs8_size, 44 and 48, size the caller’s buffers. <webcpp/crypto/pem.hpp> gives, in webcpp::crypto::pem, armour(label, der, out) and unarmour(label, text, out), with the labels public_key_label and private_key_label, and armoured_size, the text’s size. Each writes into the caller’s buffer and returns how many bytes or characters it wrote; on a refusal it writes nothing. All run on libsodium (/third_party//sodium, or the families’ aliases /webcpp/crypto//ed25519-default, /webcpp/crypto//x25519-default and /webcpp/crypto//pem-default), whose base64 runs in a time that does not depend on the bytes, those of a private key included (libsodium’s documentation).

Strict decoding. A decoder accepts an input only if encoding what it decoded gives the same bytes (design D30): the one form that OpenSSL and WebCrypto write, and nothing else. It refuses with invalid_encoding another curve’s identifier (an Ed25519 key given to X25519’s decoder), a byte left over, a length in BER’s long form where DER requires the short one, PKCS#8 version 2, which carries the public key beside the seed, attributes, and PEM with another label than the expected, lines of another length than 64, carriage returns, text before or after the key, or base64 that is not the one encoding of its bytes. A key that one library accepts and another refuses lets two programs that should agree on a key disagree on it; one form, and one verdict on every backend, closes that door. A program that receives version 2, or PEM with Windows line ends, converts it with OpenSSL’s openssl pkey first.

Example. RFC 8410’s own Ed25519 key pair read from PEM, its public key written back as PEM, which is the RFC’s to the character, and a signature; an X25519 public key’s SPKI; and the RFC’s version 2 of the same private key refused:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519/formats.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519/formats.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/pem.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace ed25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519;
namespace x25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519;
namespace pem = webcpp::crypto::pem;

namespace {

// RFC 8410 section 10.3's private key: published, never a real key.
constexpr std::string_view private_pem =
    "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n"
    "MC4CAQAwBQYDK2VwBCIEINTuctv5E1hK1bbY8fdp+K06/nwoy/HU++CXqI9EdVhC\n"
    "-----END PRIVATE KEY-----\n";

// The same key pair in RFC 5958's version 2, with an attribute and the public key.
constexpr std::string_view version2_pem =
    "-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n"
    "MHICAQEwBQYDK2VwBCIEINTuctv5E1hK1bbY8fdp+K06/nwoy/HU++CXqI9EdVhC\n"
    "oB8wHQYKKoZIhvcNAQkJFDEPDA1DdXJkbGUgQ2hhaXJzgSEAGb9ECWmEzf6FQbrB\n"
    "Z9w7lshQhqowtrbLDFw4rXAxZuE=\n"
    "-----END PRIVATE KEY-----\n";

// Prints a public key's SPKI as PEM.
bool print_public_pem(std::array<std::uint8_t, 44> const& spki) {
    std::array<char, pem::armoured_size(pem::public_key_label.size(), 44)> text{};
    auto const written = pem::armour(pem::public_key_label, spki, text);
    if (!written) {
        return false;
    }
    std::printf("%.*s", static_cast<int>(*written), text.data());
    return true;
}

// An Ed25519 key pair from PEM, its public key back to PEM, and a signature.
bool ed25519_from_pem() {
    // The PKCS#8 holds the seed: a secret<N>, which wipes itself.
    crypto::secret<ed25519::max_pkcs8_size> pkcs8;
    auto const read = pem::unarmour(pem::private_key_label, private_pem, pkcs8.writable());
    if (!read) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const pair = ed25519::decode_pkcs8(pkcs8.bytes().first(*read));
    if (!pair) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const public_key = pair->public_key();
    std::array<std::uint8_t, ed25519::max_spki_size> spki{};
    if (!public_key || !ed25519::encode_spki(*public_key, spki) || !print_public_pem(spki)) {
        return false;
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 5> const message{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'};
    auto const signature = pair->sign(message);
    return signature && ed25519::verify(*public_key, message, *signature);
}

// An X25519 public key of RFC 7748's Alice, as SPKI in PEM.
bool x25519_to_pem() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const alice_secret{
        0x77, 0x07, 0x6d, 0x0a, 0x73, 0x18, 0xa5, 0x7d, 0x3c, 0x16, 0xc1,
        0x72, 0x51, 0xb2, 0x66, 0x45, 0xdf, 0x4c, 0x2f, 0x87, 0xeb, 0xc0,
        0x99, 0x2a, 0xb1, 0x77, 0xfb, 0xa5, 0x1d, 0xb9, 0x2c, 0x2a,
    };
    auto const public_key = x25519::public_key(alice_secret);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, x25519::max_spki_size> spki{};
    return public_key && x25519::encode_spki(*public_key, spki) && print_public_pem(spki);
}

// Version 2 decodes from PEM, then the PKCS#8 is refused: strict decoding takes one form.
bool version2_refused() {
    crypto::secret<128> der;
    auto const read = pem::unarmour(pem::private_key_label, version2_pem, der.writable());
    if (!read) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const pair = ed25519::decode_pkcs8(der.bytes().first(*read));
    if (!pair && pair.error() == crypto::error::invalid_encoding) {
        std::printf("version 2 refused: invalid_encoding\n");
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    if (!ed25519_from_pem() || !x25519_to_pem() || !version2_refused()) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("signed and verified\n");
    return 0;
}

MCowBQYDK2VwAyEAGb9ECWmEzf6FQbrBZ9w7lshQhqowtrbLDFw4rXAxZuE=
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MCowBQYDK2VuAyEAhSDwCYkwp1R0i33ctD73Wg2/Og0mOBr066SpjqqbTmo=
-----END PUBLIC KEY-----
version 2 refused: invalid_encoding

Pitfalls.

  • A PKCS#8, as DER or as PEM, is the secret key: kept in a secret<N>, as the example does, it is wiped when it goes; written to a file or a database, it is sealed first, as any secret at rest (Wallets).

  • decode_spki checks the form, not the key: Ed25519’s verify refuses a public key that is not a point of the curve, and X25519’s agree one of low order (weak_public_key). A key read from outside is used through those, which check it.

  • SPKI names the algorithm, the raw 32 bytes do not: an Ed25519 key and an X25519 key of the same bytes are different keys, and the identifier keeps a program from using one as the other.

Hybrid encryption: webcpp::crypto::hybrid

Hybrid encryption joins a key agreement and a cipher: the agreement, on public keys, gives a secret key, and a fast cipher encrypts the data under it (Wikipedia). A chat app encrypts a message to a contact whose public key it knows; a feedback form encrypts a report to a key whose owner alone may read it. The namespace webcpp::crypto::hybrid holds NaCl’s and libsodium’s constructions in this version: the box, between two key pairs, and the sealed box, from anyone to a public key. Both agree with X25519 (X25519) and seal with XSalsa20-Poly1305, the secret box’s cipher (Secret boxes), or, for box_xchacha20poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305, on libsodium, their default on every target.

Which one. A box when the two parties know each other’s public keys and the recipient must know the message came from the other: a chat between two contacts. A sealed box when anyone may write and the recipient alone reads: a feedback form, a drop box, a file key sent to a recipient known by a public key (A file-sharing app: secret boxes and sealed boxes). box_xchacha20poly1305 only when the peer uses libsodium’s XChaCha20 form; otherwise box, NaCl’s format, which libsodium and its bindings in every language read. Without either, a program that encrypts to a public key by hand, an agreement and a cipher of its own choosing, risks the mistakes these constructions settle: a shared secret used as a key, a nonce reused, a weak public key accepted.

Construction X25519-XSalsa20-Poly1305 X25519-XChaCha20-Poly1305 X25519-XSalsa20-Poly1305, anonymous

Names

box

box_xchacha20poly1305

sealed_box

What it does

Authenticated encryption between two key pairs: X25519 agrees a key once per pair, then XSalsa20-Poly1305 seals each message; either party can have written it

The same, with XChaCha20-Poly1305 sealing each message

Encryption to a public key alone: a key pair drawn per message, whose public key travels with it; the recipient cannot tell who sealed it, and the sender cannot open it afterwards

Keys

the own 32-byte secret key and the peer’s 32-byte X25519 public key

the same

to seal, the recipient’s 32-byte public key; to open, the recipient’s key pair

Nonce (IV)

24 bytes, safe to draw at random (D. J. Bernstein, Extending the Salsa20 nonce, 2008)

24 bytes, safe to draw at random

none: derived from the two public keys

Overhead per message

a 16-byte tag

a 16-byte tag

48 bytes: the ephemeral public key and the tag

Standards and sources

NaCl, public-key authenticated encryption (crypto_box), libsodium’s documentation, public-key authenticated encryption

libsodium’s documentation, public-key authenticated encryption

libsodium’s documentation, sealed boxes

Choose it when

two parties who know each other’s public keys exchange messages, in NaCl’s and libsodium’s format; a peer key of small order is refused

the peer uses libsodium’s crypto_box_curve25519xchacha20poly1305; otherwise box, NaCl’s format

anyone may write to a recipient who must not learn who wrote: anonymous feedback, a drop box; it proves nothing about the sender

Boxes

hybrid::box, in <webcpp/crypto/hybrid/box.hpp>, is NaCl’s crypto_box (NaCl; libsodium’s documentation). box::make(secret_key, peer_public_key) agrees a key from the own X25519 secret key and the peer’s public key, once for the pair (libsodium’s beforenm); the box then works in place, as an AEAD without additional data: seal(iv_bytes, data_bytes) encrypts and returns the 16-byte tag, and open(iv_bytes, data_bytes, tag_bytes) checks it and decrypts, zeroing the data when it does not match. Alice’s box made from her secret key and Bob’s public key, and Bob’s made from his secret key and Alice’s public key, hold the same key: what one seals the other opens. box_xchacha20poly1305 is libsodium’s crypto_box_curve25519xchacha20poly1305, the same with XChaCha20-Poly1305. A box is moved and not copied, and wipes its key when moved from and destroyed.

A peer’s public key of small order makes the shared secret one an attacker knows: make refuses it with weak_public_key, as libsodium’s beforenm does.

Example. Alice and Bob, each with an X25519 key pair, make their boxes from the own secret key and the other’s public key; what one seals the other opens, and Mallory, who knows Alice’s public key but not Bob’s secret key, cannot:

// Each side's box: the own secret key and the other's public key give the same key.
auto alice_box = box::make(alice->secret_key.bytes(), bob->public_key);
auto bob_box = box::make(bob->secret_key.bytes(), alice->public_key);
bool send(box& sender, crypto::random_device& device, std::string_view text, sealed_message& out) {
    if (!device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    out.ciphertext.assign(text.begin(), text.end());
    auto const tag = sender.seal(out.nonce, out.ciphertext);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return true;
}

void read(char const* who, box& recipient, sealed_message message) {
    auto const opened = recipient.open(message.nonce, message.ciphertext, message.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s refused it: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("%s read: %.*s\n", who, static_cast<int>(message.ciphertext.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(message.ciphertext.data()));
}
Bob read: the meeting moved to Friday
Alice read: Friday works
Mallory refused it: the authentication tag does not match

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/hybrid/box.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <optional>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
using crypto::hybrid::box;

namespace {

// A person's X25519 key pair: the secret key stays, the public key is published.
struct person {
    crypto::secret<32> secret_key;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> public_key{};

    static std::optional<person> make(crypto::random_device& device) {
        person made;
        if (!device.fill(made.secret_key.writable())) {
            return std::nullopt;
        }
        auto const public_key = crypto::curves::x25519::public_key(made.secret_key.bytes());
        if (!public_key) {
            return std::nullopt;
        }
        made.public_key = *public_key;
        return made;
    }
};

// A message as it travels: the nonce, the tag and the ciphertext.
struct sealed_message {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, box::iv_size> nonce{};
    box::result_type tag{};
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> ciphertext;
};

bool send(box& sender, crypto::random_device& device, std::string_view text, sealed_message& out) {
    if (!device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    out.ciphertext.assign(text.begin(), text.end());
    auto const tag = sender.seal(out.nonce, out.ciphertext);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return true;
}

void read(char const* who, box& recipient, sealed_message message) {
    auto const opened = recipient.open(message.nonce, message.ciphertext, message.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s refused it: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("%s read: %.*s\n", who, static_cast<int>(message.ciphertext.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(message.ciphertext.data()));
}


}  // namespace

int main() {
    crypto::random_device device;
    auto alice = person::make(device);
    auto bob = person::make(device);
    auto mallory = person::make(device);
    if (!alice || !bob || !mallory) {
        return 1;
    }
    // Each side's box: the own secret key and the other's public key give the same key.
    auto alice_box = box::make(alice->secret_key.bytes(), bob->public_key);
    auto bob_box = box::make(bob->secret_key.bytes(), alice->public_key);
    auto mallory_box = box::make(mallory->secret_key.bytes(), alice->public_key);
    if (!alice_box || !bob_box || !mallory_box) {
        return 1;
    }
    sealed_message to_bob;
    sealed_message to_alice;
    if (!send(*alice_box, device, "the meeting moved to Friday", to_bob) ||
        !send(*bob_box, device, "Friday works", to_alice)) {
        return 1;
    }
    read("Bob", *bob_box, to_bob);
    read("Alice", *alice_box, to_alice);
    // Mallory, who knows Alice's public key, holds another key pair: not the pair's key.
    read("Mallory", *mallory_box, to_bob);
    return 0;
}

Pitfalls.

  • A box proves that one of the two key pairs wrote a message, not which one: a protocol that needs to know says so inside the message, or signs it.

  • A nonce is never repeated for one pair of keys, in either direction: draw 24 bytes at random for every message.

Sealed boxes

hybrid::sealed_box, in <webcpp/crypto/hybrid/sealed_box.hpp>, is libsodium’s sealed box, crypto_box_seal (libsodium’s documentation): anyone who knows a public key can seal a message to it, and only the key pair opens it. seal(recipient_public_key, message, out) writes to out, of the message’s size plus overhead, 48 bytes, a key pair libsodium draws for the message, its public key, the tag and the ciphertext, and wipes the drawn secret key; the nonce comes from the two public keys. open(recipient_public_key, recipient_secret_key, sealed, out) writes the message to out, of the sealed box’s size less 48 bytes, and zeroes out when the box does not open: sealed to another key pair, or changed. The sizes are checked first (invalid_input_size), then the keys (invalid_public_key, invalid_key_size).

Pitfalls.

  • A sealed box is anonymous: the recipient cannot tell who sealed it, nor whether an attacker did. Where the sender matters, use a box or a signature.

  • The sender cannot open what it sealed: it keeps its own copy of the message if it needs one.

Example. A file-sharing app seals each file’s key to its recipient: A file-sharing app: secret boxes and sealed boxes.

Parts of this chapter, the boxes’ and the sealed boxes’ descriptions and pitfalls, are adapted from libsodium’s documentation (jedisct1/libsodium-doc at 6d1ea27, ISC, LICENSE-LIBSODIUM-DOC.txt).

Choosing a backend

A backend is the C library that does an algorithm’s work: BearSSL, OpenSSL, ctaes, libsecp256k1 or libsodium. Most families have one; AES-GCM and RFC 8439’s ChaCha20-Poly1305 have several, each giving the same bytes, in code of different size, speed and pedigree. A type that names no backend, aes256_gcm or xchacha20_poly1305<>, takes its family’s default, which is fixed per target: no measurement, link line or define changes it. This chapter says what each default is and why, how a program names another backend, and what a build with threads means. The backends holds the matrices: which backend has which operation on which target, and what each costs in size and time.

The default backend per target

Each family has one default backend per target, for the reason the table gives, whatever the program links; no define changes it, and every other backend is reached by naming it in the type. AES-GCM’s is OpenSSL natively, whose assembly uses the CPU’s AES instructions on x86-64 and ARMv8 with Clang and GCC, and BearSSL on WebAssembly, the only AES-GCM backend on Emscripten and constant time by design where OpenSSL is built without assembly. On MSVC OpenSSL is built without assembly too: the default is then table-based and not constant time, and a program that timing attacks threaten names ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>>. A program that uses a default it does not link stops where it calls it, with the Jamfile line that links it and the type that names another backend (Every message, and its fix). AES-GCM’s default applies to aes128_gcm, aes256_gcm and aes256<>; the AES block cipher has none of its own, and libsecp256k1 is the only backend of secp256k1. The three ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEADs’ default is libsodium on every target; RFC 8439’s form also runs on BearSSL, on every target, and on OpenSSL, natively and on WASI, each named in the type. Every other family of this version, Ed25519, X25519, kx, the secret boxes, the boxes, the sealed box and PEM, has libsodium alone, on every target. In C++, default_backend_t<Family> names a family’s default on the target being compiled, and default_backend AES-GCM’s.

Naming another backend

A program that wants another backend than the default names it as the type’s last template argument and links its library, as ciphers::chacha20_poly1305<backends::bearssl> with /third_party//bearssl, or ciphers::gcm<ciphers::aes256<backends::bearssl>> on MSVC. The backend must have the family on the target being compiled, which supports_v<Algorithm, Backend> tells at compile time; a backend that lacks it, or that the program does not link, stops the build with a message that says what to do (Every message, and its fix). Every backend of a family gives the same bytes: the agreement tests seal with one and open with another. What differs is what each costs and what it promises of its timing: the library behind each, its constant-time design and the lane’s checks, its size and its throughput. The sizes and the throughput are dated references measured from release builds: they decide no default.

Threads and heavy operations

A heavy operation is one slow enough to stall an event loop, and gets an async_ variant that runs it on another thread. Which operations are heavy is stated, not measured (design D32): RSA key generation at every size and RSA private operations at 3072 bits and above; SLH-DSA key generation, signing and verification; ML-DSA key generation and signing; BLS12-381 verification, aggregate verification, fast aggregate verification and aggregation; KZG’s commitments and proofs over a blob and their batch verification; BN254’s pairing_check. Everything else is cheap and synchronous only. None of those families is in this version, so no operation here has an async_ variant; the list is fixed now so that a later version, or a new pin, never adds or removes one.

The variants exist only in a build with threads, where WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_THREADS is defined. A native build has threads unless the program defines WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS: the macro follows Boost.Config’s BOOST_HAS_THREADS, which Boost 1.92 defines natively on Linux, macOS and Windows whatever b2’s threading says, so threading=single alone does not remove them. On Emscripten a build has threads when it is compiled with -pthread (b2’s threading=multi); on wasip2 and wasip3 it never has.

The backends

A backend is a C library that crypto wraps; the program links the ones it names in its Jamfile, and webcpp builds each from its sources, file by file. Every table of this chapter is generated (doc/tables/generate.py) from committed data and from the tests themselves: an operation is supported on a backend and a target exactly where a test program that runs it is declared for that target, and refused where a message test stops it. The data and the tables are regenerated, and checked by the documentation’s build, at every change of a test or a pin.

A program asks the same table in C++: supports_v<Algorithm, Backend>, in <webcpp/crypto/supports.hpp>, is true exactly where the table says that the backend has the algorithm on the target being compiled, and needs neither the backend’s header nor its library, so that generic code can choose a backend at compile time. Each algorithm’s type names its family and its algorithm for it (family_type and name_type, tags of families and tags); the test that asserts every cell is generated from the same data.
