libsodium’s own test suite runs in webcpp::hash’s own lane c-suites, libs/hash/test/c_suites/Jamfile, on every target, against the same /third_party//sodium that crypto links: sign, box, box2, box7, box8, box_easy, box_easy2, box_seal, secretbox, secretbox2, secretbox7, secretbox8, secretbox_easy, secretbox_easy2, xchacha20, aead_chacha20poly1305, aead_chacha20poly13052, aead_xchacha20poly1305, kx, scalarmult, ed25519_convert, codecs.

OpenSSL is never the system’s: the superproject builds it from third_party/libs/openssl, statically, natively and on wasip2 and wasip3, and /webcpp/crypto//openssl, crypto’s name for it, stops the build on Emscripten. Natively with Clang and GCC it is built with its assembly; on MSVC, wasip2 and wasip3 it is built no-asm (INSTALL.md). A program has one copy of each library: libsecp256k1’s tables and OpenSSL’s state are global symbols, so webcpp’s build is never linked with another copy.

libsecp256k1’s precomputed tables are a size knob, the feature webcpp-secp256k1-tables: auto, the default, small on Emscripten and large elsewhere; small; or large. libsecp256k1 documents the trade: a larger window means a larger precomputed table and faster verification (configure.ac); the sizes and speeds of webcpp’s two settings are not measured yet; the fixtures sign and sign_small of Every Jamfile a user writes build both. The tables enter the canary, so a program cannot be linked with tables other than those it was compiled for. With MSVC the static library needs SECP256K1_STATIC, which the target’s usage requirements define.

Constant time

A cryptographic implementation is constant time when its running time and its memory accesses do not depend on secret data; otherwise a timing attack can recover the key (Wikipedia; BearSSL’s explanation). Each backend’s design is stated by its library’s documentation, with its source. The table’s per-target columns say what the own lane below runs on each backend and target, by checker and family, from the documentation’s data, the same as each chapter’s comparison table; "not measured yet" where the lane runs nothing. memcheck and MemorySanitizer run on Linux alone, so their native cells are Linux’s. What the lane measured where a family differs from its backend’s design is listed under the table.

Measured where a family differs from its backend’s design:

  • X25519 on libsodium, native: nothing found with arm64’s DIT (data-independent timing) bit set, as the lane runs dudect on macOS and Linux on arm64 (elsewhere its harness sets no DIT) and as Apple requires of constant-time code (Apple, Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms: enable DIT for constant-time cryptographic operations); without it, dudect times agree with an all-zero secret key against random ones at |t| 6.7 to 14.5, against the threshold 10, on an Apple M5 Max, from a release build (2026-11-19): about one nanosecond in 15 µs. libsodium does not set DIT: a program on Apple silicon sets it around its secret operations (Apple, Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms: enable DIT for constant-time cryptographic operations)

  • X25519 on libsodium, wasip2: an open finding, its cause measured: dudect times agree with an all-zero secret key against random ones at |t| 13 to 32 (2026-11-18; a fixed key against another fixed key: 22.9) and 107 to 260 (2026-11-19), against the threshold 10, under wasmtime 47 on an Apple M5 Max, from a release build. The cause is Apple silicon’s DIT (data-independent timing), which wasmtime does not set (Apple, Writing ARM64 code for Apple platforms: enable DIT for constant-time cryptographic operations): with DIT set in wasmtime’s main thread, an experiment and not the lane, the same case reads |t| 1.5 to 2.1; no branch on a secret was found in the WebAssembly or in wasmtime’s compiled code. The lane cannot set DIT from inside the WebAssembly, so it prints this value on wasip2 without judging it; the CI’s x86-64 run measures it next

The own lane constant-time (libs/crypto/test/constant_time) checks the code as webcpp compiles it. On Linux, it marks the keys, the seeds, the data and the tag secret under Valgrind’s memcheck, as ctgrind does, and, in a clang build, under MemorySanitizer, which only clang has (a gcc build runs memcheck alone): any branch or memory index that depends on them fails the run. The lane covers equal, is_all_zero and the wipe of secret<N>; BearSSL’s AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 make, seal and open; OpenSSL’s make and seal of both; ctaes’s AES; libsodium’s Ed25519 key pair and signature, X25519’s public key and agreement, its three ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEADs and two secret boxes, hybrid::box in both families, the sealed box’s seal and open, and kx; libsecp256k1’s own ctime_tests.c; and webcpp’s code around libsecp256k1: the key pair’s making, its BIP 340, recoverable and hedged ECDSA signatures and x-only tweak, ECDH in its three forms, the secret key’s tweaks and negation, PKCS#8’s encoding and decoding, ElligatorSwift’s ellswift_create and ellswift_xdh, MuSig2’s nonce_gen and partial_sign, and silent payments’ create_outputs, create_label and scan_outputs, with the wipe of their workspaces. Both checkers run the same paths, written once (paths.hpp), memcheck OpenSSL’s besides. Each check is shown to fail on a planted branch on a key byte, and each path’s output is checked to carry the mark, so that the path is traced, where the checker’s shadow keeps it: MemorySanitizer’s loses the mark through a constant-time reduction to one bit, so the result of is_all_zero, X25519’s public key and the bytes a destructor wiped are checked by memcheck alone. dudect’s statistics (Reparaz, Balasch and Verbauwhede) time BearSSL’s two AEADs’ seal and open, ctaes, equal, libsodium’s X25519 agreement and Ed25519 signing, and libsecp256k1’s ecdh_x natively, on Linux and macOS, and under wasmtime. On 64-bit ARM under macOS and Linux, each dudect program first sets the CPU’s DIT (data-independent timing) bit, with which the instructions Arm lists take a time independent of their data, and which Apple requires of constant-time code (Apple, enable DIT for constant-time cryptographic operations); it prints whether it is set, and fails where the CPU has DIT and it is not, or where macOS cannot say whether the CPU has it. Elsewhere (x86, WebAssembly, and 64-bit ARM systems the harness does not cover, MSVC on ARM64 among them) it sets nothing, prints so, and measures without DIT. The lane’s dudect_planted shows that DIT does not hide a leak: X25519’s agree after an early-exit scan of its secret key, which dudect must find. None of the C libraries sets DIT, and neither does webcpp: a program on Apple silicon sets it around its secret operations, as Apple describes (timingsafe_enable_if_supported from macOS 15.2). Without it, libsodium’s X25519 is measurably not constant time there, listed under the table.

One measurement is an open finding, listed under the table with its numbers: libsodium’s X25519 agree under wasmtime, on wasip2. Its cause is the same: wasmtime does not set DIT, and with DIT set in wasmtime’s main thread, an experiment and not the lane, the case passes. The WebAssembly cannot set it, so the lane prints its value on wasip2 without judging it, and judges everything else.

dudect’s two classes differ in the secret’s bytes and in nothing else: the preparation of each measurement reads both inputs and writes the secret with the same instructions whatever the class, since anything a class does differently before the measured call shows in its time. On a runner GitHub hosts, a virtual machine shared with other tenants whose processor changes from run to run, the lane prints each dudect |t| and judges only dudect_planted: measured there on 2026-11-20 on three processors, 23 runs of 24 stayed below 4.4 and one read 69.8, on both seeds, on a case below 4.4 in every other run, so a verdict there would pass or fail with the machine drawn. Valgrind’s memcheck and MemorySanitizer, which do not measure time, are judged there; dudect is judged wherever else the lane runs, on a machine of one’s own.

Whether a tag matched, or a shared secret came out all zero, is public by design, since the operation reports it, but it is computed from the secrets: it is the one kind of value webcpp marks public, where webcpp’s code first branches on it (BearSSL’s engines, libsodium’s engines, X25519’s agree, and each verdict of libsecp256k1’s that webcpp reads), so that the checkers report every other branch. libsecp256k1 marks its own public values (a nonce’s retry, a verdict, a public key it loads) when its context is made with SECP256K1_CONTEXT_DECLASSIFY, which webcpp’s contexts are under the checkers, as its ctime_tests.c makes its own; a key pair’s public key and a silent payments label, which webcpp reads from libsecp256k1’s structures, are marked public where webcpp reads them. libsodium branches on its own verdicts inside the functions that compute them; the lane tells memcheck of each of those functions (sodium_verdicts.supp), and libsodium is used unchanged. MemorySanitizer approximates a subtraction without its carry, so it counts every such verdict public by itself: memcheck is the check of the marks. OpenSSL’s verdict is OpenSSL’s own internal branch, which webcpp cannot mark: OpenSSL is checked with the key secret during seal only.

Size

What each cell of the capability table adds to a program, per target: a program per family and backend calls the family’s fixed operation once (test/sizes/), and its size is read against a baseline, the same harness around an operation that calls nothing of crypto, so that a cell is its operation’s code alone. The own lane sizes measures them from release builds alone (variant=release, the superproject’s webcpp.program-sizes), and the table is generated from what it wrote; a cell it has not built says so. Like the throughput below, it is a dated reference that decides nothing: a family’s default is chosen by the reason The default backend per target states.

The lane sizes measured on 2026-11-19, at variant=release: native, clang-21 on Darwin arm64, the Mach-O executable stripped, whose segments are page-aligned: a small cell can add fewer raw bytes than its code, which its gzip -9n bytes show better; wasip2, clang-wasip2, the .wasm; wasip3, clang-wasip3, the .wasm; emscripten, emscripten-6.0.11, the .wasm and its .js.

OpenSSL: its cells differ by a few bytes whatever the operation: each fetches its algorithm by name from OpenSSL’s default provider (OpenSSL 3.5’s crypto(7), algorithm fetching), and a static link brings the provider’s algorithms with it, not the operation’s alone.

libsecp256k1: a row that recovers a key or computes with a public point other than the generator (recover, MuSig2’s session, a silent payment’s output) links the precomputed table of libsecp256k1’s variable-time multiplication too, built at window 15 natively and on WASI and at window 2 on Emscripten, the small tables (libsecp256k1’s configure.ac, the precomputed tables’ trade).

Throughput

How long each family’s fixed operation takes on each backend and target, the operation the size matrix’s programs call (bench/operations.hpp). A dated reference, measured by hand, that decides nothing: every default is chosen by the reason The default backend per target states, whatever these figures say.

Measured on 2026-11-19 on Apple M5 Max (arm64), 18 cores, 128 GiB, Darwin 27.0.0; WebAssembly under wasmtime 47.0.3 (5554cc1a6 2026-07-31) (wasip2, wasip3) and node v26.13.0 (Emscripten); built with variant=release. The CI’s runners are measured when the owner runs this by hand on them.

Each cell is the median of its invocations’ medians, each of five timed runs, in microseconds per operation, with the fastest and slowest single run beside it: the spread is part of the result.

The machine’s 1, 5 and 15 minute load averages were 3/3/5 before and 3/3/5 after, on 18 cores.

OpenSSL is not built for Emscripten, so its rows are native and WASI only; on WASI it is built no-asm, natively with its assembly.

libsodium’s x86-64 assembly (design D7): Ed25519 signature, libsodium with HAVE_AMD64_ASM; X25519 agreement, libsodium with HAVE_AMD64_ASM: not measured yet. x86-64 assembly runs only on an x86-64 machine; this page’s machine is arm64. D7 asks for the rows recorded, never used: webcpp builds libsodium without it.

Wallets

A cryptocurrency wallet holds the keys that control funds on a blockchain: it makes them, keeps them secret, and signs the transactions that spend the funds (Wikipedia). Whoever holds a wallet’s secret key holds its money, and a signature over the wrong bytes spends it in a way its owner did not intend. Nothing can be recalled: a leaked key or a wrong signature is a loss.

crypto holds the primitives a wallet needs: the key pair, the signatures, their encodings and the tweak, each done by libsecp256k1. A blockchain’s rules (BIPs, EIPs) belong to a domain library built on top: it serializes the protocol’s messages, computes its hashes with Boost.Hash2, and calls these primitives. The Bitcoin steps below are what such a library builds; they are not crypto’s API.

Making and keeping a key

The problem. A wallet’s key must be unpredictable, must be a valid secret key of the curve, and must survive on disk without being readable there.

The idea. 32 bytes from random_device are a valid secp256k1 secret key with overwhelming probability; when they are not (zero, or not below the group order), make says so and the wallet draws again. At rest, the secret is sealed with AES-GCM under a key the device keeps elsewhere (a platform keystore, or a key derived from the user’s passphrase by a password hash, a hashing library’s job rather than crypto’s), with the wallet’s format version as additional data.

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
boost::system::result<secp256k1::keypair> wallet = crypto::error::backend_failure;
for (;;) {
    if (!device.fill(secret)) {
        return 1;
    }
    wallet = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
    // A secret that is zero or too large is refused: draw again. Other errors are real.
    if (wallet) {
        break;
    }
    if (wallet.error() != crypto::error::invalid_secret_key) {
        return 1;
    }
}
auto const xonly = wallet->xonly_public_key();
auto const compressed = wallet->public_key();
if (!xonly || !compressed) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("key pair made\n");
std::printf("x-only public key: %zu bytes\n", xonly->size());
// The compressed form starts with 0x02 (even y) or 0x03 (odd y).
bool const prefix_ok = (*compressed)[0] == 0x02 || (*compressed)[0] == 0x03;
std::printf("compressed public key: %zu bytes, prefix %s\n", compressed->size(),
            prefix_ok ? "ok" : "BAD");
// The device key is separate from the wallet and lives elsewhere, such as the OS keystore.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> device_key{};
std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> iv{};
if (!device.fill(device_key) || !device.fill(iv)) {
    return 1;
}
auto aead = crypto::ciphers::aes256_gcm::make(device_key);
wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(device_key)));
if (!aead) {
    return 1;
}
auto stored = secret;
wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
// "wallet v1" ties the ciphertext to its purpose and format version.
auto const tag = aead->seal(iv, bytes_of("wallet v1"), stored);
if (!tag) {
    return 1;
}

// Later: open the stored secret and make the key pair again.
if (!aead->open(iv, bytes_of("wallet v1"), stored,
                std::span<std::uint8_t const>(tag->data(), tag->size()))) {
    return 1;
}
auto restored = secp256k1::keypair::make(stored);
wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(stored)));
if (!restored) {
    return 1;
}
auto const restored_xonly = restored->xonly_public_key();
if (!restored_xonly || !crypto::equal(*xonly, *restored_xonly)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("secret sealed and restored: same public key\n");
key pair made
x-only public key: 32 bytes
compressed public key: 33 bytes, prefix ok
secret sealed and restored: same public key

Mistakes to avoid. Never derive a key from a timestamp, a counter or a general-purpose generator. Never keep the secret in clear on disk, in a log or in a backup. Wipe every copy of the secret once the key pair is made.

An ECDSA signature in DER

The problem. Bitcoin’s SegWit v0 inputs carry an ECDSA signature in strict DER (BIP 66) over a hash the protocol defines (BIP 143), in low-S form, which Bitcoin nodes require to relay a transaction (a policy; BIP 146 proposed it as a consensus rule).

The idea. The domain library computes the signature hash (SHA-256 twice over the preimage it serialized); crypto signs it, deterministically and in low-S form, and encodes the signature as strict DER. from_der decodes strict DER and refuses anything else; normalize_ecdsa gives the low-S form of a signature from a signer that does not enforce it.

// The domain library decides what is signed: here a double SHA-256 of its own preimage.
std::string_view const preimage = "example preimage";
auto const first = sha256(std::span<std::uint8_t const>(
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-reinterpret-cast)
    reinterpret_cast<std::uint8_t const*>(preimage.data()), preimage.size()));
auto const sighash = sha256(first);
auto const signature = key->sign_ecdsa(sighash);
if (!signature) {
    return 1;
}
std::array<std::uint8_t, secp256k1::max_der_size> der{};
auto const der_size = secp256k1::to_der(*signature, der);
if (!der_size) {
    return 1;
}
print("der", std::span<std::uint8_t const>(der).first(*der_size));
// The high-S twin: same r, s replaced by n - s.
auto high = *signature;
auto const flipped = order_minus(std::span<std::uint8_t const, 64>(high).last<32>());
std::ranges::copy(flipped, high.begin() + 32);
auto const refused = secp256k1::verify_ecdsa(high, sighash, *public_key);
if (refused || refused.error() != crypto::error::invalid_signature) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("high-S refused: invalid_signature\n");
// A signature from elsewhere can be brought to the low-S form before it is checked.
auto const normalized = secp256k1::normalize_ecdsa(high);
if (!normalized || *normalized != *signature ||
    !secp256k1::verify_ecdsa(*normalized, sighash, *public_key)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("normalized to low-S: verified\n");
der 30440220149707552281c27e046808f5249507fbf54ca85db51fc2d06a7ab491
    ccd7aef802202790de468aad416701a4148b2527c8aeb3ed98c95828e21affd8
    06486170617a
strict der round trip ok
verified
high-S refused: invalid_signature
normalized to low-S: verified

Mistakes to avoid. Compare the domain library’s hashes with the protocol’s published vectors: a wrong preimage signs a valid signature over the wrong thing. Never sign with a nonce of your own: RFC 6979’s deterministic nonce is what keeps a weak generator from leaking the key.

A tweaked key: Taproot

The problem. A Taproot output key is the wallet’s internal key tweaked by t = tagged_hash("TapTweak", internal_key || merkle_root) (BIP 341); spending by key path signs with the tweaked key pair.

The idea. The tweak is the protocol’s; the addition on the curve is crypto’s. The domain library computes t with Boost.Hash2’s SHA-256 (a tagged hash is SHA-256(SHA-256(tag) || SHA-256(tag) || data)) and passes it to tweak_xonly, once on the public key for the address, once on the key pair to sign:

// The tweak is the domain library's business; the library only applies it.
auto const tweak = tagged_hash("TapTweak", *internal_key);
auto const output = secp256k1::tweak_xonly(*internal_key, tweak);
if (!output) {
    return 1;
}
print("output key", output->key);
std::printf("parity %d\n", output->parity);
// The owner applies the same tweak to the key pair and signs for the output key.
if (!key->tweak_xonly(tweak)) {
    return 1;
}
auto const tweaked_public = key->xonly_public_key();
if (!tweaked_public || !crypto::equal(*tweaked_public, output->key)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("key pair tweaked: same output key\n");

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const message{};
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const aux{};
auto const signature = key->sign_schnorr(message, aux);
if (!signature || !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, output->key)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("key-path signature verified\n");
output key 418c46636d9e1a683f58e35b42336e776fdcc3b2d4e39e7a0bf1ab0716e3c5fa
parity 0
key pair tweaked: same output key
key-path signature verified

Without a script tree, as here, the Merkle root is omitted and the tweak hashes the internal key alone (BIP 341). crypto checks the key and the tweak, and wipes the pair if the tweak gives no valid key; what the tweak means is the domain library’s.

The x-only tweak is BIP 341’s arithmetic: it lifts the key to the point with an even y, and the key pair’s version negates the secret key when the public key’s y is odd. It serves the protocols built on x-only keys, such as Taproot’s output key or a pay-to-contract commitment to an x-only key. It is not BIP 32’s child derivation, which adds to the parent’s full point and secret key without that negation: for the half of the parents whose public key has an odd y, an x-only tweak derives another child than every BIP 32 wallet, whose addresses a wallet restored from the same seed never finds. BIP 32 tweaks the full key, with seckey_tweak_add and pubkey_tweak_add (Tweaks, negation and combination), and computes its tweak with HMAC-SHA-512, which is a domain library’s (BIP 32).

Mistakes to avoid. A Taproot tweak is computed from public data (the internal key and the Merkle root), so the tweaked secret key is as sensitive as the original: anyone who knows the tweak and either secret key knows the other. Check the domain library’s tweak against BIP 341’s published vectors.

Who signed this? Recoverable signatures

The problem. A wallet app receives a request that another wallet signed: a transaction to relay, or a message that proves who owns an account. The request carries the signed bytes and the signature, but no public key, and the app must know whose key signed it before it acts on it.

The idea. An ECDSA signature leaves its signer’s public key one of a few candidates; a recoverable signature adds the id, 0 to 3, of the one that verifies, so that a reader computes the signer’s key from the signature and the hash alone. Ethereum finds a transaction’s sender this way (Ethereum’s yellow paper, appendix F). sign_recoverable makes the 65 bytes, and recover finds the key (Recoverable signatures). Recovery finds some key for almost any signature and any hash: what makes it a check is the comparison with the key the reader expects.

// The reader holds no key of the wallet's: it parses the published key once, recovers the
// signer's key from the 65-byte signature and the hash, and compares the two.
auto const expected = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*published);
auto const signer = secp256k1::recover(*signature, sha256(message));
if (!expected || !signer || *signer != *expected) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("recovered the wallet's key\n");

// A changed message still recovers a key, but not the wallet's.
message = "pay 99 to bob";
auto const other = secp256k1::recover(*signature, sha256(message));
if (other && *other == *expected) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("a changed message names another signer\n");
recovered the wallet's key
a changed message names another signer

Ethereum compares addresses rather than keys, the last 20 bytes of the Keccak-256 of the uncompressed key (the yellow paper, appendix F), and a wallet signs a message after EIP-191’s prefix (EIP-191). Both are the protocol’s rules, which a domain library built on crypto, such as a future webcpp::ethereum, computes; crypto holds the signature and the recovery. This section names no application.

Mistakes to avoid. Never trust a recovered key on its own: a changed or forged message recovers some other key rather than failing, so compare the key, or the address made from it, with the one expected before acting. Hash exactly what the signer hashed: a message hashed without EIP-191’s prefix, or with another, recovers another key, which looks like a wrong signer rather than a wrong hash.

Two devices, one signature: MuSig2

The problem. A wallet split across a phone and a laptop, so that a thief who takes one device takes nothing: spending needs both. A script that asks for two signatures shows on the chain that two keys hold the coins, and costs more to spend.

The idea. MuSig2 aggregates the two public keys into one, and the two devices’ partial signatures into one BIP 340 signature under it, which the chain checks as any single signer’s (BIP 327). It takes two rounds: each device makes a nonce and sends its public half; with both in, each signs its part, and the parts add up to the signature (MuSig2: many signers, one signature).

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <utility>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace musig = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::musig;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Each device's key pair; each sends the other its public key.
    auto const phone = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x11));
    auto const laptop = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x22));
    if (!phone || !laptop) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const phone_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*phone->public_key());
    auto const laptop_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*laptop->public_key());
    if (!phone_key || !laptop_key) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Both sort the keys (BIP 327's KeySort) and aggregate them: the same key on both devices.
    // The workspace holds libsecp256k1's array of pointers; nothing is allocated.
    std::array<secp256k1::public_key, 2> keys{*phone_key, *laptop_key};
    std::ranges::sort(keys);
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, musig::workspace_size(2)> space{};
    auto const wallet_key = musig::key_aggregate(keys, space);
    if (!wallet_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("aggregate key made from %zu signers\n", keys.size());

    // The spend both approve: the transaction's 32-byte hash, as a domain library computes it.
    auto const message = repeated(0x5a);

    // Round one: each device makes a nonce for this signature and sends its public half.
    auto phone_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*phone, *wallet_key, message);
    auto laptop_nonce = musig::nonce_gen(*laptop, *wallet_key, message);
    if (!phone_nonce || !laptop_nonce) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Once both public nonces are in, each device computes the same session.
    std::array<musig::public_nonce, 2> const nonces{
        phone_nonce->public_part,
        laptop_nonce->public_part,
    };
    auto const nonce_sum = musig::nonce_aggregate(nonces, space);
    if (!nonce_sum) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const signing_session = musig::nonce_process(*nonce_sum, message, *wallet_key);
    if (!signing_session) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Round two: each signs its part, which consumes its secret nonce; the other checks it.
    auto const phone_part = musig::partial_sign(*phone, std::move(phone_nonce->secret_part),
                                                *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    auto const laptop_part = musig::partial_sign(*laptop, std::move(laptop_nonce->secret_part),
                                                 *wallet_key, *signing_session);
    if (!phone_part || !laptop_part ||
        !musig::partial_signature_verify(*phone_part, nonces[0], *phone_key, *wallet_key,
                                         *signing_session) ||
        !musig::partial_signature_verify(*laptop_part, nonces[1], *laptop_key, *wallet_key,
                                         *signing_session)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("both partial signatures verify\n");

    // The parts add up to one BIP 340 signature under the wallet's one x-only key.
    std::array<musig::partial_signature, 2> const parts{*phone_part, *laptop_part};
    auto const signature = musig::partial_signature_aggregate(*signing_session, parts, space);
    if (!signature ||
        !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, wallet_key->xonly_public_key())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the aggregate signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature\n");
    return 0;
}
aggregate key made from 2 signers
both partial signatures verify
the aggregate signature verifies as one BIP 340 signature

The wallet’s address, its transactions and the hash each device signs are a domain library’s. This section names no application.

Mistakes to avoid. Reusing a nonce: two partial signatures with one nonce give away the secret key, so a nonce is made when the signature is made, never stored, and never restored from a backup; partial_sign takes it by value and refuses one already used. Signing before every nonce is in: a device that signs while the other can still choose its nonce lets it steer the final nonce, which the two rounds exist to prevent (Nick, Ruffing and Seurin, MuSig2). A naive key sum: the plain sum of the two public keys, pubkey_combine, is not a multisignature, since a device that announces its key after seeing the other’s can choose one that cancels it and spend alone; key_aggregate weighs each key by a hash of all of them (BIP 327).

A reusable address: silent payments

The problem. A donation page wants one address to publish for good. With a plain address every payment to it is on the chain for anyone to list and add up, and a fresh address for each payer needs a server that hands them out.

The idea. A silent payment address is two public keys, scan and spend. The sender combines the secret keys of its transaction’s inputs with the scan key into a secret only it and the recipient share, an ECDH, and tweaks the spend key with it into an output key that is new for each transaction; the recipient scans each transaction with its scan secret and recognises its outputs (BIP 352; Silent payments).

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/tweak.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace silent_payments = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::silent_payments;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

using output_key = std::array<std::uint8_t, 32>;
using outpoint = std::array<std::uint8_t, silent_payments::outpoint_size>;

// The donor's wallet pays the address with one input: one output key, the transaction's.
bool pay(silent_payments::recipient const& address, secp256k1::keypair const& donor_input,
         outpoint const& smallest_outpoint, output_key& paid_key) {
    std::array<silent_payments::recipient, 1> const recipients{address};
    std::array<secp256k1::keypair const*, 1> const plain_inputs{&donor_input};
    std::array<output_key, 1> outputs{};
    // The workspace holds libsecp256k1's arrays and the input's secret; it is wiped on return.
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, silent_payments::send_workspace_size(1, 0, 1)>
        space{};
    if (!silent_payments::create_outputs(recipients, smallest_outpoint, {}, plain_inputs, outputs,
                                         space)) {
        return false;
    }
    paid_key = outputs[0];
    return true;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // The donation page: its scan and spend key pairs stay with the recipient; the address is
    // their two public keys.
    auto const scan_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x51));
    // The spend secret is kept, in a secret<32> that wipes itself, to spend what is found.
    webcpp::crypto::secret<32> spend_secret;
    std::ranges::fill(spend_secret.writable(), std::uint8_t{0x52});
    auto const spend_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(spend_secret.bytes());
    auto const donor = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x53));
    if (!scan_pair || !spend_pair || !donor) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const scan_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*scan_pair->public_key());
    auto const spend_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*spend_pair->public_key());
    auto const donor_key = secp256k1::parse_public_key(*donor->public_key());
    if (!scan_key || !spend_key || !donor_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    silent_payments::recipient const address{.scan_key = *scan_key, .spend_key = *spend_key};

    // The donor pays: the transaction spends one input, whose outpoint is its smallest.
    outpoint first_outpoint{};
    first_outpoint.fill(0x01);
    output_key first_payment{};
    if (!pay(address, *donor, first_outpoint, first_payment)) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The recipient sees the transaction: its input's public key and smallest outpoint make the
    // summary, and the scan of its outputs finds the payment.
    std::array<secp256k1::public_key, 1> const input_keys{*donor_key};
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, silent_payments::summary_workspace_size(0, 1)>
        summary_space{};
    auto const summary =
        silent_payments::make_prevouts_summary(first_outpoint, {}, input_keys, summary_space);
    if (!summary) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::array<output_key, 1> const transaction_outputs{first_payment};
    std::array<silent_payments::found_output, 1> found{};
    alignas(std::max_align_t) std::array<std::byte, silent_payments::scan_workspace_size(1)>
        scan_space{};
    auto const found_count = silent_payments::scan_outputs(*scan_pair, *spend_key, *summary,
                                                           transaction_outputs, found, scan_space);
    if (!found_count) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the recipient found %zu output\n", *found_count);

    // The spend secret plus the found tweak is the output's secret key.
    auto const output_secret = secp256k1::seckey_tweak_add(spend_secret, found[0].spend_tweak);
    if (!output_secret) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const spending_pair = secp256k1::keypair::make(output_secret->bytes());
    if (!spending_pair) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const spending_key = spending_pair->xonly_public_key();
    if (!spending_key || *spending_key != found[0].output_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("the spending key matches the output\n");

    // A second donation from the same wallet, another transaction: another outpoint.
    outpoint second_outpoint{};
    second_outpoint.fill(0x02);
    output_key second_payment{};
    if (!pay(address, *donor, second_outpoint, second_payment)) {
        return 1;
    }
    if (second_payment != first_payment) {
        std::printf("two payments to one address share no output key\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
the recipient found 1 output
the spending key matches the output
two payments to one address share no output key

The address’s encoding, the choice of inputs and the transaction are a domain library’s. This section names no application.

Mistakes to avoid. The outpoint: it must be the smallest of all the transaction’s inputs, eligible or not; with another, the sender computes another secret and the recipient never finds the payment. A dropped output: every output create_outputs makes must be in the transaction, since the recipient looks for them in order and stops at the first it does not find (libsecp256k1’s silent payments header). Scanning cost: the recipient pays one ECDH for every transaction with eligible inputs, its own or not, which a light client must plan for (BIP 352).

Peer-to-peer applications

In a peer-to-peer application the participants talk to each other rather than through a server they trust (Wikipedia): a chat between browsers over WebRTC, notes posted to public relays, files shared directly. Whatever carries the bytes, a relay or a signalling server, sees all of them and may change them. Cryptography is what lets the peers trust each other instead: a signature proves who wrote a message, and a key agreed in public keeps the conversation private.

Identities and sessions between peers

The problem. Peers of a network find each other through untrusted relays and discovery services. Each needs a name that no one else can claim, and each connection between two peers must be private and must reach the peer it names, not an impostor in the middle.

The idea. libp2p, a peer-to-peer networking stack, does it this way: a peer’s identity is a key pair, Ed25519 among the types its specification allows, and its id is derived from the public key (libp2p’s peer ids); each connection agrees fresh X25519 keys and seals with ChaCha20-Poly1305, and each side signs its connection key with its identity key, so that the other knows whom it reached (libp2p’s Noise handshake). webcpp’s primitives give each piece: an Ed25519 key pair and its signatures (Ed25519), and a session key for each direction from two X25519 key pairs, libsodium’s crypto_kx (Key exchange: crypto_kx), with ChaCha20-Poly1305 for the messages (ChaCha20-Poly1305). The handshake’s own steps, Noise’s patterns and libp2p’s framing, are a domain library’s to build from them, not this library’s API.

A peer’s identity: the key pair, a signature over what it says, and anyone’s check of it with the public key alone.

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519.hpp>

#include <webcpp/hash/algorithms.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace ed25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519;

namespace {

// Prints bytes in hex after a name, 32 bytes (64 digits) to a line, the lines after the first
// indented under the first, so that a long value stays readable on a narrow page.
void print(char const* name, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    int const indent = std::printf("%s ", name);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < bytes.size(); ++i) {
        if (i != 0 && i % 32 == 0) {
            std::printf("\n%*s", indent, "");
        }
        std::printf("%02x", bytes[i]);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// Ed25519: one message in one call.
bool sign_whole() {
    // RFC 8032 section 7.1, TEST 2: a published seed, never a real key; a program draws its
    // own with keypair::generate().
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const seed{
        0x4c, 0xcd, 0x08, 0x9b, 0x28, 0xff, 0x96, 0xda, 0x9d, 0xb6, 0xc3,
        0x46, 0xec, 0x11, 0x4e, 0x0f, 0x5b, 0x8a, 0x31, 0x9f, 0x35, 0xab,
        0xa6, 0x24, 0xda, 0x8c, 0xf6, 0xed, 0x4f, 0xb8, 0xa6, 0xfb,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 1> const message{0x72};
    auto const key = ed25519::keypair::make(seed);
    if (!key) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const public_key = key->public_key();
    auto const signature = key->sign(message);
    if (!public_key || !signature) {
        return false;
    }
    print("public key", *public_key);
    print("signature ", *signature);
    // The verifier holds the public key, the message and the signature; nothing secret.
    return ed25519::verify(*public_key, message, *signature).has_value();
}

// Ed25519ph: the message given in pieces, as a large file is read, signed once at the end,
// over SHA-512, the hash RFC 8032 fixes.
bool sign_in_pieces() {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const seed{
        0x83, 0x3f, 0xe6, 0x24, 0x09, 0x23, 0x7b, 0x9d, 0x62, 0xec, 0x77,
        0x58, 0x75, 0x20, 0x91, 0x1e, 0x9a, 0x75, 0x9c, 0xec, 0x1d, 0x19,
        0x75, 0x5b, 0x7d, 0xa9, 0x01, 0xb9, 0x6d, 0xca, 0x3d, 0x42,
    };
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 1> const first{'a'};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 2> const second{'b', 'c'};
    using signer = ed25519::ph<webcpp::hash::sha2_512>;
    auto const key = ed25519::keypair::make(seed);
    auto signing = signer::begin();
    if (!key || !signing || !signing->update(first) || !signing->update(second)) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const public_key = key->public_key();
    auto const signature = signing->sign(*key);
    if (!public_key || !signature) {
        return false;
    }
    print("public key", *public_key);
    print("signature ", *signature);
    auto verifying = signer::begin();
    return verifying && verifying->update(first) && verifying->update(second) &&
           verifying->verify(*public_key, *signature).has_value();
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    if (!sign_whole() || !sign_in_pieces()) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("verified\n");
    return 0;
}

A session: the client’s and the server’s key pairs, their session keys, and a message sealed with one side’s transmit key and opened with the other’s receive key.

#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/chacha20_poly1305.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519/kx.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace x25519 = webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519;

namespace {

// Prints bytes in hex after a name.
void print(char const* name, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    std::printf("%s ", name);
    for (auto const byte : bytes) {
        std::printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// The client sends "hello" to the server, sealed with the client's transmit key and opened with
// the server's receive key, the same key.
bool message(x25519::session_keys const& client, x25519::session_keys const& server) {
    auto sealer = crypto::ciphers::chacha20_poly1305<>::make(client.transmit.bytes());
    auto opener = crypto::ciphers::chacha20_poly1305<>::make(server.receive.bytes());
    if (!sealer || !opener) {
        return false;
    }
    // The first message of this direction: nonce 0. Each next message takes the next number;
    // a nonce is never used twice under one key.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> const nonce{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 5> data{'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o'};
    auto const tag = sealer->seal(nonce, {}, data);
    if (!tag || !opener->open(nonce, {}, data, *tag)) {
        return false;
    }
    std::printf("server read   ");
    for (auto const byte : data) {
        std::printf("%c", byte);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
    return true;
}

bool client_and_server() {
    // libsodium's kx test's seeds, published, never real ones: a program calls
    // kx_keypair<>::generate(), which draws its seed with random_device.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> client_seed{};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < client_seed.size(); ++i) {
        client_seed[i] = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(i);
    }
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> server_seed = client_seed;
    server_seed[0] = 1;
    auto const client = x25519::kx_keypair<>::make(client_seed);
    auto const server = x25519::kx_keypair<>::make(server_seed);
    if (!client || !server) {
        return false;
    }
    // Each side sends its public key; the secret keys never leave the key pairs.
    auto const client_public = client->public_key();
    auto const server_public = server->public_key();
    if (!client_public || !server_public) {
        return false;
    }
    print("client public", *client_public);
    print("server public", *server_public);
    auto const client_keys = client->client_session_keys(*server_public);
    auto const server_keys = server->server_session_keys(*client_public);
    if (!client_keys || !server_keys) {
        return false;
    }
    // Printed here only because libsodium's test publishes them; a program never prints a key.
    print("client rx    ", client_keys->receive.bytes());
    print("client tx    ", client_keys->transmit.bytes());
    return crypto::equal(client_keys->transmit.bytes(), server_keys->receive.bytes()) &&
           crypto::equal(client_keys->receive.bytes(), server_keys->transmit.bytes()) &&
           message(*client_keys, *server_keys);
}

// A peer key of low order gives an all-zero X25519 secret, which crypto_kx refuses.
bool low_order_refused() {
    auto const key = x25519::kx_keypair<>::make(std::array<std::uint8_t, 32>{});
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const zero_point{};
    if (!key) {
        return false;
    }
    auto const keys = key->server_session_keys(zero_point);
    if (!keys && keys.error() == crypto::error::weak_public_key) {
        std::printf("low order     refused: weak_public_key\n");
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    if (!client_and_server() || !low_order_refused()) {
        std::printf("failed\n");
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("agreed\n");
    return 0;
}
