Mistakes to avoid. A session key pair is drawn for each connection and never kept: the identity key signs it, so that a stolen identity key does not open past sessions. A public key received during a handshake proves nothing until its signature, by an identity the program already trusts, verifies. A nonce is never repeated under a session key: number the messages of each direction from zero.

Proving who wrote a message

The problem. Peers exchange messages through a public relay that anyone can post to. How does a reader know a message comes from its author and was not changed?

The idea. The author signs the message’s hash with a secret key; any reader verifies with the author’s public key. A valid signature proves that the holder of the secret key signed exactly these bytes. Nostr’s events, for one, are signed this way, with BIP 340 over the event’s SHA-256 (NIP-01).

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

boost::system::result<secp256k1::keypair> generate_key() {
    crypto::random_device device;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
    for (;;) {
        auto const filled = device.fill(secret);
        if (!filled) {
            return filled.error();
        }
        auto key = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
        // Not every 32 bytes are a key (zero, or too large), which is astronomically rare:
        // draw again. Any other error is real.
        if (key || key.error() != crypto::error::invalid_secret_key) {
            // The key pair keeps its own copy, which it wipes; this one goes now.
            wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
            return key;
        }
    }
}
auto const id = id_of("meet at noon");
// Fresh aux bytes make the signature unpredictable and guard against fault attacks.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> aux{};
if (!crypto::random_device().fill(aux)) {
    return 1;
}
auto const signature = author->sign_schnorr(id, aux);
if (!signature) {
    return 1;
}
// The reader needs only the message, the signature and the public key.
if (!secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, id_of("meet at noon"), *public_key)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("verified\n");
auto const altered = secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, id_of("meet at nine"), *public_key);
if (altered || altered.error() != crypto::error::invalid_signature) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("altered message refused: invalid_signature\n");
verified
altered message refused: invalid_signature

Mistakes to avoid. Verify before parsing or acting on a message. A signature proves authorship, not secrecy: sign, then encrypt what is private. A public key received with the message proves nothing; the reader must already know the author’s key.

Agreeing on a key in public

The problem. Two browsers want to talk privately through a relay that sees every byte. They have never met and share no secret.

The idea. With elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman each side combines its own secret key with the other’s public key and arrives at the same 32-byte secret, which the relay cannot compute from the public keys alone (Wikipedia). That secret is not a key yet: HKDF turns it into one, bound to the application by a label (RFC 5869). HKDF is a few lines on Boost.Hash2’s HMAC, checked here against the RFC’s first test case before it is used:

// HKDF-SHA-256 (RFC 5869): extract concentrates the input's entropy into a pseudorandom key,
// expand stretches it into as many bytes as asked, each block bound to the info string.
template <std::size_t Length>
std::array<std::uint8_t, Length> hkdf_sha256(std::span<std::uint8_t const> input,
                                             std::span<std::uint8_t const> salt,
                                             std::span<std::uint8_t const> info) {
    static_assert(Length <= std::size_t{255} * 32);
    // An empty salt stands for a block of zeros.
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const zeros{};
    if (salt.empty()) {
        salt = zeros;
    }
    hash2::hmac_sha2_256 extract(salt.data(), salt.size());
    extract.update(input.data(), input.size());
    auto prk = extract.result();
    wipe_object(extract);

    std::array<std::uint8_t, Length> out{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> previous{};
    std::size_t previous_size = 0;
    std::size_t offset = 0;
    for (std::uint8_t counter = 1; offset < Length; ++counter) {
        hash2::hmac_sha2_256 expand(prk.data(), prk.size());
        expand.update(previous.data(), previous_size);
        expand.update(info.data(), info.size());
        expand.update(&counter, 1);
        auto block = expand.result();
        wipe_object(expand);
        std::copy_n(block.data(), block.size(), previous.begin());
        wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(block)));
        previous_size = previous.size();
        std::size_t const taken = std::min(previous.size(), Length - offset);
        std::copy_n(previous.begin(), taken, out.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(offset));
        offset += taken;
    }
    // The pseudorandom key and the last block are as secret as the input, and so are the HMACs
    // keyed with them, wiped above: wipe them.
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(prk)));
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(previous)));
    return out;
}
auto alice = generate_key();
auto bob = generate_key();
if (!alice || !bob) {
    return 1;
}
// Each side sends its public key (33 bytes) and keeps its secret.
auto const alice_public = alice->public_key();
auto const bob_public = bob->public_key();
if (!alice_public || !bob_public) {
    return 1;
}
// The shared secrets live only in this block: each is a secret<32>, which wipes itself at
// the block's end, as soon as the session ciphers are made from it.
std::optional<crypto::ciphers::aes256_gcm> alice_cipher;
std::optional<crypto::ciphers::aes256_gcm> bob_cipher;
{
    auto const alice_shared = alice->ecdh(*bob_public);
    auto const bob_shared = bob->ecdh(*alice_public);
    if (!alice_shared || !bob_shared ||
        !crypto::equal(alice_shared->bytes(), bob_shared->bytes())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("shared secrets match\n");
    auto alice_made = session_cipher(*alice_shared);
    auto bob_made = session_cipher(*bob_shared);
    if (!alice_made || !bob_made) {
        return 1;
    }
    alice_cipher.emplace(std::move(*alice_made));
    bob_cipher.emplace(std::move(*bob_made));
}
hkdf matches rfc 5869
shared secrets match
bob read: hello bob

Mistakes to avoid. ECDH alone does not tell Alice that the public key really is Bob’s: an attacker in the middle can swap both keys and read everything (Wikipedia). Sign the public keys (Proving who wrote a message), or compare a fingerprint out of band. Never use the shared secret directly as a key, or as several keys: derive one key per purpose, each with its own label. Draw fresh key pairs for each session, as the example does: with long-lived key pairs, whoever later steals a secret key computes every past session’s secret from the recorded public keys, while fresh pairs wiped after the session give forward secrecy (Wikipedia); a long-lived key signs the fresh public keys instead. ecdh returns libsecp256k1’s hashed form, the SHA-256 of the compressed shared point, as a secret<32> that wipes itself: both sides must use the same form, and a protocol that takes the raw x coordinate, such as Nostr’s NIP-44, needs ecdh_x (Three forms of ECDH).

A shared key in Nostr’s direct messages

The problem. A Nostr chat app sends a private message to a contact through public relays, which keep every event and serve it to anyone who asks. The two users know each other only by their public keys, the secp256k1 keys that sign their notes.

The idea. Each side combines its secret key with the other’s public key, an ECDH, and both find the same shared point. Nostr’s encrypted payloads take its x coordinate unhashed, and derive from it a conversation key, HKDF-extract with the salt nip44-v2, then a key for each message (NIP-44). ecdh_x gives the x coordinate as a secret<32> (Three forms of ECDH); the conversation key and everything after it, the message keys, the padding and the payload’s format, are NIP-44’s, which a domain library built on crypto and hash, such as a future webcpp::nostr, derives. The example computes the conversation key only to show where the x coordinate goes:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/sha2.hpp>
#include <boost/system/result.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string_view>
#include <type_traits>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;
namespace hash2 = boost::hash2;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

// Wipes an object of key-derived state, such as an HMAC whose inner and outer states hold the
// key: its bytes are all it is, so overwriting them leaves nothing of the key.
template <class T>
void wipe_object(T& object) {
    static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(&object, 1)));
}

std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes_of(std::string_view text) {
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-reinterpret-cast)
    return {reinterpret_cast<std::uint8_t const*>(text.data()), text.size()};
}

void print_hex(char const* label, std::span<std::uint8_t const> bytes) {
    std::printf("%s", label);
    for (std::uint8_t const octet : bytes) {
        std::printf("%02x", static_cast<unsigned>(octet));
    }
    std::printf("\n");
}

// NIP-44's conversation key: HKDF-extract (RFC 5869), an HMAC-SHA-256 keyed with the salt
// "nip44-v2" over the shared x coordinate. A NIP-44 library computes it; the message keys,
// the padding and the payload's format that follow are the protocol's too.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> conversation_key(crypto::secret<32> const& shared_x) {
    auto const salt = bytes_of("nip44-v2");
    hash2::hmac_sha2_256 extract(salt.data(), salt.size());
    extract.update(shared_x.bytes().data(), crypto::secret<32>::size());
    auto digest = extract.result();
    wipe_object(extract);
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> key{};
    std::span<std::uint8_t const> const digest_bytes(digest.data(), digest.size());
    std::ranges::copy(digest_bytes, key.begin());
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(digest.data(), digest.size())));
    return key;
}

boost::system::result<secp256k1::keypair> from_secret(std::uint8_t fill) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
    secret.fill(fill);
    auto made = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
    // The key pair keeps its own copy, which it wipes; this one goes now.
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
    return made;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Fixed secrets, so that the output is fixed. A real program draws its secret keys from
    // random_device, as wallet_key.cpp does.
    auto const alice = from_secret(0x11);
    auto const bob = from_secret(0x22);
    if (!alice || !bob) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const alice_public = alice->public_key();
    auto const bob_public = bob->public_key();
    if (!alice_public || !bob_public) {
        return 1;
    }
    // Each side combines its secret key with the other's public key: the same x coordinate,
    // a secret<32> that wipes itself.
    auto const alice_x = alice->ecdh_x(*bob_public);
    auto const bob_x = bob->ecdh_x(*alice_public);
    if (!alice_x || !bob_x || !crypto::equal(alice_x->bytes(), bob_x->bytes())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("shared x coordinates match\n");

    // A real program never prints a shared secret; this one does to show the fixed value.
    print_hex("x: ", alice_x->bytes());
    auto key = conversation_key(*alice_x);
    print_hex("conversation key (what a NIP-44 library derives): ", key);
    wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(key)));
    return 0;
}
shared x coordinates match
x: 77e0510d5042e2f5e9e59c977b81eeed590cf7d20c1c51da451a8eaa9fdc45ff
conversation key (what a NIP-44 library derives): 2cbdf074f601178c24da3f829b504507a1f550f97d472af0f3f2cc59ab7757d1

This section names no application.

Mistakes to avoid. Hashing the x coordinate differently on the two sides: ecdh hashes the compressed shared point with SHA-256, libsecp256k1’s default, and a side that uses it while the other takes the raw x coordinate gets another key, so that every message fails to open with nothing pointing at the cause. Reusing the conversation key as a message key: it is the same for every message between the two users, in both directions; NIP-44 derives each message’s keys from it and a fresh 32-byte nonce, and a program that encrypts with the conversation key itself repeats its keys across messages.

A handshake an observer cannot recognise

The problem. A node of a peer-to-peer network, a Bitcoin node or a messenger, opens connections that a box on the path may want to recognise and block. A handshake that starts with a public key is easy to spot: a compressed key begins with 02 or 03, and its next 32 bytes are always the x coordinate of a point of the curve, which only about half of all random strings are.

The idea. Bitcoin’s version 2 transport sends each peer’s key as an ElligatorSwift encoding instead: 64 bytes, made from the key pair and fresh randomness, that cannot be told from random ones; both peers compute the same secret from the two encodings (BIP 324; ElligatorSwift: keys that look like noise). The secret feeds the protocol’s key schedule; that schedule and the protocol’s packets are BIP 324’s, a domain library’s.

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/ellswift.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/equal.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;

namespace {

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> repeated(std::uint8_t value) {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> bytes{};
    bytes.fill(value);
    return bytes;
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // Each peer's key pair and the randomness of its encoding (random_device in a real program).
    auto const initiator = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x11));
    auto const responder = secp256k1::keypair::make(repeated(0x22));
    if (!initiator || !responder) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Each peer sends the 64 bytes ellswift_create makes from its key pair.
    auto const initiator_message = secp256k1::ellswift_create(*initiator, repeated(0x33));
    auto const responder_message = secp256k1::ellswift_create(*responder, repeated(0x44));
    if (!initiator_message || !responder_message) {
        return 1;
    }

    // Each message decodes to its sender's public key; any 64 bytes decode to some key.
    auto const initiator_key = initiator->public_key();
    auto const responder_key = responder->public_key();
    if (!initiator_key || !responder_key ||
        secp256k1::serialize_public_key(secp256k1::ellswift_decode(*initiator_message)) !=
            *initiator_key ||
        secp256k1::serialize_public_key(secp256k1::ellswift_decode(*responder_message)) !=
            *responder_key) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("each 64-byte message decodes to its sender's key\n");

    // Both pass the two messages in the same order, the initiator's first, and name their own
    // side; the shared secret is the input of the protocol's key schedule, not a key itself.
    auto const initiator_secret = secp256k1::ellswift_xdh(
        *initiator, *initiator_message, *responder_message, secp256k1::ellswift_party::initiator);
    auto const responder_secret = secp256k1::ellswift_xdh(
        *responder, *initiator_message, *responder_message, secp256k1::ellswift_party::responder);
    if (!initiator_secret || !responder_secret ||
        !crypto::equal(initiator_secret->bytes(), responder_secret->bytes())) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("initiator and responder agree\n");
    return 0;
}
each 64-byte message decodes to its sender's key
initiator and responder agree

The encodings hide that a key exchange happens, not who takes part: both peers’ addresses stay visible to whoever watches the connection. This section names no application.

Mistakes to avoid. Draw fresh randomness for every encoding: the same key with the same randomness gives the same 64 bytes, which links two connections of one node. Pass the two encodings in the protocol’s order, the initiator’s first, and name the right party: a side that passes them in its own order computes another secret, and the connection fails with nothing pointing at the cause. Never use the secret as a key by itself: BIP 324 derives its session’s keys from it with HKDF.

Everyday applications

Most programs that need cryptography are not about cryptography: a login form, a shop, a file-sharing app, a program that updates itself. Each needs a few primitives used exactly right. This chapter gathers them; each section links to the chapter that teaches the primitive.

A file-sharing app: secret boxes and sealed boxes

The problem. A file-sharing app stores files on a server, or in a cloud bucket, that its users do not control. Whoever runs the storage, or breaks into it, reads every file, and can change one before the recipient downloads it. The recipient is known only by a public key, published once; the sender and the recipient are never online together.

The idea. age, a file encryption tool and format, does it this way (the age format): the file is encrypted once under a key drawn for that file alone, and that file key is encrypted to each recipient’s X25519 public key, with a key pair drawn for the purpose, so that the recipient’s secret key alone recovers it. webcpp’s primitives do the same in libsodium’s formats: the file in a secret box (Secret boxes) under a fresh 32-byte key, and the key in a sealed box to the recipient (Sealed boxes). Each file has its own key, so a leaked key opens one file; the tag of each box makes any change to the upload fail to open, never decrypt to something else. age’s own steps, its header, its recipient stanzas and its chunked payload, are a domain library’s to build from these primitives; this program does not read age files.

// The sender: a key for this file alone, the file in a secret box under it, the key sealed to
// the recipient.
bool share(crypto::random_device& device, std::span<std::uint8_t const> recipient_public_key,
           std::string_view contents, upload& out) {
    crypto::secret<32> file_key;
    if (!device.fill(file_key.writable()) || !device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    auto box = secretbox<>::make(file_key.bytes());
    if (!box) {
        return false;
    }
    out.file.assign(contents.begin(), contents.end());
    auto const tag = box->seal(out.nonce, {}, out.file);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return sealed_box::seal(recipient_public_key, file_key.bytes(), out.sealed_key).has_value();
}
// The recipient: the file key out of the sealed box, then the file out of the secret box.
void receive(char const* who, std::span<std::uint8_t const> public_key,
             std::span<std::uint8_t const> secret_key, upload received) {
    crypto::secret<32> file_key;
    auto const key_opened =
        sealed_box::open(public_key, secret_key, received.sealed_key, file_key.writable());
    if (!key_opened) {
        std::string const reason = key_opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s: the file key refused: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    auto box = secretbox<>::make(file_key.bytes());
    if (!box) {
        return;
    }
    auto const opened = box->open(received.nonce, {}, received.file, received.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s: the file refused: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("%s read: %.*s\n", who, static_cast<int>(received.file.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(received.file.data()));
}
on the wire: 80 bytes of sealed key, 24 of nonce, 16 of tag, 25 of file
the recipient read: quarterly report, draft 3
the recipient, the upload changed: the file refused: the authentication tag does not match
another key pair: the file key refused: the authentication tag does not match

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/secretbox.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/hybrid/sealed_box.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/secret.hpp>

#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>
#include <vector>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
using crypto::ciphers::secretbox;
using crypto::hybrid::sealed_box;

namespace {

// What the app uploads: the sealed file key, the file's nonce and tag, and the sealed file.
struct upload {
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32 + sealed_box::overhead> sealed_key{};
    std::array<std::uint8_t, secretbox<>::iv_size> nonce{};
    secretbox<>::result_type tag{};
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> file;
};

// The sender: a key for this file alone, the file in a secret box under it, the key sealed to
// the recipient.
bool share(crypto::random_device& device, std::span<std::uint8_t const> recipient_public_key,
           std::string_view contents, upload& out) {
    crypto::secret<32> file_key;
    if (!device.fill(file_key.writable()) || !device.fill(out.nonce)) {
        return false;
    }
    auto box = secretbox<>::make(file_key.bytes());
    if (!box) {
        return false;
    }
    out.file.assign(contents.begin(), contents.end());
    auto const tag = box->seal(out.nonce, {}, out.file);
    if (!tag) {
        return false;
    }
    out.tag = *tag;
    return sealed_box::seal(recipient_public_key, file_key.bytes(), out.sealed_key).has_value();
}


// The recipient: the file key out of the sealed box, then the file out of the secret box.
void receive(char const* who, std::span<std::uint8_t const> public_key,
             std::span<std::uint8_t const> secret_key, upload received) {
    crypto::secret<32> file_key;
    auto const key_opened =
        sealed_box::open(public_key, secret_key, received.sealed_key, file_key.writable());
    if (!key_opened) {
        std::string const reason = key_opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s: the file key refused: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    auto box = secretbox<>::make(file_key.bytes());
    if (!box) {
        return;
    }
    auto const opened = box->open(received.nonce, {}, received.file, received.tag);
    if (!opened) {
        std::string const reason = opened.error().message();
        std::printf("%s: the file refused: %s\n", who, reason.c_str());
        return;
    }
    std::printf("%s read: %.*s\n", who, static_cast<int>(received.file.size()),
                reinterpret_cast<char const*>(received.file.data()));
}


}  // namespace

int main() {
    crypto::random_device device;
    // The recipient's key pair, made once on the recipient's device; only the public key is
    // published.
    crypto::secret<32> secret_key;
    if (!device.fill(secret_key.writable())) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const public_key = crypto::curves::x25519::public_key(secret_key.bytes());
    if (!public_key) {
        return 1;
    }

    upload sent;
    if (!share(device, *public_key, "quarterly report, draft 3", sent)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("on the wire: %zu bytes of sealed key, %zu of nonce, %zu of tag, %zu of file\n",
                sent.sealed_key.size(), sent.nonce.size(), sent.tag.size(), sent.file.size());
    receive("the recipient", *public_key, secret_key.bytes(), sent);

    // The storage service changes the file.
    upload changed = sent;
    changed.file[0] ^= 0x01U;
    receive("the recipient, the upload changed", *public_key, secret_key.bytes(), changed);
    // Someone else's key pair cannot open the file key.
    crypto::secret<32> other_secret;
    if (!device.fill(other_secret.writable())) {
        return 1;
    }
    auto const other_public = crypto::curves::x25519::public_key(other_secret.bytes());
    if (!other_public) {
        return 1;
    }
    receive("another key pair", *other_public, other_secret.bytes(), sent);
    return 0;
}

Mistakes to avoid. Never reuse a file key for a second file, nor a nonce under one key. Open the file key and the file before using a byte of either: a box that does not open is an attack or a corruption, never a reason to fall back on an unencrypted copy. A sealed box says nothing of who sent it: an app where the sender matters signs the upload (Ed25519) or uses a box between the two key pairs (Boxes). A large file cut into separate boxes is safe only when each chunk’s tag also covers its number and a flag marking the last chunk, in the additional data or in a nonce built from them, and a reader refuses chunks out of order and a stream that ends without the last flag: otherwise whoever holds the ciphertext reorders, drops, repeats or truncates chunks and each one still opens. The STREAM construction (Hoang, Reyhanitabar, Rogaway and Vizár, 2015) and libsodium’s secretstream (libsodium’s documentation) do this; this version of crypto offers neither.

A login: session tokens and reset links

A session token or a password-reset link is a bearer secret: whoever has it is the user. It is drawn from random_device, 32 bytes. The server stores the token’s SHA-256 (Boost.Hash2’s sha2_256), not the token, and looks the hash up when the token comes back, so that a leaked database hands out no live session or reset link (OWASP asks that reset tokens be stored securely, Forgot Password Cheat Sheet); a random token of 32 bytes needs no slow password hash. equal is for a token or a MAC checked against one value the program already knows. Entropy shows the program, reset_token. A password itself is never encrypted: it is hashed with a slow password hash, Argon2id or scrypt, which webcpp::hash’s password hashing gives, not crypto.

A webhook: checking an HMAC

A payment provider or a source-code host signs each call to a program’s webhook with an HMAC under a shared secret. The program recomputes it with Boost.Hash2 and compares with equal, never ==: Comparing tags.

A database field, a cookie, a file

Data stored where someone else may read it, a database, a cookie, a cloud bucket, is sealed with AES-GCM, with what it belongs to (the user’s id, the cookie’s name, the file’s path) as additional data, so that it cannot be moved to another place: AES-GCM. A large file is sealed in records: Encrypting what does not fit in memory.

A software update or a licence file

The problem. A program downloads its updates, or reads a licence file. Anyone who can change the download, a compromised mirror, a network in the middle, could ship code that the program then runs.

The idea. The publisher signs the SHA-256 of each update with ECDSA; the program ships with the publisher’s public key and accepts an update only when its signature verifies. Only the publisher’s secret key can produce a signature the program accepts.

// The program hashes the bytes it downloaded and checks the signature against the hash.
if (!secp256k1::verify_ecdsa(*signature, sha256(update), *shipped_key)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("update accepted\n");

update[7] = update[7] == '2' ? '3' : '2';
auto const tampered = secp256k1::verify_ecdsa(*signature, sha256(update), *shipped_key);
if (tampered || tampered.error() != crypto::error::invalid_signature) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("tampered update refused: invalid_signature\n");
update accepted
tampered update refused: invalid_signature

The whole program:

#include <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/error.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/random_device.hpp>

#include <boost/hash2/sha2.hpp>
#include <boost/system/result.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;
namespace secp256k1 = webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1;

namespace {

// Overwrites a secret through a volatile pointer, which the optimiser cannot drop as a dead
// store: crypto wipes its own copies of keys this way, and the program wipes its own.
void wipe(std::span<std::byte> secret) {
    std::byte volatile* const bytes = secret.data();
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < secret.size(); ++i) {
        bytes[i] = std::byte{0};
    }
}

std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> sha256(std::string_view text) {
    boost::hash2::sha2_256 hash;
    hash.update(text.data(), text.size());
    auto const digest = hash.result();
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> out{};
    std::copy_n(digest.data(), out.size(), out.begin());
    return out;
}

boost::system::result<secp256k1::keypair> generate_key() {
    crypto::random_device device;
    std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
    for (;;) {
        auto const filled = device.fill(secret);
        if (!filled) {
            return filled.error();
        }
        auto key = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret);
        if (key || key.error() != crypto::error::invalid_secret_key) {
            // The key pair keeps its own copy, which it wipes; this one goes now.
            wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
            return key;
        }
    }
}

}  // namespace

int main() {
    // The publisher signs once, offline; the secret never leaves the publisher.
    auto publisher = generate_key();
    if (!publisher) {
        return 1;
    }
    // The compressed public key (33 bytes) is what the program ships with.
    auto const shipped_key = publisher->public_key();
    std::string update = "update v2.1 payload";
    auto const signature = publisher->sign_ecdsa(sha256(update));
    if (!shipped_key || !signature) {
        return 1;
    }

    // The program hashes the bytes it downloaded and checks the signature against the hash.
    if (!secp256k1::verify_ecdsa(*signature, sha256(update), *shipped_key)) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("update accepted\n");

    update[7] = update[7] == '2' ? '3' : '2';
    auto const tampered = secp256k1::verify_ecdsa(*signature, sha256(update), *shipped_key);
    if (tampered || tampered.error() != crypto::error::invalid_signature) {
        return 1;
    }
    std::printf("tampered update refused: invalid_signature\n");
    return 0;
}

Mistakes to avoid. Verify the bytes that will run, not a copy of them. Keep the publisher’s secret key off the build machines that anyone can reach. Never fall back on an unsigned update when verification fails.

Allocation

An audio worklet, a game loop or an embedded device must not allocate on its hot path, or must allocate only from its own arena. crypto’s own code allocates one thing: a secp256k1 key pair’s signing context, once, in keypair::make, from the std::pmr::memory_resource the program passes, which must outlive the key pair. Every buffer is the caller’s.

  • Nothing allocates per message, on any backend: seal, open, begin_seal, update, result, encrypt, decrypt, fill, the signatures (hedged and recoverable too), ecdh, ecdh_x, ecdh_point, the verifications, recover, parse_public_key, serialize_public_key, the tweaks and negations, pubkey_combine (in a workspace the caller lends), the SPKI and PKCS#8 encoders and decoders (decode_pkcs8 makes a key pair, whose context is the one allocation above), and ellswift_*, MuSig2’s functions and silent payments’ (each over a workspace the caller lends, where it takes one). The counting tests of test/ prove it, every operator new and the C library’s allocator counted.

  • BearSSL and ctaes allocate nothing, make included: the key schedule lives inside the object.

  • OpenSSL’s make allocates its cipher context through OpenSSL’s own allocator, outside the program’s resource; the first make of a process also initialises OpenSSL. The test allocation_openssl counts and prints these allocations on each target at every run, and fails if a message allocates; the count depends on the target and on OpenSSL’s build, so the page does not copy it. A program that needs every allocation in its arena uses BearSSL, or OpenSSL with the memory option of OpenSSL’s allocations in your own memory resource, natively.

  • Keys are wiped. The key schedules that live inside crypto’s objects (BearSSL’s, ctaes’s, libsecp256k1’s key pair) are overwritten on destruction and on move by stores the optimiser cannot drop; OpenSSL wipes its own contexts when they are freed.

  • No type is shareable. An object holds a key, and OpenSSL’s hold pointers into OpenSSL’s heap: none is placed in memory shared with another process, and a key never should be.

Example. A key pair whose context comes from an arena on the stack, through a resource that counts what it gives:

// Counts allocations and forwards them to the arena.
class counting_resource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {
public:
    explicit counting_resource(std::pmr::memory_resource* upstream) : upstream_(upstream) {}

    [[nodiscard]] std::size_t allocations() const { return count_; }

private:
    void* do_allocate(std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) override {
        ++count_;
        return upstream_->allocate(bytes, alignment);
    }

    void do_deallocate(void* pointer, std::size_t bytes, std::size_t alignment) override {
        upstream_->deallocate(pointer, bytes, alignment);
    }

    [[nodiscard]] bool do_is_equal(std::pmr::memory_resource const& other) const noexcept override {
        return this == &other;
    }

    std::pmr::memory_resource* upstream_;
    std::size_t count_ = 0;
};
// The buffer is the only memory there is: the upstream refuses everything else.
std::array<std::byte, 8192> storage{};
std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource arena(storage.data(), storage.size(),
                                          std::pmr::null_memory_resource());
counting_resource counting(&arena);

// A demonstration secret, so that the output is the same on every run; a real one is drawn
// from random_device.
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> secret{};
secret.fill(0x42);
auto key = secp256k1::keypair::make(secret, &counting);
wipe(std::as_writable_bytes(std::span(secret)));
if (!key) {
    return 1;
}
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> message{};
message.fill(0x17);
std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const aux{};
auto const public_key = key->xonly_public_key();
auto const signature = key->sign_schnorr(message, aux);
if (!public_key || !signature || !secp256k1::verify_schnorr(*signature, message, *public_key)) {
    return 1;
}
std::printf("allocations in the arena: %zu\n", counting.allocations());
allocations in the arena: 1
signed and verified

OpenSSL’s allocations in your own memory resource

By default OpenSSL allocates with the C library’s malloc, outside every allocator of the program’s. A native program that keeps its memory in its own arena, such as an audio engine whose real-time thread may not touch the system’s heap, or an embedded server that gives each part a fixed budget, finds OpenSSL bypassing that arena: its first make initialises OpenSSL, which takes many blocks from the system’s heap, and Beast’s TLS and libdatachannel’s DTLS, which link the same OpenSSL, allocate there for every connection. The arena’s accounting is then wrong, a budget is exceeded with no warning, and a real-time thread can wait on the system allocator’s lock. The memory option sends every allocation OpenSSL makes in the process to a std::pmr::memory_resource the program defines. It is for native programs only: on WebAssembly the backend is BearSSL, which allocates nothing.

How. Three things, each needed:

  1. The define and OpenSSL, in the requirements of the program’s project, so that every target of the program gets both, its own libraries and a tool that only calls random_device included. config.hpp stops a target that has the define without OpenSSL, and any build for WebAssembly, with an #error (OpenSSL’s memory option):

    project app
  : requirements <define>WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE <library>/webcpp/crypto//openssl ;

exe app : app.cpp /webcpp/crypto//crypto ;

  2. webcpp::crypto::openssl_memory_resource(), defined once in the program. Without it the program does not link. It returns a resource that is thread-safe and is never destroyed: create it with new and never delete it. OpenSSL frees through it after main returns, so a static resource object, or a local variable of main, would be used after its destruction:

    // Declared by crypto under WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE, defined once by the program.
// Never destroyed: OpenSSL frees through it after main returns. The synchronized pool serves
// OpenSSL on any thread.
std::pmr::memory_resource& webcpp::crypto::openssl_memory_resource() noexcept {
    // Never deleted, on purpose; a new that fails this early ends the program, which has no
    // resource for OpenSSL.
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(cppcoreguidelines-owning-memory,bugprone-unhandled-exception-at-new)
    static auto* const resource = new std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource;
    return *resource;
}

  3. backends::openssl::install_memory_functions(), the first statement of main, before any thread starts and before anything uses OpenSSL; the program stops when it returns an error:

    // The first statement of main: before any thread starts and before anything uses OpenSSL.
auto const installed = crypto::backends::openssl::install_memory_functions();
if (!installed) {
    std::string const message = installed.error().message();
    std::printf("install: %s\n", message.c_str());
    return 1;
}

Example. The whole program seals and opens one block on OpenSSL, every allocation of OpenSSL’s in the program’s pool:

#include <webcpp/crypto/backends/openssl.hpp>
#include <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aes256_gcm.hpp>

#include <openssl/crypto.h>

#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <memory_resource>
#include <string>
#include <thread>

namespace crypto = webcpp::crypto;

// Declared by crypto under WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE, defined once by the program.
// Never destroyed: OpenSSL frees through it after main returns. The synchronized pool serves
// OpenSSL on any thread.
std::pmr::memory_resource& webcpp::crypto::openssl_memory_resource() noexcept {
    // Never deleted, on purpose; a new that fails this early ends the program, which has no
    // resource for OpenSSL.
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(cppcoreguidelines-owning-memory,bugprone-unhandled-exception-at-new)
    static auto* const resource = new std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource;
    return *resource;
}

int main() {
    // The first statement of main: before any thread starts and before anything uses OpenSSL.
    auto const installed = crypto::backends::openssl::install_memory_functions();
    if (!installed) {
        std::string const message = installed.error().message();
        std::printf("install: %s\n", message.c_str());
        return 1;
    }

    bool ok = false;
    std::thread worker([&ok] {
        // A zero key and IV keep the output stable: a real program draws its key from
        // random_device and never reuses an IV under it.
        std::array<std::uint8_t, 32> const key{};
        std::array<std::uint8_t, 12> const iv{};
        std::array<std::uint8_t, 16> data{};
        {
            auto aead = crypto::ciphers::aes256_gcm::make(key);
            if (aead) {
                auto const tag = aead->seal(iv, {}, data);
                ok =
                    tag && aead->open(iv, {}, data, *tag) && data == std::array<std::uint8_t, 16>{};
            } else {
                std::string const message = aead.error().message();
                std::printf("make: %s\n", message.c_str());
            }
        }
        // The thread's last call into OpenSSL, on every path: it gives the thread's own blocks back
        // to the resource now. On Windows, whose static libcrypto is never told that a thread ends,
        // they would otherwise stay in the resource until the process ends.
        OPENSSL_thread_stop();
    });
    worker.join();
    auto const name = crypto::ciphers::aes256_gcm::backend_type::name;
    std::printf("aes256_gcm %s backend=%.*s\n", ok ? "ok" : "FAILED", static_cast<int>(name.size()),
                name.data());
    return ok ? 0 : 1;
}
aes256_gcm ok backend=openssl

What to know.

  • The whole process. The resource receives every allocation of the OpenSSL the program links, not only crypto’s: Beast’s TLS and libdatachannel’s DTLS too. The test neighbours links Asio’s TLS and libdatachannel beside the option, with the objects of libdatachannel whose static initialisers name OpenSSL, and the install still succeeds; the test handshake runs a TLS 1.3 handshake through libssl, and counts no call of the C library’s allocator over the whole exchange: the key, the certificate, both contexts, the handshake, a record each way and every free.

  • Nothing else may call CRYPTO_set_mem_functions. If another library has called it before, install_memory_functions() returns memory_functions_refused; if it calls it after the install, the next make returns memory_functions_not_installed, and only when that call has finished before the make. The damage is done by then: OpenSSL accepts the replacement after the install, and from then on frees the blocks it took from the resource through the other party’s free, which corrupts that party’s heap; the error that make then returns does not undo it.

  • memory_functions_refused although the install is the first statement of main means that something used OpenSSL before main: a static object of another library. OpenSSL then keeps its own malloc for the rest of the process. A libcrypto DLL, which webcpp never builds (a program built without b2), is refused the same way.

  • memory_functions_not_installed from a make means that the install was not called, or that something replaced OpenSSL’s functions after it.

  • One module. The program’s code that uses crypto’s OpenSSL backend lives in one module: a DLL, or a shared library of the program’s that hides its symbols, that includes the backend’s header has its own copy of crypto’s functions, and its make returns memory_functions_not_installed. An ELF shared library with default visibility usually binds to the executable’s copy instead, but nothing guarantees it.

  • Threads on Windows. OpenSSL gives a thread’s own blocks back when the thread ends, except on Windows, where the static libcrypto that webcpp always builds is never told that a thread ends. Every thread that used OpenSSL, a make, Beast’s TLS or libdatachannel’s DTLS, leaves its error queue and its list of handlers in the resource, never given back, not even at exit, unless it calls OPENSSL_thread_stop() before it ends. A resource of a fixed size under a thread pool that replaces its threads, or a thread per connection, then runs out over time, and the failure lands in a later make or inside a TLS handshake. The example’s worker thread ends so, and so does the second thread of the test everything, whose exit check fails on Windows without it:

    // The thread's last call into OpenSSL, on every path: it gives the thread's own blocks back
// to the resource now. On Windows, whose static libcrypto is never told that a thread ends,
// they would otherwise stay in the resource until the process ends.
OPENSSL_thread_stop();

  • When the resource cannot allocate. The resource must serve OpenSSL’s initialisation, which the first use of OpenSSL in the process runs, usually the first make. On an OpenSSL built with threads, which is MSVC’s only build and b2’s threading=multi elsewhere, a failure during OpenSSL’s base initialisation is not recoverable: OpenSSL reports it through its error queue, whose state needs the initialisation that is running, so OpenSSL re-enters its own initialisation and that call never returns. The process aborts on macOS, deadlocks on Linux and spins on Windows. Only an OpenSSL built without threads, b2’s default on macOS and Linux, returns from that failure, and OpenSSL stays unusable for the rest of the process: make gives backend_failure from then on. When the failing allocation is OpenSSL’s base initialisation (with OpenSSL 3.5.9, its first lock), OpenSSL never registers its cleanup, and OPENSSL_cleanup frees nothing: the blocks it took meanwhile stay in the resource until the process ends, and the thread’s error queue takes no entry from then on. The test fail_init pins this on an OpenSSL without threads and prints how many blocks stay; with threads, as fail_init_threads, it prints how many blocks the first make took instead. After the initialisation, make gives not_enough_memory or backend_failure. seal and open allocate nothing. A resource of a fixed size needs room for the first make, whose allocations the test allocation_openssl prints on each run. Without exceptions, a resource that throws ends the process; one that returns null reports the failure.

  • Two allocations stay outside the resource, because no hook of OpenSSL’s reaches them: the C library’s FILE and its buffer while OpenSSL reads its configuration file at initialisation (one or two blocks, by C library, freed when the file closes), and OpenSSL’s secure heap, if the program turns it on with CRYPTO_secure_malloc_init.

  • Native only. A WebAssembly build of the same program is a project of its own, in a directory of its own, with neither the define nor OpenSSL, and names /third_party//bearssl.

The backends of openssl_memory_resource, backends::openssl::install_memory_functions, from the test programs that run it:

Testing

crypto is tested by lightweight_test programs under test/, each declared in test/Jamfile, and each public header is compiled alone, as the only include of its translation unit, with the libraries it needs. Every test program is built twice, with exceptions and with exception-handling=off, by the Jamfile’s rule crypto-run. Every example of this page is built and run, and its output compared with its .expected.

Each lane builds from scratch, as the continuous integration does, from the root of a webcpp checkout:

b2 -a --build-dir=bin/lane-native libs/crypto/test libs/crypto/example

The 402 tests and 33 examples natively, and each of the 42 public headers compiled alone.

b2 -a --build-dir=bin/lane-wasip2 toolset=clang-wasip2 testing.launcher=tools/boost/asio-wasip2/run.sh libs/crypto/test libs/crypto/example

The same for wasm32-wasip2: 307 tests, each run by wasmtime. toolset=clang-wasip3 with tools/boost/asio-wasip3/run.sh does the same for wasm32-wasip3: 292 tests.

b2 -a --build-dir=bin/lane-emscripten toolset=emscripten libs/crypto/test libs/crypto/example

The same on Emscripten: 231 tests, each run by node.

MSVC and Apple Clang run in the continuous integration only. The own lane c-suites runs the C libraries’ own test suites (BearSSL’s, ctaes’s and libsecp256k1’s) on webcpp’s build of them, on every target, on every push: the target’s lane command with libs/crypto/test/c_suites//c-suites in place of the two directories. libsodium’s own suite runs in webcpp::hash’s lane c-suites (libs/hash/test/c_suites//c-suites), on every target, against the same build of libsodium that crypto links: each program of its test/default, those of crypto’s operations among them (sign, box, box2, box7, box8, box_easy, box_easy2, box_seal, secretbox, secretbox2, secretbox7, secretbox8, secretbox_easy, secretbox_easy2, xchacha20, aead_chacha20poly1305, aead_chacha20poly13052, aead_xchacha20poly1305, kx, scalarmult, ed25519_convert, and codecs, the base64 functions PEM’s engine calls), compared with its .exp. The own lane constant-time checks constant time (Constant time): natively, Valgrind and clang’s MemorySanitizer on Linux and dudect’s statistics on Linux and macOS, and dudect’s under wasmtime on wasip2, whose |t| a runner GitHub hosts prints without judging it (Constant time says why); the native lane’s command with libs/crypto/test/constant_time//constant-time in place of the two directories.

What the tests check:

  • The vectors. AES-GCM against the GCM specification’s cases and Project Wycheproof’s vectors, on BearSSL and on OpenSSL; AES against FIPS 197 on ctaes and OpenSSL; secp256k1 against BIP 340’s vectors, Wycheproof’s ECDSA, ECDH and DER vectors and libsecp256k1’s own recovery edge cases, the x-only tweak against BIP 341’s, the tweaks, negations and sums of keys against libsecp256k1’s C API, and the SPKI and PKCS#8 encodings against Wycheproof’s SPKIs, OpenSSL (natively and on WASI) and node’s crypto module (under Emscripten). Ed25519 against RFC 8032’s tests, Wycheproof’s EdDSA vectors and the twelve edge cases of "Taming the many EdDSAs"; X25519 against RFC 7748’s and Wycheproof’s; ChaCha20-Poly1305 and XChaCha20-Poly1305 against RFC 8439’s and the XChaCha20 draft’s examples and Wycheproof’s vectors, on every backend that has them.

  • node’s WebCrypto as an outside oracle, on Emscripten: 200 Ed25519 key pairs, messages and signatures from a fixed seed, each verified and signed again by crypto.subtle, which must give the same public key and signature, and 200 X25519 agreements, each derived again to the same public key and shared secret (oracle_25519, which prints oracle ok 400). oracle_25519_corrupted flips one signature and one shared secret, and passes only when WebCrypto disagrees on exactly those two.

  • The backends against each other, on random keys, IVs, additional data and messages of every size around a block’s: BearSSL and OpenSSL seal the same bytes with AES-GCM and each opens what the other sealed, with BearSSL on its x86-64 instructions and on its portable code; ctaes and OpenSSL encrypt the same blocks. Natively, on wasip2 and on wasip3, from a fixed seed and from a seed drawn at each run, which a disagreement prints.

  • <windows.h>, bare, included before and after every public header with every backend linked: no macro of it breaks a header, and the headers leave NOMINMAX and WIN32_LEAN_AND_MEAN as they found them. Its teeth are on the continuous integration’s MSVC lanes.

  • Every guard and every error, on a mock backend whose checks every real backend’s test runs as well, and the limits natively.

  • Allocation: every operator new and the C library’s allocator counted around each operation.

  • The default backend of every family on every target, the same with every backend linked, with none, with each alone and with the defines that no longer choose one (The default backend per target).

  • Every message, word for word, by a message test with clang on the targets it names; on MSVC, each case proven to stop the build (Every message, and its fix).

  • The user’s Jamfiles, by the superproject’s tools/test/crypto_jamfiles_test.py, which builds each fixture on a scratch superproject (Every Jamfile a user writes).

  • A backend named and not called adds no byte, by programs built with and without its library and compared.

The documentation’s tables are checked by its build: doc/tables/generate.py --check fails when a generated table differs from what the data and the tests give.

The test matrix of every lane is published with the documentation, at https://webcpporg.github.io/report/.

Reference

Every name crypto declares, in the namespaces webcpp::crypto, backends, ciphers, curves and hybrid, from the Doc Comments of its headers: each class, function, type and enumerator with its declaration, what it does, what it asks of its caller and how it fails. The other sections teach the library; this one is where a name is looked up.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_BEARSSL

Defined by /third_party//bearssl when the program links BearSSL; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_CTAES

Defined by /third_party//ctaes when the program links ctaes; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself, and compiles webcpp’s src/canary_ctaes.c with ctaes.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_OPENSSL

Defined by /webcpp/crypto//openssl when the program links OpenSSL; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself. Refused on Emscripten, where OpenSSL is not built.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SECP256K1

Defined by /third_party//secp256k1 when the program links libsecp256k1; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself, and builds libsecp256k1 with webcpp’s src/canary_secp256k1.c.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_SODIUM

Defined by /third_party//sodium when the program links libsodium; a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself, and links libsodium built with webcpp’s src/canary_sodium.c.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_THREADS

Defined when the build has threads (design D23): natively when Boost.Config defines BOOST_HAS_THREADS, on Emscripten when the program is built with -pthread (b2’s threading=multi), never on wasip2 or wasip3, and never when the program defines WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS. Only then do the heavy operations’ async_ variants run on another thread; without it, a program that calls one stops with the synchronous name to call instead.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_THREADS

Defined in a build with threads, where the heavy operations’ async_ variants exist (design D23): natively unless the program defines WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS (Boost.Config’s BOOST_HAS_THREADS, which b2’s threading=single leaves defined), on Emscripten with -pthread, never on WASI.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Defined when webcpp::crypto is built without exceptions: when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the developer defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), or when the developer defines it alone.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_NO_THREADS

Defined by a program that wants no threads from webcpp::crypto: WEBCPP_CRYPTO_HAS_THREADS stays undefined, and the heavy operations’ async_ variants refuse to compile.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_MEMORY_RESOURCE

Defined by a native program, in its project’s requirements beside /webcpp/crypto//openssl, to send every allocation of OpenSSL’s in the process to a resource of the program’s: the program then defines openssl_memory_resource() once and calls backends::openssl::install_memory_functions() as the first statement of main. Refused on every WebAssembly target, and natively without OpenSSL linked.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_SECP256K1_SMALL_TABLES

Defined by /third_party//secp256k1 when libsecp256k1 is built with its small precomputed tables (<webcpp-secp256k1-tables>small, and Emscripten’s default); a program built without b2 defines it to 1 itself when it builds libsecp256k1 with ECMULT_WINDOW_SIZE=2 and COMB_BLOCKS=2, COMB_TEETH=5. The canary refuses a program and a library that disagree.

WEBCPP_CRYPTO_WEBASSEMBLY

Defined on the WebAssembly targets, wasip2, wasip3 and Emscripten.

Installs webcpp’s adapter as OpenSSL’s memory functions, so that every allocation of OpenSSL’s in the process goes to openssl_memory_resource(). Called as the first statement of main, before any thread starts and anything uses OpenSSL. The first use of OpenSSL after it, usually the first make, runs OpenSSL’s initialisation through the resource: on an OpenSSL built with threads (MSVC’s only build) a failure during its base initialisation makes that call never return; on one built without threads every make then gives backend_failure.

webcpp::crypto::ciphers::aead

An AEAD of the family Family on Backend, one shot: authenticated encryption in place, the tag apart.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aead.hpp>

template<
    class Family,
    class Backend>
class aead;

Description

An object holds a key: it is used by one thread at a time. A nonce (the IV) is never repeated under one key: two messages under one key and one nonce reveal the XOR of their plaintexts and let an attacker forge tags. Drawn at random, ChaCha20-Poly1305’s 12-byte nonce lets a key seal at most 2^32 messages, and the original’s 8 bytes are too few: a counter numbers them. XChaCha20-Poly1305’s 24-byte nonce, and the secret boxes’, are safe to draw at random.

webcpp::crypto::ciphers::aead::open

Opens a message in place: data_bytes holds the ciphertext before and the plaintext after.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aead.hpp>

[[nodiscard]]
boost::system::result<void>
open(
    std::span<uint8_t const> iv_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t const> additional_data_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t> data_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t const> tag_bytes) noexcept;

Description

When the tag does not match, or the backend fails, data_bytes is zeroed; a guard’s refusal leaves it untouched.

Return Value

Nothing; invalid_state moved from; invalid_iv_size; invalid_tag_size; invalid_input_size for additional data given to a family that takes none; message_too_long; authentication_failed; backend_failure.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

Parameters

Name Description

iv_bytes

The nonce of the seal.

additional_data_bytes

The additional data of the seal.

data_bytes

The ciphertext.

tag_bytes

The seal’s tag, tag_size bytes, which may lie anywhere, data_bytes included.

webcpp::crypto::ciphers::aead::seal

Seals a message in place: data_bytes holds the plaintext before and the ciphertext after.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/aead.hpp>

[[nodiscard]]
boost::system::result<result_type>
seal(
    std::span<uint8_t const> iv_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t const> additional_data_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t> data_bytes) noexcept;

Description

The nonce is read before the first byte of data_bytes is written, so it may lie in data_bytes. The additional data may touch data_bytes, as a wire format that puts it just before the message does, but not overlap it: BearSSL’s ChaCha20-Poly1305 reads it after it encrypts, in one call over the whole message, so an overlap would authenticate other bytes than the caller’s additional data; the backends would give different tags, and an open with the original additional data would fail.

When the backend fails, data_bytes is zeroed, as a failed open’s is: a backend may fail after it began to encrypt, and neither the plaintext nor bytes that look sealed are left; a guard’s refusal leaves it untouched.

Return Value

The tag; invalid_state moved from; invalid_iv_size; invalid_input_size for additional data given to a family that takes none; message_too_long; backend_failure.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

Parameters

Name Description

iv_bytes

The nonce, iv_size bytes, never repeated under this key.

additional_data_bytes

Authenticated, not encrypted; empty for a family that takes none (max_additional_data_size 0).

data_bytes

The message.

webcpp::crypto::ciphers::gcm

AES-GCM (NIST SP 800-38D) with the key size of Cipher, on the backend of Cipher, which must export GCM over its own AES: BearSSL or OpenSSL.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/ciphers/gcm.hpp>

template<class Cipher>
class gcm;

Description

An object holds a key and the state of one message: it is used by one thread at a time, and it is not shareable. An IV is never reused under one key, and with random IVs, or IVs other than 12 bytes, a key seals at most 2^32 messages (NIST SP 800-38D section 8.3).

    std::span<uint8_t const> iv_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t const> additional_data_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t> data_bytes,
    std::span<uint8_t const> tag_bytes) noexcept;

Description

While it runs, the decrypted bytes are in data_bytes before the tag is checked; when the tag does not match, or the backend fails, data_bytes is zeroed. A guard’s refusal leaves it untouched.

Return Value

Nothing; invalid_state moved from or during an incremental message, which goes on; invalid_iv_size; invalid_tag_size; message_too_long; authentication_failed; backend_failure.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

Parameters

Name Description

iv_bytes

The IV of the seal.

additional_data_bytes

The additional data of the seal.

data_bytes

The ciphertext.

tag_bytes

The seal’s tag, 16 bytes, which may lie anywhere, data_bytes included.

webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519

Types

Name Description

basic_keypair

An Ed25519 key pair (RFC 8032): its secret key, kept by the backend and wiped by every move and by the destructor, and its public key.

ph

Ed25519ph (RFC 8032 section 5.1), the Ed25519 signature of a message’s SHA-512, given in pieces.

strict

Ed25519 verification as libsodium does it: S below the group order, A and R canonical, neither of small order (design D31).

Type Aliases

Name Description

keypair

The key pair on the default backend.

Functions

Name Description

decode_pkcs8

The key pair of a PKCS#8, refused unless it is exactly RFC 8410’s version 1 form: the 16 bytes of Ed25519’s prefix, then the seed, and nothing after.

decode_spki

The public key of an SPKI, refused unless it is exactly RFC 8410’s form: the 12 bytes of Ed25519’s prefix, then the key, and nothing after.

encode_pkcs8

Writes a key pair’s PKCS#8 (RFC 8410, version 1: the seed, without the public key) into out, which then holds the secret key: a program wipes it, or seals it, when it is done.

encode_spki

Writes a public key’s SPKI (RFC 8410) into out.

to_x25519_public

The X25519 public key of an Ed25519 public key (the birational map from edwards25519 to Curve25519), so that a peer known by its Ed25519 key can be agreed with by curves::x25519::agree; the key pair’s own side is basic_keypair::x25519_secret.

verify

Verifies an Ed25519 signature under a verification policy (design D31).

Variables

Name Description

max_pkcs8_size

The PKCS#8’s size, 48 bytes: version 1, with the seed alone.

max_spki_size

The SPKI’s size, 44 bytes: the one size RFC 8410 gives an Ed25519 public key’s.

webcpp::crypto::curves::ed25519::ph

Ed25519ph (RFC 8032 section 5.1), the Ed25519 signature of a message’s SHA-512, given in pieces.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/ed25519.hpp>

template<
    class Hash,
    class Backend = default_backend_t<families::ed25519>>
class ph;

Description

A large message need not be held whole: the signer is begun, updated with each piece, then signs with a key pair or verifies with a public key, either of which ends the message. Its state is wiped by every move, by the end of a message and by the destructor.

Its signature is not Ed25519’s of the same message: a verifier is told which of the two a protocol uses.

Namespaces

Name

musig

silent_payments

Types

Name Description

basic_keypair

A secp256k1 key pair on libsecp256k1, with a signing context of its own in the resource it is given, randomised from the random device as libsecp256k1 recommends.

public_key

A secp256k1 public key, parsed: a point on the curve, never the identity (libsecp256k1’s secp256k1_pubkey).

tweaked_xonly_key

A tweaked x-only key: the key and the parity of its point’s y.

Type Aliases

Name Description

keypair

A key pair on libsecp256k1.

workspace

Memory a caller lends to a function over many keys, nonces or outputs, for libsecp256k1’s arrays of pointers, which crypto builds there and allocates nowhere.

Enums

Name Description

ellswift_party

The two sides of ellswift_xdh (BIP 324’s initiator and responder).

point_form

The two SEC1 encodings of a point.

Functions

Name Description

combine_workspace_size

The workspace pubkey_combine needs for key_count keys, in bytes.

decode_pkcs8

The key pair of a PKCS#8 that is exactly what encode_pkcs8 writes for its secret, made as basic_keypair::make makes it.

decode_spki

The public key of an SPKI in exactly one of the two forms encode_spki writes.

ellswift_create

The encoding of a key pair’s public key, made from its secret with the key pair’s context (secp256k1_ellswift_create), so that the public key is never computed apart.

ellswift_decode

The public key of any 64 bytes (secp256k1_ellswift_decode): every input decodes.

ellswift_encode

A public key’s ElligatorSwift encoding (secp256k1_ellswift_encode): one of many, chosen by the randomness, each of which decodes to the key.

ellswift_xdh

The shared secret of an ElligatorSwift key exchange, hashed as BIP 324 hashes it (secp256k1_ellswift_xdh with secp256k1_ellswift_xdh_hash_function_bip324): a tagged hash of both encodings and the shared point’s x coordinate.

encode_pkcs8

Writes a key pair’s PKCS#8 into output_bytes, in OpenSSL’s form: version 0, and RFC 5915’s ECPrivateKey of version 1 with the uncompressed public key and no parameters inside.

encode_spki

Writes a public key’s SPKI (RFC 5480, the secp256k1 OID) into output_bytes.

from_der

Decodes a strict DER ECDSA signature (BIP66, secp256k1_ecdsa_signature_parse_der) to its compact form.

normalize_ecdsa

The low-S form of a compact ECDSA signature (secp256k1_ecdsa_signature_normalize), the only form verify_ecdsa accepts; a low-S signature is returned unchanged.

parse_public_key

Parses a public key: 33 bytes with prefix 02 or 03, or 65 with prefix 04 (X9.62’s hybrid prefixes 06 and 07 are refused, as everywhere in crypto).

pubkey_combine

The sum of public keys (secp256k1_ec_pubkey_combine), in a workspace the caller lends for libsecp256k1’s array of pointers.

pubkey_negate

The negation -P of a public key (secp256k1_ec_pubkey_negate), which never fails.

pubkey_tweak_add

A public key P plus t times the generator (secp256k1_ec_pubkey_tweak_add).

pubkey_tweak_mul

A public key P times t (secp256k1_ec_pubkey_tweak_mul).

recover

The public key that made a recoverable signature of a 32-byte hash (secp256k1_ecdsa_recover), as Ethereum identifies a transaction’s signer.

seckey_negate

The group order minus a secret key (secp256k1_ec_seckey_negate).

seckey_tweak_add

A secret key plus a tweak modulo the group order (secp256k1_ec_seckey_tweak_add).

seckey_tweak_mul

A secret key times a tweak modulo the group order (secp256k1_ec_seckey_tweak_mul).

serialize_public_key

Serialises a public key in Form.

to_der

Encodes a compact ECDSA signature as strict DER (BIP66), with libsecp256k1’s own encoder.

tweak_xonly

Tweaks an x-only public key by a 32-byte tweak t: P + t*G, with libsecp256k1’s static context, which allocates nothing (secp256k1_xonly_pubkey_tweak_add).

verify_ecdsa

Verifies an ECDSA signature in compact form with the static context, after its self-test; a high-S signature is refused, as libsecp256k1 refuses it.

verify_schnorr

Verifies a BIP340 signature with libsecp256k1’s static context, which allocates nothing, after its self-test (include/secp256k1.h:235-247).

operator==

Equal when the points are equal.

operator<=>

Ordered as their compressed encodings, BIP 327’s KeySort (secp256k1_ec_pubkey_cmp).

webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::musig

Types

Name Description

aggregate_key

The signers’ aggregate key and what signing needs of it (libsecp256k1’s keyagg cache), with the tweaks a protocol applies to it: public data, copied freely, made only by key_aggregate.

aggregate_nonce

The sum of the signers’ public nonces, parsed (libsecp256k1’s aggnonce): public, copied freely, made only by nonce_aggregate and parse_aggregate_nonce.

nonce_pair

What nonce_gen returns: the secret nonce to keep, the public nonce to send.

partial_signature

One signer’s partial signature, parsed (libsecp256k1’s partial_sig): public, copied freely, made only by partial_sign and parse_partial_signature.

public_nonce

A signer’s public nonce, parsed (libsecp256k1’s pubnonce): public, copied freely, made only by nonce_gen and parse_public_nonce.

secret_nonce

A signer’s secret nonce: move-only, wiped on move and destruction, made only by nonce_gen.

session

The session of one message (libsecp256k1’s session): the final nonce and the challenge, public, copied freely, made only by nonce_process.

Functions

Name Description

key_aggregate

Aggregates the signers’ keys in the order given (secp256k1_musig_pubkey_agg).

nonce_aggregate

Sums the signers’ public nonces (secp256k1_musig_nonce_agg), as one of them or a coordinator does once every public nonce is in.

nonce_gen

A fresh nonce for one signature (secp256k1_musig_nonce_gen), its 32 bytes of session randomness drawn inside from crypto’s random device, with the key pair’s secret, its public key and the aggregate key.

nonce_process

The session of one message (secp256k1_musig_nonce_process): the final nonce and the challenge every signer signs.

parse_aggregate_nonce

Parses an aggregate nonce (secp256k1_musig_aggnonce_parse): two compressed points, either of which may be the point at infinity, written as 33 zero bytes.

parse_partial_signature

Parses a partial signature (secp256k1_musig_partial_sig_parse).

parse_public_nonce

Parses a signer’s public nonce (secp256k1_musig_pubnonce_parse): two compressed points.

partial_sign

This signer’s partial signature (secp256k1_musig_partial_sign), consuming the nonce: it is taken by value, wiped by the call and destroyed at its end.

partial_signature_aggregate

The BIP 340 signature of the partial signatures (secp256k1_musig_partial_sig_agg), which verify_schnorr checks under aggregate_key::xonly_public_key().

partial_signature_verify

Verifies one signer’s partial signature (secp256k1_musig_partial_sig_verify), which tells a dishonest or faulty signer apart before the signature is aggregated.

serialize_aggregate_nonce

Serialises an aggregate nonce (secp256k1_musig_aggnonce_serialize).

serialize_partial_signature

Serialises a partial signature (secp256k1_musig_partial_sig_serialize).

serialize_public_nonce

Serialises a signer’s public nonce (secp256k1_musig_pubnonce_serialize).

workspace_size

The workspace key_aggregate, nonce_aggregate and partial_signature_aggregate need for count items, in bytes.

webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::musig::secret_nonce

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/musig.hpp>

class secret_nonce;

Description

It is consumed by partial_sign, which takes it by value, so that a nonce cannot be passed to a second signature without an explicit std::move of an object already moved from (which partial_sign refuses with invalid_state). Reusing a nonce in two signatures reveals the secret key.

A fresh nonce for one signature (secp256k1_musig_nonce_gen), its 32 bytes of session randomness drawn inside from crypto’s random device, with the key pair’s secret, its public key and the aggregate key.

nonce_gen(

    aggregate_key const& signers_key,
    std::span<uint8_t const> message_hash = {},
    std::span<uint8_t const> extra_input = {}) noexcept;

Description

Tip: make the nonce when the signature is to be made, and keep it nowhere else: a nonce survives no restart of the program, which is what keeps it from being used twice.

The pair; invalid_state moved from; invalid_input_size for a message or an extra input that is neither empty nor 32 bytes; entropy_unavailable; backend_failure.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::silent_payments::create_outputs

The sender’s outputs (secp256k1_silentpayments_sender_create_outputs): one x-only key per recipient, in the recipients’ order, from the secret keys of the transaction’s eligible inputs, Taproot inputs (their keys negated for an odd y, as BIP 352 says) apart from the others, and the smallest outpoint, which the caller determines.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp>

template<class Backend = default_backend_t<families::secp256k1_silent_payments>>
[[nodiscard]]
boost::system::result<void>
create_outputs(
    std::span<recipient const> recipients,
    std::span<uint8_t const, outpoint_size> smallest_outpoint,
    std::span<basic_keypair<Backend> const const*> taproot_inputs,
    std::span<basic_keypair<Backend> const const*> plain_inputs,
    std::span<std::array<uint8_t, 32>> output_keys,
    workspace pointer_space) noexcept;

Description

The context is the first Taproot input’s key pair’s, else the first plain input’s.

Tip: every output made must be in the transaction, and the outpoint must be the transaction’s smallest, or the recipient never finds the payment.

Return Value

Nothing; invalid_input_size (no recipient, no input at all, outputs not one per recipient, a short workspace, more than group_limit recipients sharing a scan key, which webcpp counts only when there are more recipients than that); invalid_state (a moved-from key pair, or a null pointer among the inputs); invalid_secret_key when libsecp256k1 refuses: the inputs’ keys sum to zero, or a recipient’s spend key gives no output, which only a key chosen against the sender can.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::silent_payments::label_lookup

Whether LabelLookup can look up a label for scan_outputs.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1/silent_payments.hpp>

template<class LabelLookup>
concept label_lookup = std::is_nothrow_invocable_v<LabelLookup const&, std::span<std::uint8_t const, 33>> &&
    std::same_as<std::invoke_result_t<LabelLookup const&, std::span<std::uint8_t const, 33>>,
                 std::optional<std::span<std::uint8_t const, 32>>>;

Description

Called with a candidate label’s 33 bytes, it returns exactly std::optional<std::span<std::uint8_t const, 32>>: a span over the label’s 32-byte tweak, or std::nullopt. The lookup owns the bytes the span points into for the call: they stay valid until the lookup is called again, since libsecp256k1 reads them after the lookup returns. A result returned by value, such as a std::array or a std::optional of one, would be gone by then, so no other result type is accepted, a convertible one included. The lookup is noexcept, since libsecp256k1’s C frames are between the scan and the lookup.

Template Parameters

Name Description

LabelLookup

The lookup’s type.

webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::basic_keypair::tweak_xonly

Tweaks this key pair in place by a 32-byte tweak t: its x-only public key P becomes P + t*G, and its secret key follows (secp256k1_keypair_xonly_tweak_add).

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>

[[nodiscard]]
boost::system::result<void>
tweak_xonly(std::span<uint8_t const, 32> tweak_bytes) noexcept;

Description

The caller computes the tweak, as a protocol defines it.

Allocates nothing; the pair keeps its context, its wiping and its behaviour when moved from.

Return Value

Nothing; invalid_state moved from; invalid_secret_key for a tweak not below the group order, or one that gives no valid key (negligible, but checked), after which the pair is wiped and empty, as moved from.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

Parameters

Name Description

tweak_bytes

The 32-byte tweak, a big-endian scalar.

webcpp::crypto::curves::secp256k1::basic_keypair::make

Makes a key pair from a secret key.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/secp256k1.hpp>

[[nodiscard]]
static
boost::system::result<basic_keypair>
make(
    std::span<uint8_t const> secret_bytes,
    std::pmr::memory_resource* memory_resource = std::pmr::get_default_resource());

Return Value

The key pair; invalid_key_size; invalid_secret_key; entropy_unavailable, also where there is no generator at all (an Emscripten audio worklet), whatever the generator’s own error; backend_failure, should libsecp256k1 refuse the context’s randomisation or the key pair after the secret’s check, which v0.8.0 does not (its secp256k1_context_randomize fails only on the static context, and secp256k1_keypair_create only on a secret secp256k1_ec_seckey_verify refuses). A failed allocation is the resource’s to report; the seed is wiped then too.

Note

The return value should not be discarded.

Parameters

Name Description

secret_bytes

32 bytes, not zero and below the group order.

memory_resource

The resource of the signing context, the one allocation; it must outlive the key pair.

webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519

Types

Name Description

algorithm

X25519 (RFC 7748) on a backend: the type supports_v names, whose functions the free functions below call.

kx_keypair

A crypto_kx key pair: its secret key, kept by the backend and wiped by every move and by the destructor, and its public key, which the peer receives.

session_keys

The session keys of one side: what it receives with and what it transmits with.

Functions

Name Description

agree

The shared secret, refused when all zero: algorithm<Backend>::agree.

decode_pkcs8

The secret key of a PKCS#8, refused unless it is exactly RFC 8410’s version 1 form: the 16 bytes of X25519’s prefix, then the secret key, and nothing after.

decode_spki

The public key of an SPKI, refused unless it is exactly RFC 8410’s form: the 12 bytes of X25519’s prefix, then the key, and nothing after.

encode_pkcs8

Writes a secret key’s PKCS#8 (RFC 8410, version 1: the secret key, without the public key) into out, which then holds the secret key: a program wipes it, or seals it, when it is done.

encode_spki

Writes a public key’s SPKI (RFC 8410) into out.

public_key

The public key of a secret key: algorithm<Backend>::public_key.

Variables

Name Description

max_pkcs8_size

The PKCS#8’s size, 48 bytes: version 1, with the secret key alone.

max_spki_size

The SPKI’s size, 44 bytes: the one size RFC 8410 gives an X25519 public key’s.

webcpp::crypto::curves::x25519::kx_keypair

A crypto_kx key pair: its secret key, kept by the backend and wiped by every move and by the destructor, and its public key, which the peer receives.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/curves/x25519/kx.hpp>

template<class Backend = default_backend_t<families::kx>>
class kx_keypair;

Description

A client computes its session keys with client_session_keys from the server’s public key, the server with server_session_keys from the client’s: each side’s transmit is the other’s receive.

The session keys are libsodium’s construction, BLAKE2b-512 of the X25519 shared secret and both public keys, client first: only another crypto_kx derives them.

webcpp::crypto::hybrid::basic_box

crypto_box: authenticated encryption between two key pairs.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/crypto/hybrid/box.hpp>

template<
    class Family = families::box_xsalsa20poly1305,
    class Backend = default_backend_t</* implementation-defined */>>
class basic_box;

Description

make agrees a key from the own secret key and the peer’s public key, once per pair of keys (libsodium’s beforenm); seal and open then work in place, the tag apart, under that key. Either party of the pair can have written a message: the box proves that it comes from one of them, not which.

An object holds the agreed key, the state that every message uses: it is used by one thread at a time, moved and not copied, and wiped when moved from and destroyed. A nonce (the IV) is never repeated for one pair of keys, in either direction: two messages under one pair and one nonce reveal the XOR of their plaintexts and let an attacker forge tags. Its 24 bytes are safe to draw at random for every message.
